Sustainable aviation fuel may cost 2-3 times more than conventional jet fuel: Centre’s draft policy
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is an alternative fuel made from non-petroleum feedstocks that reduces air pollution from air transportation, according to the US Department of Energy.
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) could cost at least two to three times as much as conventional jet fuel, according to a draft policy by the Centre, which proposes financial incentives to encourage its production as India prepares to introduce blending mandates for airlines.
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is an alternative fuel made from non-petroleum feedstocks that reduces air pollution from air transportation, according to the US Department of Energy.
The draft proposes a phased blending mandate for international aviation, requiring fuel suppliers to ensure a 1% SAF blend in 2027, 2% in 2028, 3% in 2029 and 5% in 2030. Targets beyond 2030, including 20% by 2040, are mentioned as ‘indicative’. The National Council on SAF will decide which of these become mandatory, taking into account factors such as supply-chain readiness, technology and market conditions.
The draft states that SAF can reduce lifecycle carbon dioxide emissions by up to 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.
The proposed mandate will initially apply to international flights covered under the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) CORSIA framework, with fuel suppliers required to blend SAF with ATF. As per the draft, only domestically manufactured SAF will qualify under the policy.
According to the draft, the government may consider extending financial incentives and support measures to promote SAF production. These could include support through existing or new schemes, green bonds and tax concessions, it said.
The proposed fiscal measures include exemption or reduction in goods and services tax (GST), import duty waivers, income-tax holidays and accelerated depreciation, subject to consideration by the relevant ministries and departments, the draft said.
India has an estimated 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue that could produce the fuel, alongside feedstocks such as used cooking oil and ethanol.
To support research and development in the sector, the policy also proposes an SAF Innovation Seed Fund of about ₹500 crore under the Centre for High Technology, which functions under the petroleum ministry.
The draft also seeks to build a domestic supply chain, stating that SAF used to meet the blending requirements must be manufactured in India. The fuel would be blended with conventional ATF at a production facility, refinery or intermediate storage point before being supplied to airports, it said.
It further proposes a digital National SAF Registry, to be maintained by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), to track SAF production, blending and transactions. Each transaction would be supported by a digitally secured certificate carrying details such as the fuel batch, feedstock origin, producer and emissions reduction, it stated.
- ABOUT THE AUTHORNeha LM Tripathi Neha LM Tripathi is a Special Correspondent with the National Political Bureau of Hindustan Times. She covers the aviation and railways ministries, and also writes on travel trends. Her work spans national developments, with a focus on policy, people, and the evolving travel landscape. She has 13 years of experience. Before moving to Delhi, she was based in Mumbai, where she began her journey as a journalist. Outside the newsroom, Neha enjoys trekking and travelling.Read More

WASHINGTON – Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterm elections may have significant implications for the upcoming negotiations over a key funding source for the Food and Drug Administration, in part by empowering a major critic of the program.
The FDA collects user fees from pharmaceutical companies to fund the agency’s reviews of their medicines. The Prescription User Fee Drug Act must be renewed before the current law expires on Sept. 30. Otherwise, it could disrupt the FDA’s ability to approve medicines.
The power to shape that legislation will fall to senior Democrats, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who will likely lead the Senate’s health committee. Sanders is one of the few lawmakers who have opposed the core premise of the user fee structure.

Ulster's Augustus enjoying South Africa homecoming
- Published
Ulster back row Juarno Augustus says he is "enjoying his rugby again" after recovering from the ankle surgery he underwent in the summer.
This weekend the 28-year-old is preparing to go back to where it all began in terms of his professional playing career as the Irish province face the Stormers in a United Rugby Championship encounter.
Augustus, who played for the Cape Town-based side between 2017 and 2021, is relishing the prospect of coming up against his former team while also spending some precious time with his family.
"It's nice just to be at home. I'll probably need a lot of tickets, everyone's been asking me!" said the former Northampton Saints forward.
"It's always nice to play against the team you grew up playing for. I'll just try to play my game to the best of my ability.
"I had surgery and I was struggling a bit in pre-season to put it behind me but it's all gone now and I've had a run of games. That's the main thing - to keep training and being fit again. "
- Four games, no wins - Ulster aim for URC turnaround 
  - Published5 days ago
Ulster remain without a victory in their URC campaign to date, their 34-26 defeat by the Bulls in Pretoria extending their winless run in the competition this season to four games.
"I don't think huge things need to change. It's just a bounce of the ball, just small things that we need to work on and get right," added Augustus.
Ulster and the Stormers played out a pulsating 38-38 draw in Belfast last term but the number eight is hoping Richie Murphy's side can go one better on Saturday (12:45 GMT) against a Stormers outfit who have won three and lost one of their four URC matches.
"It's at their home this time so we need to be sharper, need to be ready for what they're going to bring. From minute one to minute 80, we need to give it our best. That's what we are going after.
"They have a lot of dangerous players who can make anything happen in a second. We need to be aware of it.
"Richie and his coaching staff gave us some detail on how they play and it's up to us now to go out and execute.
"We just need to be on our game every single moment."

Three ways Democrats could reshape U.S. foreign policy after the midterms
Democrats will control Congress. Will it change Trump's approach to foreign policy?
One thing is clear from this week's midterm elections: The Trump administration's foreign policy decisions were no longer just about what happened abroad. The war in Iran has driven up gas prices, while Trump's tariffs have raised costs for American businesses.
According to the Voter Poll conducted by SSRS for several news outlets, including The Associated Press, 51% of voters said U.S. support for Israel had been too strong, while 63% said the war in Iran was the wrong decision. Nearly three-quarters (74%) considered the war a major or crucial factor in their vote. The economy weighed even more heavily, with 89% calling it a major or crucial factor.
And while Americans were making their views known at the ballot box, the rest of the world had plenty to say, too. Sometimes with a little more humor. The election results have inspired AI-generated videos, social media memes and newspaper headlines abroad.
What could the results actually change?
Anne Applebaum, a Pulitzer Prize-winning historian and staff writer at The Atlantic, has spent years studying authoritarianism and the erosion of democratic institutions. In a February interview with NPR, she warned about corruption in U.S. foreign policy, saying people around Trump and his family had accepted money from foreign governments and others.
Now, with Democrats set to control Congress, Applebaum sees reason for U.S. allies to regain some confidence in American democracy. But whether that translates into changes in foreign policy is another question.
On Morning Edition, Applebaum outlined three ways Congress could influence U.S. foreign policy, from the war in Iran to Ukraine, and where its power would stop. Read her takeaways below.
1. How Congress could influence the war in Iran
The U.S. and Israel have carried out military campaigns against Iran since June 2025. The war has cost American taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion as of mid-October, according to Pentagon figures obtained by The Associated Press. Iranian retaliatory strikes have also targeted U.S. military bases in the Gulf.
"I don't expect Trump to change," Applebaum said. "He's not that interested in what Americans think of his policies."
There is also a question of timing. Iran remains wary of renewed attacks, and some supporters of the war may see the next two months, before the new Congress takes office, as their last chance to escalate the conflict, Trita Parsi, an Iran expert at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, told NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi.
Once Democrats take control of both chambers, they could use one of Congress's most important powers: deciding how federal money is spent. Lawmakers can seek restrictions in spending bills that would limit the use of federal funds for certain military operations.
"You could see them trying to use the power of the purse, the appropriations committees, to end the war or to influence politics," Applebaum said.
She expects that pressure to "change the trajectory of the war sooner or later."
2. What congressional investigations could reveal
Congress can also investigate how the administration makes foreign policy decisions, even when it cannot directly reverse them.
Applebaum expects lawmakers to examine potential corruption involving people close to Trump and decisions made by his foreign policy team. She raised questions about Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's competence and the advice Trump received during the Iran war.
Such investigations could bring more information into public view, but they would not necessarily produce a change in policy.
"Congress can't force the president to make changes," Applebaum said, noting that Trump can veto legislation.
Congress could, however, offer "a different narrative, both about this war and more broadly about American foreign policy," she said.
For that to matter, Applebaum said, Democratic leaders would need to move quickly, decide what to investigate and establish their priorities.
3. What could change for Ukraine
Support for Ukraine has crossed party lines in Congress, even as the Trump administration's approach to Russia has raised questions among lawmakers.
Applebaum expects that bipartisan coalition to become more active under Democratic control, including through legislation that would require the president to reimpose sanctions on Russia.
"I would expect legislation forcing the president to reimpose sanctions," she said.
The question is whether enough lawmakers would support such legislation to override a presidential veto. Applebaum said she could not predict that outcome, though she considered it possible given the level of congressional support for Ukraine.
Congress has already sought answers about disruptions to Ukraine's satellite communications. In October, the Pentagon's inspector general declined a bipartisan request to investigate slowdowns to Starlink and Starshield services, which Ukrainian officials said had hampered their ability to intercept Russian drones. The Trump administration and SpaceX have offered conflicting accounts of who was responsible.
Applebaum expects lawmakers to examine those disruptions further, along with the administration's negotiations with Russia and Ukraine, including allegations of business dealings involving negotiators.
She expects those issues to become "more open, more part of the conversation, more part of criticism."

Breast cancer begins long before the lump: why diet and lifestyle matter
While genetic predisposition is one factor, a majority of breast cancers develop in women with no family history: metabolic health and physical inactivity play a role too, and it is important for women to know about these factors
Students seen taking part in a ‘Pink Umbrella’ walk to create awareness on breast cancer. Image used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: VELANKANNI RAJ B
Last month, celebrated as Breast Cancer Awareness Month, reminded us, as it does every year, about the importance of mammograms, early diagnosis, and advances in treatment. These messages save lives and deserve continued attention. However, there is another conversation that often receives far less attention: the role of food, physical activity, obesity, diabetes, physical activity, and metabolic health in breast cancer.
In my oncology clinic, patients are often surprised when I bring up these topics. They say, “Doctor, I knew breast cancer was related to family history. I didn’t know that lifestyle diseases such as diabetes and obesity had anything to do with it.”

A cancer medicine supplied to a retailer for ₹2,700 carries a maximum retail price (MRP) of ₹27,000. Who accounts for this tenfold difference? This was among the examples highlighted by the Supreme Court in September 2026, when it questioned the gap between the prices paid for medicines and what patients ultimately pay.
Subsequently, on October 17, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) announced a 30% cap on trade margins for 137 anti-cancer drugs, effective from November 9. This intervention could reduce prices substantially for some products. It also raises a broader question: how does India decide what medicines should cost?

The National Police Agency said Thursday it will start an initiative to share data on bank accounts used in scams with financial institutions nationwide amid continued heavy losses from special fraud.
Under the initiative, to be launched Monday, the NPA will ask financial institutions to promptly report customers who have transferred money to such accounts, aiming to identify potential fraud victims at an early stage and enable police officers to intervene to prevent further losses.
According to the NPA, losses from special fraud nationwide totaled ¥261 billion from January to September, up ¥48.3 billion from a year earlier, and were on track to exceed last year’s record high. Social media-based investment scams and fraud schemes involving people impersonating police officers have been particularly prevalent.
Against this backdrop, the NPA will compile a list of bank accounts identified by prefectural police departments across the country as having received funds from fraud victims and share this information via a file-sharing system with 807 financial institutions nationwide that have signed agreements with the agency.
If a financial institution’s transfer records show that a customer has sent money to one of these accounts, the institution will report the customer’s name, address and other relevant information to the NPA.
Since the sender may be an unidentified victim, a police officer with jurisdiction over the area will promptly meet with the person to issue a warning and confirm whether the individual has been defrauded.
Previously, each prefectural police force had individually entered into similar agreements with regional banks and credit unions. With the NPA acting as an intermediary and megabanks and online banks also joining the framework, a system will be established to allow inquiries to be made to financial institutions nationwide simultaneously, the agency said.
The NPA is stepping up efforts to combat fraud in cooperation with financial institutions, aiming to prevent the unauthorized use of bank accounts and stop funds obtained through fraud from being transferred elsewhere.
The NPA has concluded agreements with 20 financial institutions, including megabanks, under which the institutions provide the agency with information on suspicious transactions detected through their monitoring systems. It has also begun checking bank accounts online to speed up the tracing and freezing of stolen funds.

Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children's and teenagers' use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.
The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans' exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.
Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.
However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on November 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared.
According to the civil society coalition Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organised crime.
“I don't think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”
The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.
Benigno Gomez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities' need to reduce students' time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren't allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.
During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico's Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”
Parents seek reassurance
Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of October 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town -- which relies on mango and shrimp production -- was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.
More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.
“Just hearing my daughter's voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community -- admitting that she didn't hesitate to interrupt her daughter's class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”
In defence of the regulation
For Israel Sanchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government's decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organisation, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sanchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.
Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialisation and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximise our attention.”
The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.

I was 30 days into a hospital stay when I learned the difference between a friend and someone who used to be one. I didn't know it yet, but that lesson was about to cost me most of my friend group and give me something better in return.
In 2018, I had a widow-maker heart attack. Then two bilateral lower limb amputations. I was flat on my back, trying to figure out what was left of my body and what was left of my life. That's when the visitors started sorting themselves into neat piles.
Friends were there when I needed them
Tijuana was the one my husband called the day I was rushed to the ER. We met on my first day of new-teacher orientation, and she became my department chair soon after. Somewhere along the way, she also became auntie to my daughter, and I became auntie to her five. She also became my best friend. Tijuana was the only person I let come around consistently, and she did, every time. She helped me. She cried with me. She loved on me in the specific, unglamorous way that has nothing to do with flowers and everything to do with showing up to a room that smelled like antiseptic and fear and staying anyway.
Kimberly is my line sister. We were initiated into the same sorority, which means she's been mine and I've been hers since the moment we decided, as grown women with full lives already built, that we still had room for a sisterhood we both wanted. She showed up unannounced one day and ran straight into my mother in the hospital lobby. She came bearing gifts, one set for me and one for my parents, because I guess she knew they were scared too and needed something in their hands besides worry. Once home, relearning what my body could and couldn't do, she showed up again. She's been around ever since.
Others didn't show up at all
I used to think friendship was proven in the good years, the weddings, the birthdays, the Saturday brunches. Turns out it gets proven in a hospital room when you have nothing to offer anybody, and the only thing left to see is who still shows up. Some people bring gifts because they actually care. Some people show up because that's what's expected. Or they're just nosy. Either way, you can usually tell which by whether there's a second visit. For some people, there isn't one.
I didn't see any of this as an upgrade while it was happening. It felt like a loss. It wasn't.
Within a year, my friend group went from dozens of people I called "friends" to 12. Nobody got a dramatic goodbye text. They just stopped calling. I stopped being easy to invite to places. My disability made them uncomfortable. A lot of people didn't know how to deal with that, so they didn't.
I'm not angry about my group shrinking
I'm not angry about it anymore. That took a while. For the first year or two, I kept a mental list of who hadn't called, replaying visits that never happened, holding onto invitations that quietly stopped coming. It's an ugly thing to sit with, watching your world shrink in real time and knowing exactly whose choice that was.
But after almost a decade, here's the truth: I wouldn't trade the 12 women I do have for the several I used to.
"The Twelve" know what my new normal actually looks like because they loved me through the year it became normal. They saw me on the days I couldn't get out of bed and the days I could barely stand to be looked at. They never performed concern. They just showed up. They still do.
A hundred people who show up for the good years will tell you they love you. Twelve people who show up for a hospital room, a home health aide schedule, and a body that doesn't look or work the way it used to will show you. Turns out I didn't need the crowd. I needed the women who would love me for real. And they did. And they do. That's not a loss I'm grieving. That's the best trade I never chose to make.

Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
- Published
The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.
Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.
He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.
El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.
El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.
The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.
Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.
One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."
Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.
Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.
A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.
However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.
While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.
Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.
Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances.
The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.
It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones.
In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.
Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.
But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.
These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody.
A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.
As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.
Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%.
"Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products.
"Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.
El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.
For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women.
"Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.
Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.
In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.
Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests.
"Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC.
"The latter cannot be understood without the former."
Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.
Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".
She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.
For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important.
"It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."
El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.
For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.
However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system.
The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.
When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.
While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts.
"I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
"Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."

All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.
Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.
But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.
“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”
André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.
“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.
Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.
These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.
The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.
“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.
The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.
About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the tropical forests forever facility, a fund aiming to preserve forests, to which the UK contributed £400m and other countries combined contributed about $7bn.
The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.
In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.
Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu, where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

Raymond van Barneveld secures World Darts Championship spot as Tommy Morris stuns Luke Humphries in Players Championship 34
Raymond van Barneveld ensured he will be at Alexandra Palace next month as the final Players Championship event took place in Leicester; Tommy Morris stunned Luke Humphries in the final to also book a World Championship spot while Ricky Evans will need to come through qualifying
Thursday 5 November 2026 20:17, UK
Five-time world champion Raymond van Barneveld has secured a spot at this year's World Darts Championship, while non-tour card holder Tommy Morris stunned Luke Humphries to win the final Players Championship event.
England's Morris defeated Humphries 8-5 in the final of Players Championship 34 by winning the last three legs, sealing victory with a 161 checkout.
It means he has qualified for the Grand Slam of Darts, which takes place from November 14-22, and next month's World Darts Championship, both live on Sky Sports.

"You have no idea, I'm so happy!" said Morris, who was overcome with emotion.
"I've come from nothing. I haven't even got a tour card. For me to come here and do that, I'm just flying my flag from where I live and doing it for my family. I don't even know what's going on.
"I had a target at the start of the year to reach the Worlds and now my next target is to get a tour card and be with these boys full time. I've won nothing. For me to win one of these PDC events is very overwhelming for me."
Earlier on, darts legend Van Barneveld ensured he will be at Alexandra Palace by securing his place in the top 40 on the ProTour Order of Merit.
Van Barneveld beat Dutch compatriot Jimmy van Schie in his opening match, which was enough to reach the World Championship for a record 34th time in his career.
However, crowd favourite Ricky Evans will need to come through a tour-card-holder qualifier to be at Alexandra Palace after an early exit on Thursday.
Evans needed a strong run but lost 6-0 in the second round to Morris, while Dutch players Wesley Plaisier and Jeffrey de Zwaan will also need to come through qualifying matches.

Who has qualified for the Players Championship Finals?
The main purpose of the 34 indoor Players Championship events that have been held over the last nine months is to set a 64-player field for the Players Championship Finals, which take place in Minehead at the end of this month.
The top 64 from this season's Players Championship Order of Merit qualify, and some big names have missed out.
Luke Littler did not enter enough events to qualify, a decision he took after his quarter-final exit at the World Series Finals in September, so he will not defend his title.
Nathan Aspinall has missed out, while Josh Rock's second-round defeat on Thursday means he has also not qualified.
Although Van Barneveld secured a spot at the World Championship, he will not feature at the Players Championship Finals, and neither will former world champion Peter Wright.
Gary Anderson squeaked through after his quarter-final run in Players Championship 33, which was backed up with a first-round win on Thursday, while former world champions Gerwyn Price and Michael Smith also just did enough.
World No 2 Humphries will be the favourite for the tournament, while Dutch star Wessel Nijman is the top seed after his six Players Championship event wins this year.
Fan favourites Michael van Gerwen, James Wade and Stephen Bunting are in the field, as is Welsh No 2 Jonny Clayton.
When are the Players Championship Finals?
The Players Championship Finals will take place at Butlins in Minehead from November 27-29.
The winner of the event takes home £130,000, with a total prize pot of £750,000 on the line for the 64 players.
The World Youth Championship final between Cam Crabtree and Jan Schmidt will be played on the same weekend on November 29.
