Quick Answer
Apple’s new iPad mini features IP67 water resistance, an Acoustic Display with no grilles, a lighter body, and an 8.5-inch 60Hz OLED display with nano-texture options. Powered by the A20 Pro chip, it adds a landscape front camera, fast charging, and Pencil support. However, it lacks ProMotion, starts at $699/Rs 82,990, and comes in only two colors.
Apple has taken the wraps off a new iPad. This one is an iPad mini, and it comes with perhaps the most radical overhaul of Apple’s smaller tablet. The new iPad mini – which is being referred to as the iPad mini (A20 Pro) – comes with a truckload of new features, some of which have never been seen on any other iPad (including the Pros). Of course, it is also more expensive than ever before (such are the expensive memory times we live in), but is it worth sinking bucks in? Here are twelve things we think you should know about Apple’s new smaller iPad:
Table of Contents
First iPad with IP67 rating
Dust and water resistance have finally – FINALLY – come to the iPad. The new iPad mini comes with IP67 dust and water resistance, making this the first Apple tablet that can survive a spell in the rain or even a fall in the water. The iPad just got pool and beach friendly!
First iPad with an “Acoustic Display”: Look ma, no speaker grilles!
The new iPad mini is also the first to come with no speaker grilles at all. Apple says that its latest tablet has an Acoustic Display, which has specially designed woofers that are “paired through the display” for better bass and volume. There are also tweeters between the glass and aluminum enclosure for better highs. That’s some very impressive audio tech right there. What’s more, it comes with a sealed enclosure that enables the iPad mini to be dust- and water-resistant. Not many openings on this one!
The biggest display on an iPad mini – and the first OLED display on a non-Pro iPad
The new iPad mini comes with an 8.5-inch display, which is the largest seen on an iPad mini. The earlier generations of the tablet had 7.9-inch displays, while more recent ones had larger, 8.3-inch displays. It also comes with a higher resolution, 2316 x 1512, as compared to 2266 x 1488 of the previous iPad mini, although both have the same pixel density (326 ppi). The new iPad mini is also the first non-Pro iPad to sport an OLED display. In the past, the iPad Pros had what Apple calls a Tandem OLED display. That said, the display on the iPad mini is different from those on the Pros – the iPad Pros have an Ultra Retina XDR display, while the new iPad mini has what Apple has termed a Super Retina XDR display.
First iPad mini with TWO display options (and a “polishing cloth” in the box too!)
The new iPad mini actually gives consumers two display options. While the base 128 GB storage option has a “regular” display, the 256 GB and 512 GB variants also come with a “nano texture display glass” option, similar to those seen on the iPad Pro models. What’s more, those who go with this option will also get a “polishing cloth”. Such perks.
Not ProMoted to ProMotion: Bigger, brighter display…but STILL with a 60 Hz refresh rate
The iPad mini comes with a larger and brighter (600 nits) display than on the previous iPad mini (500 nits) and even the iPad Air M4 (500 nits), but, surprisingly, comes with the same 60 Hz refresh rate display that is seen in most non-Pro iPads. The new iPad mini does not come with a ProMotion display, which enables higher and lower refresh rates. No ProMotion for the new tablet in this regard. Pun intended.
Bigger display, but still smaller and lighter than the previous iPad mini (only slightly heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max)
Rather remarkably, even though the new iPad mini comes with a larger display than the previous iPad mini, it is actually more compact and even lighter as compared to its predecessor. It is slightly shorter (195.3 mm vs 195.4 mm), less wide (132.6 mm vs 134.8 mm) and slimmer (5.4 mm vs 6.3 mm) as compared to the previous iPad mini. Making this possible are incredibly thin bezels – 24 percent thinner than on its predecessor. At 255 grams, the new iPad mini is also the lightest iPad ever (the previous mini was 293 grams) and is only a feather heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max (249 grams) and even the iPhone Duo (255 grams). This is the easiest iPad to carry, by a mile, for miles (pun intended).
Driven by the latest iPhone chip, with differences across storage models
The iPad mini runs on the same processor that we have seen on the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the iPhone Duo – the A20 Pro. Interestingly, however, there are subtle differences between the processors on different storage variants. The 128 GB and 256 GB storage variants come with a chip with a 5-core CPU and 3 efficiency cores, while the 512 GB variant has a 6-core CPU and 4 efficiency cores. The processor on the 128 GB and 256 GB variants also has a 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512 GB one has a dual 16-core Neural Engine. We are not too sure what difference those make in everyday performance, but if you are a spec and high-performance chaser, then the 512 GB iPad mini might be the one for you.
A better front camera, and now on the landscape side
The new iPad mini has a similar rear camera to that of the previous one – a 12-megapixel camera with f/1.8 aperture – but the front-facing camera, or “selfie and video call” camera, is very different. While it has the same megapixel count (12) as its predecessor, it has a larger aperture (f/2.0 as compared to f/2.4) and, most interestingly of all, is now on the landscape edge rather than the portrait one. Apple has almost always shown the iPad mini being used in portrait mode (apart from when gaming), so this is a significant change.
Compatible with both Apple Pencils
The new iPad mini plays fine with both Apple Pencils, the Apple Pencil (USB-C) and the Apple Pencil Pro, making this pretty much a proper sketching, scribbling tab.
No smart connector, so don’t expect Apple keyboard covers
The new iPad mini has no smart connectors (those tiny metallic dots) on its side or back, so in spite of the bigger display and powerful specs, we do not expect to see keyboard covers from Apple for this one.
Fast charging comes to a non-Pro iPad (but the bundled adapter is a slow one)
While its battery life remains at the classic “up to 10 hours of surfing the web on Wi-Fi or watching video”– that is an iPad standard, the new iPad mini comes with support for fast charging. This enables it to get charged up to 50 percent in about half an hour with a 35W or higher adapter. Mind you, you will need to shell out extra bucks for that adapter, as the one that comes in the box is a 20W USB-C Power Adapter.
Also Read: Apple iPad mini (A20 Pro) vs Apple iPad mini (A17 Pro)
Kinda pricey: Priced close to the iPad Air 11 (M4)
The new iPad mini is the most expensive iPad mini ever released by Apple. The iPad mini (A17 Pro) started at USD 499 (Rs 49,900 in India), but the new iPad mini starts at a much higher USD 699 (Rs 82,900 in India). That places it incredibly close to the iPad Air (M4), which comes with a bigger display, a desktop-level processor, and an official price tag of USD 749 ( Rs 89,900 in India), but which is often available at lower prices.
And one more thing…ONLY TWO COLORS
The iPad Mini has generally had a wide range of color options. The 2021 iPad mini and the iPad mini (A17 Pro) had four color options each – space grey, blue and starlight, as well as blue for the A17 Pro and pink for the 2021 edition. The new iPad mini has, however, trimmed the product color palette – it is available in just two shades: midnight and starlight. Hopefully more colors will come along soon!

The country of 630,000 on track to become the EU’s 28th member state
The EU says Montenegro is the candidate country that is closest to membership

The European Union could conclude accession negotiations with Montenegro by the end of this year, the European Commission said on Wednesday.
“For the first time since 2011, when the EU closed accession negotiations with Croatia, the EU is in a position to soon close accession negotiations with another candidate country, Montenegro,” the EU’s executive said in its annual enlargement policy report.
“This is testament to Montenegro’s sustained efforts to advance on the European path and implement the reforms needed to turn EU membership into reality,” it said.
It added that “it considers that accession negotiations could realistically be closed by the end of 2026” and an accession treaty could be signed by June 2027.
Montenegro, with a population of just 630,000, aims to become the 28th member of the EU in 2028.
Joining the bloc requires all current 27 member countries to ratify an accession treaty.
“In the weeks and months ahead, it will be essential that Montenegro maintains a steady focus on completing the preparations for EU membership, sustaining the adopted reforms and ensuring continuous cross-party support to its EU path,” the Commission said.
Earlier this year, President Jakov Milatovic expressed confidence that Montenegro was on track to fulfil its ambitious goal by 2028.
"We can achieve it. I am optimistic about it,” he said from his presidential office in the capital, Podgorica.
The EU sees Montenegro as the candidate country that is closest to membership, with Albania, Ukraine and Moldova also considered frontrunners.
The Western Balkan nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and Kosovo are also at different stages of the process.
In its assessment of Albania's progress, the Commission said: "cross-party cooperation and inclusive and constructive dialogue in the Parliament and with civil society are needed to move ahead on EU key reforms, in particular in the context of the ongoing largest protests since the country’s democratic transition".
"Albania needs to continue adopting key reforms to fulfil closing benchmarks across all chapters of negotiations.
“This is important for Albania to meet its ambitious but achievable target of closing negotiations by the end of 2027," it added.

With a huge and still-growing catalog of exoplanets, researchers are eager to take the next steps: trying to infer what conditions are like on them, either by imaging them directly or by capturing the light that has passed through their atmosphere. Both are substantial challenges, given the presence of stars that are far, far brighter than light that has come to us via the planet.
While telescopes can be fitted with devices called coronagraphs that block out much of a star’s light, there are limits to their effectiveness, caused by noise from subtle variations in the telescope’s configuration and pointing between observations. Now, researchers have developed a new software package that optimizes a physical model of the telescope in a way that allows us to better model these differences, producing low-noise imaging of exoplanets.
Point spreads
Central to this work is the concept of a point spread function. If you use a telescope to image a single point of light, it will not appear that way in the actual image. Instead, it will be slightly blurry and spread out, due to imperfections in the telescope hardware and the limits of our ability to keep it pointed accurately through the time it takes to image something. The mathematical description of how a telescope distorts a point of light is called its point spread function.
There are two ways to figure out what the point spread function is. One is to use the telescope to image a known target and use those observations to derive a mathematical description of the point spread function. This is effective at reducing noise but has its limits, as the behavior of the telescope hardware can change over time, and the point spread function may vary with the wavelengths being imaged.
The alternative is to try to model the hardware’s behavior and use that model to derive a point spread function. But modern telescopes are incredibly complicated instruments, with many, many factors feeding into their performance in ways that can be difficult to ascertain, even with the full engineering schematics. As a result, these models simply contain too many parameters that need to be tuned to make this route computationally tractable.

Keeper Owono 'would never intentionally hurt anyone'
- Published
Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono "would never intentionally hurt anyone" and has been "deeply affected" by the death of Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel, his team-mate said on Wednesday.
Tenerife player De Miguel, 30, died after suffering a serious injury in a collision with Owono during a Spanish second-division match on Monday.
The world of football has paid tribute to De Miguel, a father-of-one who joined Tenerife in summer 2025, with a minute's silence being held at all European games this week.
Writing on social media, Andorra centre-back Lautaro Spatz said Owono was devastated.
He paid tribute to De Miguel but added: "I also want to say a few words about my team-mate, goalkeeper and friend, who is deeply affected by what has happened.
"Those of us who know him know the kind of person he is, how much he is suffering at this moment and that he would never intentionally hurt anyone.
"In football, unfortunate incidents can happen but no-one could imagine that one of them might end with such tragic consequences."
- Football world mourns Tenerife striker De Miguel 
  - Published14 hours ago
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Police in Spain opened a routine investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
Owono has made 47 international appearances for Equatorial Guinea.
The Equatoguinean Football Federation said in a statement on Tuesday the 25-year-old was going through a "situation of profound sorrow and grief".
Period of mourning
On Tuesday, mourners laid flowers and lit candles beneath a black and white image of De Miguel at the Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez.
Tenerife said in a statement they will commence six official days of mourning, with all club activities suspended during this time.
The club's players, staff and officials will attend De Miguel's funeral, which will take place in Navahermosa, Toledo.
Tenerife will also open their home ground on Saturday evening to allow supporters to "bid a fitting farewell".
"Jesus de Miguel's family would like to thank everyone for their messages of support and, from the bottom of their hearts, ask that their privacy be respected at this terrible time. May he rest in peace," added the statement.

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Virendra Tiwari, former officer on special duty (OSD) to transport and school education minister Uday Pratap Singh, reportedly continues to work with the minister despite being relieved of his duties and sent back to his parent department, the Urban Administration and Development Department, around two months ago.
Amid controversies surrounding him, Tiwari has reportedly continued to be seen at the minister's office and the Mantralaya, raising questions about his association with Singh. According to the information, Tiwari was sent back to his parent department following his promotion.
This is the second instance in the past month of an OSD attached to a minister being removed following allegations. Recently, Deputy Chief Minister Jagdish Devda relieved his OSD, Deepam Raichura, of his responsibilities after allegations surfaced regarding his connection with liquor shop contracts in Bhopal.
Ministerial OSDs have faced controversies in the past as well. During the previous Congress government, two OSDs, Arun Nigam and Harish Kumar Khare, were also removed from their assignments after their names surfaced in the chargesheet in the alleged honey-trap case.
Nigam was attached to the office of the then mining minister Pradeep Jaiswal, while Khare was OSD to the then food and civil supplies minister Pradyuman Singh Tomar.
Tiwari appointed OSD in 2024
According to an order issued by the MP State Open School Board (MPSOS) on Mar 15, 2024, Tiwari, then a chief municipal officer from the Urban Administration and Development Department, was initially sent to MPSOS on deputation against the post of section officer.
On the same day, he was attached to the office of the school education minister as OSD until further orders.
Meanwhile, Tiwari has denied all the allegations; he told Free Press that he was not working with the minister since his service ended.

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) has warned banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) and fintech startups against the growing trend of cyberattackers using AI agents for financial frauds. In an advisory issued on November 3, the National Cybercrime Threat Analysis Unit (NCTAU), under the I4C, flagged that attackers were exploiting unpatched software and misconfigured internet-facing servers to gain access to financial infrastructure. The cybersecurity agency also said that it has unearthed multiple “individual” cases, where malicious agentic AI systems were exploiting compromised financial systems to undertake unauthorised transactions running into crores of Rupees. Describing the modus operandi of these AI-led cyberattacks, the agency noted that perpetrators exploit unpatched software to compromise banking systems. Customer-facing complaint interfaces can also serve as potential entry points, added I4C. Once inside, NCTAU noted that attackers potentially target automated fund disbursement systems and APIs used for payments and transfers. The agency added that these cyberattackers then route funds through mule accounts across different banks and quickly move to withdraw the proceeds of the crime via IMPS and NEFT. The perpetrators then delete records and hide their tracks so that investigation becomes difficult, added the NCTAU. As such, the agency has advised financial institutions to take the following measures: Implement CERT-In’s critical advisories “urgently” on payment and disbursement APIs as well as AI agents Report cyber incidents to CERT-In within six hours, and to RBI as well in the cases of banks or NBFCs Test payment APIs and strengthen customer-facing infrastructure Set transaction limits, verify beneficiary details and monitor sudden changes in transaction speeds, volumes and patterns Ensure KYC and approval checks are completed before funds are transferred Improve coordination between security, transaction monitoring and IT teams Conduct authorised red-team exercises to test how quickly security and payment controls respond to machine-speed attacks The warning highlights how AI is accelerating the threat of cyber fraud for financial services firms. At the Global Fintech Fest (GFF) 2026 in September, both Prime Minister Narendra Modi and RBI Governor Sanjay Malhotra had urged fintechs to bolster cybersecurity and strengthen consumer trust. At the same event, National Payments Council of India (NPCI) MD and CEO Dilip Asbe had also called on banks and payments companies to invest in AI to combat cyber threats. In line with this, CERT-In had also issued a critical advisory last month, raising concerns over cyberattackers using publicly-available agentic AI tools for financially motivated intrusions into Indian entities. The advisory follows disclosures by global AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic about their agents taking unauthorised actions during internal cybersecurity evaluations.

The Delhi High Court has given the National Medical Commission (NMC) and the Delhi government’s Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) two weeks to submit a joint inquiry report on the medical qualifications of two doctors accused of mishandling a child during treatment.
Justice Neena Bansal Krishna passed the order on October 30 while hearing a contempt petition filed by the child’s mother, Sapna Jain, on behalf of her minor son.
According to the petition, the child suffered severe brain damage “after being mishandled by two unqualified doctors (misrepresenting as super-specialists) in the Neonatal ICU of Fortis Hospital, Shalimar Bagh”.
The petition claims that the child is now in a permanent vegetative state and suffers from West Syndrome, epilepsy and cerebral palsy. It also states that he continues to experience severe pain and suffering.
In March 2025, the High Court had called for affidavits clarifying whether the qualifications claimed by the two doctors “are qualifications entitling these Respondents (doctors) to undertake specialisation practice in this country.”
In May 2026, the court further directed the NMC Secretary and the DGHS to conduct a joint inquiry into the doctors’ qualifications and submit a report within eight weeks.
However, the fresh contempt petition alleged that the deadline of July 24, 2026, passed without the authorities submitting the report or seeking an extension from the court.
“The matter concerns the qualifications of doctors treating critically ill newborns. The NMC, being the statutory regulator, is duty-bound to ensure transparency and accountability, and its continued failure to place a clear and conclusive report before this Court raises serious questions regarding its fairness and credibility and that of its officers. The DGHS has likewise failed to discharge the joint duty cast upon it by this Court,” the plea said.
The court has posted the case for hearing on December 16.

It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave
The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.
Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.
In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.
Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.
"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.
"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.
Blue wins, red losses
In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)
In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.
A big recruiting effort
Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action, a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.
The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton, says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.
"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.
Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.
Naughton attributes that success to health care and affordability being front of mind. Also, polls show the public trusts doctors, and the candidates effectively countered messaging from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has downplayed ongoing measles outbreaks.
"People were sick of it," Naughton says. "We should not have American children dying — or anyone dying — of measles in 2026. And yet, not only did we have that happening, we had a health secretary that only made the situation worse."
A key vote, a damaging investigation
Outgoing chair of the powerful Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committee, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., spoke often from the dais about how his experience as a physician shaped his perspective as a lawmaker and committee chair.
During Kennedy's confirmation hearing in Jan. 2025, Cassidy memorably spoke about the root of his passion for vaccination. "In the early 2000's, I was loading a patient onto an air ambulance, an 18-year-old young woman, to go to get a liver transplant from acute liver failure due to hepatitis B," he said, noting the expensive surgery and ongoing hospital bills she would face, if she lived. "It was the worst day of my medical career, because I thought: $50 of vaccines could have prevented this all."
Still, Cassidy ultimately cast a key vote to confirm Kennedy into the job, despite Kennedy's long history of anti-vaccine activism. Kennedy flaunted vaccine-related promises Cassidy said he made to earn that vote, and even supported the Republican primary challenger who managed to unseat Cassidy earlier this year.
In a surprise Tuesday night, Dr. Roger Marshall, R.-Kan., also lost his reelection bid — another senior member of the HELP committee. Marshall is an OBGYN and staunch supporter of Kennedy. In September, the New York Times reported that Marshall had sued more than 700 patients for unpaid medical bills. One of the patients filed a class action lawsuit against him last week. Marshall described his actions as a way to "keep the lights on" in a last-minute social media video. He lost to challenger Adam Hamilton, a Methodist minister, by four points.
All the way back to 1776
Dr. Chadd Kraus has studied physicians in Congress. Kraus is now an emergency room doctor and the vice chair for research for the Department of Emergency and Hospital Medicine at Jefferson Health Lehigh Valley in Pennsylvania. Two decades ago, after studying political science as an undergrad and pursuing a masters in public health, he worked on an analysis of the physicians in Congress.
"In 1776, 10.7% of the signers of the Declaration of Independence were physicians," the paper notes. Kraus explains that was an era where practicing medicine involved leeches; germs hadn't been discovered and antibiotics hadn't been invented. Kraus suggests those physicians happened to be "part of a class that owned land that was educated."
In the next two hundred years, medicine transformed, and for a time, very few physicians served as federal lawmakers. "In the period of time that we studied [from 1960-2004], there were 25 physicians total who had served in the U.S. Congress, whether the House or the Senate," he explains. "In the current Congress, there are as many physicians — nearly — as there were in that whole period of time that we studied, which was several decades."
The new count
To be specific, there are 20 physicians in the current Congress, and Republicans outnumber Democrats two to one. There are six Democrats and 10 Republicans who serve in the House. All four doctors in the Senate are Republicans.
In the new Congress, there will be at least 18 physicians in Congress, 10 of them Democrats. Depending on the outcome of several House races, Democratic physician-lawmakers may outnumber Republican physician-lawmakers. Another notable win was in Ohio, where oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker flipped a Republican House seat. Nurse Lauren Underwood, a Democrat, held onto her House seat in Illinois.
In addition to Republicans Cassidy and Marshall losing their Senate seats, in the house, Rep. Neal Dunn of Florida, a urologist, retired, and Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, an ophthalmologist in Iowa, and Jen Kiggans, a nurse in Virginia lost their seats.
Kraus says, when it comes to making laws, "physicians have a valuable perspective, not a monopoly on good policy," he says. "And the need for physician voices in government has grown, I think, over the course of time, as healthcare has become more complex and politically consequential."
He says the emergency department, especially, is a place where you can see the effect of health policy in real time. He recalls at the beginning of the opioid crisis, how emergency physicians were among the first to sound the alarm to policymakers. When the uninsured rates increase, they see patients coming in sicker than they would otherwise be, he says. "We see the challenges of health policy and the consequences of it," he says
A health policy shake up?
Many of the new members of Congress campaigned on health policy issues, like the cost of health insurance and prescription drugs. There's widespread dissatisfaction with the cost of health care across the political spectrum. Democratic leaders have said that reversing Republican cuts to premium subsidies for health insurance and work requirements for Medicaid will be at the top of their agenda.
Beyond those immediate issues, more than 15 years after the passage of the Affordable Care Act, there may be political appetite and public demand for major new health legislation in the coming years. Some candidates ran on Medicare-for-all, a national health insurance plan, which has become increasingly popular in public opinion surveys.
"I think we all certainly agree, no matter one's political views or perspective, that there is the potential for a better system," Kraus says. "I do think that having physicians and other health care professionals meaningfully incorporated into the policymaking process is really critical to finding what those innovations might be."
Naughton of 314 Action says the health-professional candidates her group supported care about and have ideas about how to change the health care system, but that hasn't been their only pitch to voters.
"I do think that they really lead with what they essentially are, which is problem solvers," she says. "We can fix this problem — we can make health care accessible and affordable — and not make it a choice between life or debt."
Lexie Schapitl contributed reporting to this story.

Earlier this year, Patrick Woodard had to have a talk with one of the hundreds of clinicians that work at Monument Health, where he is chief information officer. The South Dakota and Wyoming-based health system had decided to block access to OpenEvidence, the popular free artificial intelligence tool, and Woodard had gotten a few objections.
One of them, Woodard recounted, was from a super user. This doctor was storing more than a hundred patient records inside OpenEvidence, and feeding them to the artificial intelligence tool for help making medical decisions. That would have to end, Woodard told him.
In the last year, free chatbots built to answer clinician questions — including OpenEvidence, Doximity Ask, and ChatGPT for Clinicians — have grown in popularity. Hundreds of thousands of doctors use the tools, in part, because they claim to be compliant with the federal health data privacy law HIPAA, allowing users to share a patient’s protected health information directly with the AI after signing an agreement. That assurance is meant to address one potential risk of the technology, while making it more valuable day-to-day.

Hong Kong pro-democracy activist faces sentencing in 2nd national security case
Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong is expected to be sentenced Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law
HONG KONG -- Prominent Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong is expected to be sentenced Thursday for his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say reflects the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.
Wong was charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security under the law. In September, he pleaded guilty, facing a prison term ranging from three years to life imprisonment. Pleading guilty typically reduces the sentence.
The 30-year-old is already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term for the city's biggest national security case linked to an unofficial primary after entering a guilty plea in that case. Before being prosecuted for the collusion-related charge, Wong had been expected to be freed in January 2027.
Judge William Tam is scheduled to hand down the penalty Thursday morning. Some members of the public started queuing outside the court building as early as Tuesday to secure a seat in the public gallery.
Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society marked by its vibrant protest and media scenes. But after an anti-government movement rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for their reports critical of the government shut down, and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.
Observers say Wong's sentencing shows the authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible, further chilling civic activism.
“NSL charges can be repeatedly weaponized to keep a specific political prisoner in jail, if the government deems necessary," said Eric Lai, a research fellow at Georgetown Center for Asian Law, referring to the national security law.
But Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities also said the security law is crucial for the city’s stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.
The prosecution previously alleged that Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination. It said that before the security law was introduced, the pair had been calling for sanctions and other adverse measures against Hong Kong and China. It pointed to his meetings with U.S. politicians like Nancy Pelosi and Marco Rubio in 2016 and 2019.
After the law was enacted, Law and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw foreign countries’ attention and bolster the request for sanctions, blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.
His lawyer Derek Chan earlier urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.
His friends said during his nearly six years in prison, Wong kept reading books and exercising, teaching himself guitar while maturing in his thinking.
To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.
Despite being held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern, at least for the pro-Beijing camp.
In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for “beautifying” his crimes. The city’s security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.
But the documentary then shot to the top of Netflix’s popular chart in Hong Kong.

A 47-year-old woman in California has admitted to defrauding her employer of almost $18 million ( approximately ₹170 crore) over a period of 10 years, using the stolen money to finance an extravagant lifestyle involving luxury shopping, private jet journeys, and expensive home renovations. Lizbeth Sherman, a resident of El Dorado Hills, pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud charges on Monday, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of California. The woman spent the money on designer handbags, Rolex watches, luxury holidays and other high-value purchases. Sherman's alleged fraud began in 2015 when she took up a position as an executive assistant to a retired venture capitalist from the San Francisco Bay Area. As part of her responsibilities, she was given access to her employer's bank account to manage credit card payments. However, she gradually misused this access to divert large sums of money towards her personal expenses. Between September 2015 and May 2025, she repeatedly transferred funds to cover her own credit card bills, prosecutors said. “Between September 2015 and May 2025, Sherman abused this access and stole nearly $18 million from her employer in order to pay off her own extravagant credit card expenses,” federal prosecutors said. The stolen money enabled Sherman to make expensive purchases and maintain a lavish lifestyle for years. Her spending reportedly included designer handbags from Louis Vuitton, luxury watches, expensive holidays and private jet journeys. She also spent a substantial amount on vehicles and renovations to her $2 million home in El Dorado Hills. “In this manner, Sherman spent tens of thousands of dollars on luxury handbags, Rolex watches, resort-level vacations, private jet travel, vehicles, and improvements to a $2 million residence in El Dorado Hills.” Over time, Sherman also began selling some of the luxury products she had purchased using her employer's money through online marketplaces. This allowed her to convert the expensive purchases into cash. “Sherman began reselling designer products that she bought with the employer’s money on online platforms, thus converting her credit card purchases into cash,” the release explained. 'I cannot teach you integrity': How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
- Published
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.
"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.
Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.
"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.
"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.
The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.
"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.
She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.
"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"
Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.
"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."
"What else would we do?"
Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.
In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.
The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.
"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.
The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.
A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.
The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.
At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.
Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.
Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.
Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."
Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.
For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.
"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.
The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.
Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.
"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.
Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.
The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.
His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.
Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.
"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.
While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.
"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.
The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.
When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.
"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.
His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.
For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.
"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"
Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.
Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.
Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.
This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.
For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.
What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.
Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.
At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.
Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.
Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.
Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.
If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.
The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.
She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.
"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

Supreme Court ends distinction between detention and arrest, says 24-hour clock starts when liberty is curtailed
SC made clear that the 24-hour deadline is sacrosanct and even a person detained for search and seizure must be produced before a magistrate within that period.
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that law enforcement agencies cannot circumvent the constitutional protection against prolonged custody by keeping a person in detention without formally showing an arrest, holding that the mandatory 24-hour period for producing an individual before a magistrate begins from the moment his liberty is curtailed, irrespective of when the arrest is officially recorded.
Rejecting attempts by some high courts to draw a distinction between detention and arrest, the court held that there could be no artificial “buffer period” during which a person’s liberty could be curtailed without triggering the safeguards under Article 22(2) of the Constitution.
The apex court made clear that the 24-hour deadline is sacrosanct and that even a person detained for search and seizure must be produced before a magistrate within that period.
The endeavour of several high courts, including Orissa, Kerala and Madras, to create a distinction between detention and arrest is highly problematic and wholly unwarranted, noted a bench of justices Ujjal Bhuyan and AS Chandurkar.
“There is nothing like a temporary disruption in liberty and any such interpretation is absolutely unconstitutional. There cannot be an artificial distinction between arrest and detention for creating a buffer period,” said Justice Bhuyan while reading out the operative portion of its judgment.
The case
The judgment arose from appeals filed by four persons arrested in a case under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, involving the seizure of 11.03 kg of yaba tablets in Tripura. The four were detained on September 29, 2025, at 2 pm during search and seizure operations but were formally shown as arrested only at 11 am the following day.
The bench held that they ought to have been produced before a magistrate within 24 hours of their detention at 2 pm on September 29. Their continued detention without judicial oversight for about 18 hours violated Article 22(2)and warrants their immediate release.
The Tripura high court had rejected their bail pleas, holding that the stringent twin conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act had to be satisfied before granting bail in a case involving a commercial quantity of contraband. It had also rejected their challenge to the alleged breach of arrest procedure under Section 36 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
What the ruling settles
The ruling settles an important question concerning the reach of Article 22(2), which mandates that a person arrested and detained in custody must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest, excluding the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the court. By holding that the constitutional clock starts ticking from the moment a person’s liberty is effectively curtailed, the court has taken away the discretion of investigating agencies to decide when the period of judicial oversight should begin merely by choosing when to formally record an arrest.
“The words 'arrest' and 'detained' under Article 22(2) are conjunctive and must be read together. The period of 24 hours shall start from the very moment a person is detained, and the person must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours,” Justice Bhuyan said.
The court also rejected the proposition that a brief period of detention before formal arrest could be treated as a temporary or permissible interruption of liberty, holding that such an interpretation would dilute the fundamental protection guaranteed by the Constitution.
“A statute, special or otherwise, cannot be a guide to the Constitution. It has to be the other way round. The interpretation has to be in a manner that upholds the fundamental right,” said the bench, adding that detention of a person for search and seizure beyond 24 hours runs contrary to Article 21, which guarantees the right to life and personal liberty.
The bench specifically disapproved of the judgments of the Orissa high court in Aryaman Pattanaik (2025), the Kerala high court in Arun K Thomas (2026), and the Madras high court in Kannan (2025), which had allowed the period preceding formal arrest to be excluded while computing the 24-hour deadline.
The court underscored that the constitutional safeguard was particularly important in the context of custodial violence, which often takes place when individuals are kept in police custody without being formally shown as arrested.
“The endeavour of this court is to eliminate custodial violence, which often takes place when a person is detained and not shown as formally under arrest. Custodial violence is unfortunately a recognised truth acknowledged by this court in several past judgments and incidents, including the Bhagalpur blinding case,” it said.
The bench further directed that the 24-hour period would commence from the date and time at which a person's liberty is curtailed, including when the person is intercepted by law enforcement authorities. No period spent in custody before the formal recording of arrest can be excluded, except the time genuinely necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the magistrate.
The bench also said that any detention without warrant must be for a reasonable period and that the magistrate receiving the detained person must specifically record the exact date and time from which the person’s liberty was curtailed and examine whether the 24-hour constitutional deadline had been observed. In the event of a breach, the person would have to be released.

Canva announces major job cuts after 'our hardest year yet'

Canva, one of Australia's best known start-ups, has announced a shake up of the business that will affect 22% of its workers, including job cuts.
In what was "without doubt the hardest moment in our thirteen-year history" co-founder and CEO Melanie Perkins said 1,271 people would either lose their jobs, be asked to relocate or change roles.

The company, which has staff in 37 countries, said Sydney would become the "primary home" for more of its product teams and that as of next year hybrid workers would be expected to spend two to three days in the office.

"New technology is transforming what people can create, how they create it, and what they expect from the products they use," Perkins said in her note on Wednesday.
Perkins, who left university at 19 to found her first venture, launched Canva in 2013.

A 22-second-long clip shared by X user Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) showing a massive crowd in a large open area went viral on November 1.
Thottathil posted the video with the caption, “Early in the morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed #ChaloDilli,” thus claiming that the crowd had gathered for the INDIA’s bloc’s rally on November 1 to protest against electoral irregularities and demand the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Early morning itself Ramlila Maidan is packed ✊🏼 🔥
#ChaloDilli https://t.co/oM5kSpCNoH
— Vijay Thottathil (@vijaythottathil) November 1, 2026
The post by Thottathil, who was till recently a social media manager of Kerala Congress, amassed over 243,000 views and was reshared over 1,400 times. (Archive)
Congress leader Harish Rawat, too, shared the video on Instagram, claiming that the visuals were from the November 1 protest rally.

Various other X handles posted the same 22-second clip, claiming that they are visuals from the ‘Chalo Dilli’ rally held on November 1. A few of them are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
In the comments of the video posted by Vijay, X users were quick to point out that the video was not from the November 1 ‘Chalo Dilli’ protest, and instead was from another rally held at an earlier date.
To determine the veracity of these claims, we ran a reverse image search on a few of the keyframes, which led us to a video uploaded by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on December 14, 2025.
This video, captioned “‘वोट चोरी’ के खिलाफ जनसैलाब 🔥🔥” (A public outpouring against “vote theft”), was uploaded during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests of December 2025.
View this post on Instagram
The comparison of certain keyframes of both videos reveals stark similarities, including the backdrop, the size of the crowd, a flag being waved in the front, and even a blue tent visible in the clip. See below:
A deeper dive revealed that Congress leader Harish Rawat had himself shared the video during the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhodo” protests on December 14, 2025. He has now shared the same clip again as scenes from the INDIA bloc rally of November 1, 2026.
To sum up, the viral clip with the massive crowds gathered at Ramlila Maidan shared by Thottathil is an old clip from the “Vote Choro, Gaddi Chhoro” protests that was organised by Congress in December last year. The leader of a German conservative party is found dead at a Berlin hotel
Hubert Aiwanger, leader of a conservative party influential in Bavarian politics, has been found dead in a Berlin hotel
BERLIN -- Hubert Aiwanger, the leader of a conservative party that has become a mainstay of Bavarian politics and sought to expand its influence across Germany, has been found dead at a Berlin hotel.
Berlin police and prosecutors said the body of Aiwanger, who was Bavaria's deputy governor and the southern state's economy minister, was found in his hotel room in the center of the capital on Wednesday evening. An investigation into the cause of death was opened.
German news agency dpa reported, without naming sources, that the 55-year-old Aiwanger had planned to make a speech Wednesday afternoon at the opening of a Berlin office of his party, the Free Voters, but pulled out of the event for health reasons.
Aiwanger had been the party's leader in Bavaria since 2006 and its national leader since 2010.
The combative politician with a strong regional accent and a populist touch made his party a serious rival to Bavaria's long-dominant Christian Social Union, which is part of the center-right bloc that currently leads Germany. On his watch, it entered the state legislature in Munich in 2008. Ten years later, when the CSU lost its majority in the state legislature, it entered Bavaria's government as the junior coalition partner.
Shortly before Bavaria's 2023 election, Aiwanger faced a furor that started with allegations — denied by the politician — that he was responsible for an antisemitic flyer when he was a high school student 35 years earlier. The Free Voters emerged unscathed from the election, gaining support and remained part of the state government.
Aiwanger's party has made only limited inroads outside Bavaria and he wasn't able to lead it into the national parliament.
Bavarian governor Markus Söder wrote on X that “the sudden death of Hubert Aiwanger is an absolute tragedy.”
Aiwanger is survived by his partner, Free Voters politician Tanja Schweiger, and two children.

Some of the health harms of climate change grew faster in the decade since the Paris Agreement entered into force (2016-2025) than in the previous decade (2006-2015) as climate action fails to keep pace, according to the 10th Lancet Countdown Report on Health and Climate Change.
The report, which was released on Wednesday, said the annual average heat-related deaths rose by nearly 36% globally after the Paris Agreement was introduced.
"In 2023 alone, heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths with more than 70 per cent of that toll attributable to human-caused climate change," it said.
The analysis represents the work of 146 multidisciplinary researchers from more than 100 institutions across more than 30 countries. It tracks 54 indicators of the health impacts of climate change and the health effects of climate action.
The report highlights that cleaner energy, more resilient health systems, more health-protecting legislation and growing scientific evidence have brought real health benefits to local communities since the Paris Agreement, but these gains are still too slow, too insufficient, and too inconsistent to offset the growing risks.
"Rising overall energy demand and slow system change means fossil fuels still supply over 80% of the world's energy, and climate-heating emissions reached a record high in 2024," it said.
The report added that despite gains in some countries, fossil-fuel air pollution still kills an estimated 2.8 million people a year worldwide.
Moreover, adaptation funding is falling far short of what's needed.
According to the report, the health adaptation needs quantified so far by developing countries put the minimum cost at $3.3 billion a year, based on data from only 48 of the 79 countries that have completed these estimates.
However, only around a third of this declared need, $1.1 billion, was committed in 2024.
"This substantial financing gap is reflected in countries' ability to translate adaptation priorities into action, with finance and human resourcing identified as the top barriers to implementation of Health National Adaptation Plans," said the report.

Amid the India-China standoff in Arunachal Pradesh (here, here), a video purportedly showing Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh criticising the Indian Army is being widely shared on social media (here, here, here). He claims that the India-China border tensions are not a major concern and that the government is fully supporting the Indian Army by providing adequate funds. The concerns raised by some soldiers over the government’s support are dismissed, and the clashes between the two neighbouring countries are described as minor, with trade relations continuing between them. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Union Defence Minister Rajnath Singh criticising the Indian Army amid the India-China standoff in Arunachal Pradesh.
Fact: The viral video has been manipulated using AI. The original video, published by ANI on 26 October 2026, shows Defence Minister Rajnath Singh criticising Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge’s remarks about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father. He made no remarks criticising the Indian Army. PIB Fact Check also confirmed that the viral video was AI-manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
We did not find any credible reports confirming that Union Minister Rajnath Singh made such statements as claimed in the viral video.
After conducting a reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video, we found that the news agency ANI published the original video on 26 October 2026. However, in the original video, Rajnath Singh is heard expressing shock and disappointment over Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge’s remarks about Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s late father in Patna. He criticises the Congress for defending Kharge’s remarks instead of acknowledging the mistake and expressing regret. The original audio has been replaced with a fabricated audio track. We also reviewed the full original video and found that Rajnath Singh made no remarks criticising the Indian Army.
We also noticed certain inconsistencies in the viral video. An unnatural rhythm in the speech and variations in tone are prominently seen. On verifying the video’s audio using Hive AI and Resemble AI, we found it to be a deepfake.
Further, the Press Information Bureau (PIB) Fact Check issued a clarification on 31 October 2026, debunking the viral video and confirming that it had been manipulated using AI.
To sum up, this viral video of Rajnath Singh criticising the Indian Army is AI-Manipulated.

Just days before Diwali, Delhi-NCR is already choking on “hazardous” air on Thursday, while Mumbai continues to be in the “unhealthy” band. Weather experts believe that there could be a sharp spike in pollution the day after Diwali. With the Air Quality Index (AQI) deteriorating and winter setting in, India's top metropolises are facing a sudden rise in cases of persistent, unyielding cough. Clinics are crowded with patients presenting with sore throats, chest tightness, and fatigue. But a common question among the masses is: Is this cough a reaction to the toxic air, or is it a seasonal viral infection like the flu? Quick answers to key questions Pollution-related symptoms often build gradually and cause throat or eye irritation without fever. Influenza usually starts suddenly and is more likely to bring fever and body aches, though symptoms can overlap. Yes. Pollution can worsen airway inflammation during a viral infection, while an infection can make airways more sensitive to polluted air. A viral infection can leave the airways unusually reactive, causing a cough to continue for several weeks after the infection has resolved. Pollution may aggravate that irritation. Seek medical advice if the cough comes with breathlessness, chest pain, fever, reduced oxygen saturation or bloody sputum. A clinician can assess the symptoms and decide whether tests are needed. A gradual onset with throat or eye irritation and no fever may point to pollution. If symptoms improve indoors or when you leave the city, that can also suggest an air-quality trigger. Medical experts told LiveMint that the confusion is entirely justified — The physiological responses to smog, seasonal influenza, and common colds look remarkably alike, making self-diagnosis tricky and complicating treatment. The primary diagnostic challenge is that the respiratory system reacts similarly to both environmental irritants and viral invaders, the experts noted. “At this time of year, the symptoms overlap considerably,” Dr Rommel Tickoo, Senior Director, Internal Medicine at Max Super Speciality Hospital, Saket, New Delhi, explained. A patient presenting with persistent dry cough, fatigue and chest tightness could be “due to the polluted air, seasonal influenza, or a bacterial infection on top of irritated airways,” he said. Dr Sagar Srivastava, Consultant Pulmonologist at Kailash Hospital in Greater Noida, agreed, noting that this mimicry makes clinical assessments difficult. “The factors that lead to air pollution, the common cold, and the flu have some similar symptoms, including coughing, sore throat, blocked nose, and trouble breathing,” he said, adding that “this similarity makes it hard to identify the exact cause of the problem because while irritation from pollution does not include fever, infections can also begin without having a fever first.” While the initial scratchy throat might feel identical, doctors suggest patients look for specific patterns in how the symptoms evolve to narrow down the culprit. The onset speed and the presence of systemic symptoms are key indicators. “Influenza usually begins suddenly and comes with fever and body aches, whereas symptoms from pollution tend to build up gradually and are mostly irritation in the throat and eyes, without fever,” Dr Tickoo noted. Environmental triggers, he said, also offer a major clue. “If a patient improves when they are indoors or when they travel out of the city, that points towards the air.” Dr Tickoo explained that medical professionals also watch closely for secondary infections — “If someone was getting better and then develops a fresh fever with coloured sputum, we start considering a secondary bacterial infection.” In many cases, the persistent cough isn't an “either/or” situation, Dr Divya Gopal, Additional Director of Internal Medicine at Sir H.N. Reliance Foundation Hospital in Mumbai, noted. The toxic air actually paves the way for viruses, and viruses leave the airways highly sensitive to pollution. “Pollution can exacerbate existing inflammation of the airways in addition to the presence of viral infection in an individual, which means that a patient can have several causes of his/her condition,” Dr Gopal said. This combination, she said, often leads to a prolonged, nagging cough long after the initial illness has passed. “There can be post-viral airway hyperreactivity, which leads to a cough lasting several weeks after the infection resolves.” Physicians rely heavily on a detailed patient history to understand the primary cause of overlapping conditions. “Symptoms, including when the first signs started, the duration of time and severity, along with other symptoms, will assist in narrowing down the cause,” said Dr Srivastava. He said that doctors inquire about recent exposure to pollutants, contact with sick individuals, and pre-existing conditions like asthma or COPD. Then, depending on this history, doctors may order a complete blood count, CRP levels, viral panels (Influenza/COVID-19), or a chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia. Therefore, Dr Gopal warned against dismissing severe symptoms as mere smog irritation. “Do not jump to conclusions that persistent coughing is due to pollution,” she advised. “It is necessary to see a doctor if breathlessness, chest pain, fever, reduced oxygen saturation, or bloody sputum is present. Correct diagnosis will help prevent unnecessary use of antibiotics.” While individuals have limited control over the city's air quality, doctors strongly recommend focusing on what they can control—specifically, getting vaccinated against the flu. “While vaccination does not rule out influenza completely, it reduces the likelihood and helps us narrow down the cause,” Dr Tickoo said, urging older adults, pregnant women, young children, and those with comorbidities to get their shots. “It takes about two weeks to take effect, so it is better to get it now than to wait.” Arshdeep Kaur is a Senior Content Producer at Mint, where she reports and edits across national and international politics, business and culture‑adjacent trending stories for digital audience. As the air quality of the national capital deteriorated to the 'very poor' category for the first time this winter season, the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and adjoining areas (CAQM) on Monday (November 2, 2026) announced Stage 2 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
The air quality is likely to be in the 'very poor' category for the next three days, as per the Central government’s Air Quality Early Warning System for Delhi. The last time Delhi’s air quality was in the 'very poor' category was on February 11 this year.
Stage 2 of the GRAP mandates NCR State governments to enhance vehicle parking fees to discourage use of private vehicles. The GNCTD (Delhi government) and NCR State governments also have to “stagger timings for public offices and municipal bodies in the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the districts of Gurugram, Faridabad, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar”.
Considering the restrictions on vehicles, the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC) has decided to run additional trips on weekdays. While the DMRC was running 20 trips since October 28, when the GRAP-1 was enforced, 20 more trips will be run now. “This is to encourage people to use public transport rather than their private vehicles and help mitigate pollution,” said a senior Metro official.
Other directions to State governments include implementing existing measures to control air pollution, such as mechanical sweeping of roads or sprinkling water on roads, among others
The GRAP is a set of short-term emergency measures to reduce air pollution and is divided into four stages. The CAQM announces the different stages depending on the level of pollution recorded or forecast for the near future.
The 24-hour average Air Quality Index (AQI) of Delhi stood at 324 (very poor) at 4 p.m. on November 2, 2026, up from 261 (poor) a day earlier, as per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)’s daily bulletin, which is treated as the day’s AQI. A higher AQI indicates worsening air quality.
‘Very poor' levels of air pollution could lead to “respiratory illness on prolonged exposure”, as per the CPCB. On February 11, 2026, the AQI was 305 (very poor).
Every winter, air pollution spikes in the Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Pollution from stubble burning during October and November and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season also add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

Top U.N. court to rule on Myanmar’s Rohingya genocide case
A view of the Peace Palace, which houses the Permanent Court of Arbitration and the International Court of Justice, in The Hague, Netherlands, on June 18
| REUTERS
The Hague – The top United Nations court on Nov. 19 will deliver a landmark ruling on whether Myanmar’s crackdown against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority constituted a genocide, officials said on Tuesday.
Judges at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) have for seven years been weighing accusations by The Gambia that Myanmar’s brutal repression of the Rohingya breached the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention.
While the ICJ has no means of enforcing its decisions, a ruling that Myanmar committed genocide would heap more international pressure on its leader Min Aung Hlaing.

Ahead of its premiere on November 13, Student of the Year: After Dark has released a new track titled ‘Jo Hona Hai Ho Jayega’. Featuring Shanaya Kapoor alongside singer-composer Chaar Diwaari, the song offers a glimpse into the series' unusual and darker setting.
Student of the Year: After Dark song ‘Jo Hona Hai Ho Jayega’: Chaar Diwaari and Samad Khan bring experimental sound to Shanaya Kapoor’s series
Sung, written and composed by Chaar Diwaari and Samad Khan, the track combines elements of different musical styles, including qawwali and mid-tempo sounds. Its unconventional arrangement and lyrics revolve around the idea of accepting uncertainty and allowing events to take their course.
The music video features Shanaya Kapoor and Chaar Diwaari in a setting where things take unexpected turns. The video also ends on a supernatural note, with Chaar Diwaari transforming into a werewolf.
Talking about the track, Chaar Diwaari said, “I think the fun part about this song is that it doesn't really behave the way you expect it to. We are exploring different genres such as qawali and mid-tempo in this in a way where the transitions feel effortless. The lyrics talk about Murphy's Law in a way where it feels liberating. The lyrics reflect positive nihilism. Samad and I have been close friends for a while so making this song felt like it was long overdue.”
Samad Khan also spoke about the creative process behind the song. He said, “Diwaari and I didn't want to make something that sounded too polished or predictable. We wanted the track to have its own personality, something that feels slightly off in places but in a good way. We played around with different sounds and ideas until we found something that felt right for this world. I think that's what I enjoy most about working with Diwaari. We can try the weirdest things without worrying too much about whether they make sense to anyone else and somehow, they end up making sense in the song.”
‘Jo Hona Hai Ho Jayega’ is now available on streaming platforms through Sony Music India.
