In 1904, two scientists, Henry Wheeler and Treat Johnson, synthesised a variant of cytosine, one of the building blocks of DNA, in the laboratory.
The variant they synthesised contained a chemical tag called a methyl group (-CH3) attached to cytosine, so they called it 5-methylcytosine. Their motivation for doing so was based on the observation that two other building blocks of DNA and its chemical cousin RNA, called thymine and uracil, differed only by the presence of a methyl group.
So Wheeler and Johnson figured that a methylated version of cytosine might also exist in nature.
In 1925, Johnson, while working with another scientist named Robert Coghill, finally discovered 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. Two more decades later, Rollin Hotchkiss found 5-methyl-cytosine in the DNA of cows. Soon, scientists found that it existed in nearly all animals.
However, nobody knew why it existed — or why some of the cytosines in DNA were methylated while others were not.
Genes on and off
That insight came in 1975, when Robin Holliday and John Pugh proposed that the methylation of the cytosine could be a way for the body to use the information stored in DNA.
DNA is segmented into genes, and each gene contains the information necessary to make a particular protein. These proteins perform their specific functions in the cells. Since every cell in the body has two copies — one from each parent — of all human DNA, all cells technically have the blueprint to make a whole organism.
However, cells also have specialised functions. A brain cell will not need the genes for the proteins used to digest food. So Holliday and Pugh suggested that chemical modifications such as the methylation of cytosine could help establish and activate genes that a cell wants while silencing those it does not.
This idea, that cells could use chemical tags on DNA to control which genes were active, has come to be called epigenetics. (The British biologist Conrad Waddington had actually coined the term in 1942 itself.) Soon, scientists found enzymes that could add and remove these chemical tags to and from DNA.
Today, we know that cells use many other chemical tags, not only on DNA itself but also on the proteins around which DNA is wrapped like a vine around a stick.
Together, all these chemical marks help control which genes are switched on or off. Problems in this system can lead to changes in gene activity, which in turn can lead to diseases like cancers.
Functional cure
Now, according to a paper that appeared in Nature Biomedical Engineering on September 21, scientists have used this epigenetic control to treat a hepatitis B infection.
This is a remarkable development because, instead of targeting the virus directly, the work silenced the viral DNA. This is promising because current treatments rarely eliminate the DNA, which allows the virus to rebound. By silencing this residue, the treatment could offer a path to a lasting functional cure for hepatitis B.
The hepatitis B virus mainly infects liver cells. After entering a cell, the virus’s DNA serves as the template to make new viral particles. In many people, the immune system clears the infection, but if it does not, the viral DNA can persist for years or even decades in the host’s liver.
In this time, the virus can remain silent, meaning the viral DNA is still present in the cell but its genes are not active to produce new viruses. This allows the virus to ‘hide’ from the immune system. Then, at a later point, the virus can activate again and produce new virus particles.
And studies have shown that one of the mechanisms by which the virus stays silent is by methylating the cytosines.
Locator and effector
The authors of the new study have reported a new experimental therapy called CRMA-1001, which, they have claimed, can silence the DNA of the hepatitis B virus by selectively adding methylation marks to the viral genome.
The study is innovative because it uses several different technologies to overcome three major challenges. To epigenetically silence viral DNA, scientists first need to be able to target the virus’s DNA without methylating any of the cytosines in the host’s DNA. Then, the silencing mechanism must switch off the virus’s DNA effectively. Finally, all of this should happen without causing any unwanted side-effects to the host.
The study authors solved the first two problems by combining two substances called a ‘locator’ and an ‘effector’. The locator used the CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing tool to find and bind to a specific DNA sequence: in this case, that was a sequence within the viral DNA. This allowed the CRISPR system to take the ‘effector’, the methylation machinery, to the correct location. The effector had proteins that could add methyl groups to nearby cytosines in the viral DNA and proteins that help switch off genes.
Finally, the researchers packed the entire system and delivered it on an mRNA platform (similar to the mRNA vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic). This made the system transient: once a cell had read the instructions to make the required proteins, it degraded them, stopping the production of those proteins too.
Novel therapy
The researchers gave mice infected with hepatitis B virus either a single dose of CRMA-1001 or three doses, one month apart, and regularly tested them for six months for the signs of infection. They reported that after one dose, the levels of several hepatitis B virus markers, including the viral DNA and two viral proteins called HBsAg and HBeAg, dropped significantly. When they tested the viral DNA, they found new methyl groups, suggesting that the treatment was working as intended. The effect was even stronger after three doses: six months after the first dose, as many as 90% of the animals had less viral DNA than could be detected.
CRMA-1001 is not a cure in the traditional sense of the word. The hepatitis B virus DNA is still present in the liver cells. Instead, the study demonstrated a functional cure: when the virus is not necessarily eliminated but is kept so thoroughly suppressed that, for all intents and purposes, the patient has no active signs of disease.
In this study, the team followed up with the mice for six months after treatment, and the researchers found sustained suppression of the virus in that period. However, the study did not establish whether the virus could eventually become active again after those six months, since the viral DNA was still present.
Further studies are needed to examine the long-term effects of CRMA-1001, including whether the silencing effect can persist over many years and whether the virus can ever become active again after treatment. An ongoing phase I/II clinical trial includes these among other questions.
If CRMA-1001 is eventually approved as a therapy for the market, it will represent a novel way to tackle a viral infection: where instead of fighting the threat, the cell ignores it.
Arun Panchapakesan is an assistant professor at the Y.R. Gaitonde Centre for AIDS Research and Education, Chennai.

Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguay's lower house voted unanimously Thursday to impeach President Santiago Peña just minutes after he announced his resignation, as the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings, sent protesters surging into the streets and turned his own party against him.
The 78-0 vote marked a stunning repudiation of Peña by lawmakers from his long-ruling Colorado Party, who joined the opposition in backing his impeachment after three days of demonstrations rocked the capital, Asunción. The vote sends the charges to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority is required to convict the president and formally remove him from office.
The impeachment came as thousands protested for a third day, as they attempt to recoup lost savings, wages and pensions from Ueno Bank, a major digital lender.
Peña, a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, announced his decision in a video posted to X as lawmakers debated his impeachment, saying he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."
The president, who until last year held a stake in a company related to Ueno Bank, expressed contrition but stopped short of accepting responsibility for the banking crisis that has plunged a South American nation long prized by foreign investors for its stability into financial and political turmoil.
"I also want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."
The extraordinary turn of events set the stage for a transfer of power later Thursday. Congress was expected to formally accept Peña's resignation at 5 p.m., clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in as president an hour later. Alliana would serve out Peña's term through August 2028, with lawmakers expected to choose a new vice president.
From star lender to seized bank
Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. They are now left scrambling to recoup their savings, government pensions, and, for 7,000 employees impacted by the bank's closure, unpaid wages.
Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president, who until last year had a stake in Ueno's holding company, could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its dubious lending practices.
The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth made Paraguay a darling of international investors in recent years.
"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."
Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.
Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.
As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies.
Peña repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
Long lines outside branches but customers are locked out
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.
Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left.
Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.
Officials appealed for calm and said they had begun repaying depositors, opening new accounts elsewhere for about 280,000 who had banked only with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Peña's request.
Authorities have detained eight senior Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud. Lawyers for several of the detained said they needed time to review the allegations before they could comment.
Protesters in the streets
Hundreds of employees of Ueno Bank and other companies belonging to Grupo Vázquez, the bank's parent conglomerate, protested outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages with their jobs in limbo and their salaries trapped at the failed bank. A day earlier, hundreds of retirees, depositors, university students and workers flooded the streets of Asunción, the capital.
"We want your head, Peña!" they shouted. Their signs demanded Peña's impeachment, called him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber pellets to push back the crowds.
Many demonstrators saw Ueno's collapse not just as the result of risky banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on the latest index of perceived corruption from Transparency International, a global watchdog.
"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said protester Belarmino Balbuena.
At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. But across the capital, fresh graffiti denounced politicians as thieves.

The Indian government has moved to reduce the price of cancer drugs after a retired bank clerk took her case to the supreme court.
From next month, 137 cancer drugs in India will be cheaper as the government tries to tackle the tragedy of poorer patients either forgoing treatment, selling land or falling into debt to meet the high cost of some medicines, which are making large profits for hospitals and pharmacists.
Sarojam Radhakrishnan, a former bank employee in Kerala, was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2021. Doctors prescribed life-saving targeted treatments but the monthly cost, of more than 63,000 rupees (£500), was far beyond her family’s means.
Realising that thousands of families were being ruined by the cost of such drugs, Radhakrishnan filed a petition to the Kerala high court in 2022 demanding government intervention to lower the costs.
When the case reached the supreme court, the judges looked at hospitals’ and retailers’ mark-ups on cancer drugs and called the situation “carnage” and “extortion”.
During a hearing on 29 September, justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta noted how a life-saving cancer drug supplied to hospitals at 2,700 rupees carried a vastly marked-up price of 27,000 rupees.
The judges found that hospitals, distributors and chemists enjoyed large margins on medicines. Analysis by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority revealed a trade mark-up on some cancer drugs averaging 170%, with some extreme examples stretching to more than 700%.
A 30% trade margin cap on the price of 42 drugs has been in place for some years but many others remained off this list. Now, prodded by the supreme court’s findings, the government has imposed the cap on 137 other drugs.
“The measure is expected to reduce medicine prices by up to 70% and help cancer patients save 2,500 crore rupees [£199m] annually, significantly reducing the amount they pay from their own pockets,” a statement from the Department of Pharmaceuticals said.
People on low incomes in India dread illness, as the cost of treatment can mean financial ruin, particularly for cancer patients.
Whenever the Indian Cancer Society holds a free diagnosis camp in Gurgaon where he lives, Krishan Kalra urges local drivers, maids, cooks and tailors to turn up because tests they cannot afford are offered free.
As a former member of the council of the Rajiv Gandhi Cancer Institute and Research Centre, Kalra knows the importance of early diagnosis, but he said very few people attended. “When I ask why, they say they’re too scared – if something serious like cancer is detected, they haven’t got the money to pay for the treatment so they prefer to remain in the dark,” he said.
With the cost of cancer drugs ranging in price from 38,000 to 380,000 rupees, many families quietly walk out of the doctor’s consulting room upon hearing the estimated cost of treatment.
Studies by the Public Health Foundation of India show that spending on healthcare pushes about 55 million Indians a year below the poverty line.
Few Indians can afford the premiums for comprehensive health insurance. The government’s nationwide insurance scheme, Ayushman Bharat, covers treatment for some cancers but it provides only 500,000 rupees’ worth of annual cover for a family – the cost of just one dose of Kadcyla (ado-trastuzumab emtansine), a drug used to treat breast cancer. Patients may need up to 14 doses.
Dr Ravi Kannan is a surgical oncologist and director of Cachar cancer hospital and research centre in Silchar, Assam. He has worked in hospitals elsewhere in India and is familiar with doctors’ trauma of seeing patients walk out to go home and die.
“Some families start the treatment, hoping against hope to manage the cost. They start but they don’t come back for chemotherapy or radiation. They can’t sustain the cost,” he said. “The decision is a welcome step if the outcome is that more patients can access the drugs they need.”
India records about 1.56m new cancer cases annually – up from 1.39m cases in 2020 – making it a significant public health challenge.
As the supreme court delves deeper into the subject, what was clear, said Jyotsna Singh, co-convener of the Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments, a civil society network, was that a “total overhaul” of the healthcare system was needed.
“Right from the cost of manufacturing a drug to the point of sale, we need to make the system transparent and regulate the entire supply chain. Only then will these drugs become available to those who need them,” she said.
Singh said companies and hospitals were likely to try to find legal loopholes to wriggle out of the 30% cap, suggesting that hospitals may offset the lower price charged for a drug by raising charges on other items.
The supreme court judges have also asked the government’s lawyers why the cap should apply only to cancer drugs and not the entire range of non-patented drugs. The court has given the government until 27 October to respond.
Unfortunately, the court’s ruling came too late for Radhakrishnan, who died in September 2022 while her case was still pending in Kerala.

Hajra Begum rolls a potato in her hands, checking its skin for cuts, soft spots and signs of rot. After a day harvesting in her family’s field in Chorwan, a remote mountain village in Gurez, Indian-administered Kashmir, she is sorting the crop for winter storage. Some of the potatoes will feed her family through the cold months; others will be saved for planting in spring.
“It should be perfect for planting,” she says. “If you keep a bad potato, you will waste the whole next year.”
Begum, 40, is preparing to lower the potatoes into a khraw, a traditional underground storage pit lined with straw and sealed against the cold. For generations, khraws have kept potatoes, turnips and cabbages through Himalayan winters, when heavy snowfall cuts villages off from the Kashmir valley and temperatures fall below -20C (-4F) – cold enough to crack pipes and freeze diesel.
But the practice is slowly dying out. As roads have improved and young people have left for work and education, fewer families maintain the pits. Their decline threatens not only a traditional way of storing food but also the local potato varieties themselves and the knowledge of which ones store well, resist rot and produce reliable harvests.
“When I was young, almost every family had three or four pits,” Begum says. “Now, down in the main valley, they have abandoned the practice altogether. Only a handful of families still use them. The rest buy from the market or subsidised ones from the government.”
Begum learned from her mother how to tell potatoes that store well from those that rot or sprout too quickly. She is passing this on to her daughter, but is unsure whether the skill will survive into another generation.
Gurez is a high-altitude Himalayan valley perched near the Line of Control, the heavily militarised boundary separating Indian- and Pakistani-administered Kashmir. About 80 miles (125km) from Srinagar, the valley remains cut off each winter when snow closes Razdan pass, its main road link, which sits at roughly 3,600 metres.
It is home to the Dard-Shin people, an Indigenous community who speak Shina and have a culture that is distinct from Kashmiri, with community links across the border in Gilgit-Baltistan, administered by Pakistan.
Potatoes account for about 45% of Gurez’s cultivated area, according to a 2019 study by the Indian Council of Agricultural Research’s National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources (ICAR-NBPGR), a government body that studies and conserves India’s crop diversity. Yet the genetic diversity of the valley’s potatoes has not been systematically documented.
Dr Sheikh M Sultan, a senior scientist based at ICAR-NBPGR’s Srinagar station, surveyed the valley and later struggled to find some of the varieties he had once encountered. “When I first visited, I saw many varieties,” he says. “Later, I could hardly locate even one sample of some. The loss of genetic diversity is tremendous.”
Sultan says migration, improved roads and changing lifestyles have contributed to the decline. As traditional farming disappears, so does knowledge about selecting, cultivating and preserving local varieties.
“When people stop producing their own seeds and start relying entirely on commercial varieties, the loss can be irreparable,” he says.
He warns that research institutions often prioritise introduced varieties over indigenous crops whose characteristics remain poorly understood. “Our indigenous varieties may possess valuable characteristics, including tolerance to cold and resistance to certain pests and diseases,” he says.
“These are resources we should be studying and improving, rather than neglecting.”
Climate breakdown is adding to the pressures on farmers across the Himalayas. People in Gurez report drier springs, reduced snowfall and water shortages, which they say have affected potato production.
Abdul Jabbar Mapnoo, 70, a farmer in Chorwan, remembers winters when deep snow covered the valley. “Every house used to have two or three khraw, each holding about five quintals – 500kg – of potatoes,” he says. “The springs are drying up, and there is less snow in winter. Potato production has fallen. I remember winters when six feet of snow would cover the valley in January or February.”
As farming becomes more difficult and markets easier to access, households have less incentive to grow their own potatoes. Varieties adapted to local conditions over generations could disappear from cultivation before researchers establish what makes them distinctive.
Dr Parveen Kumar, a scientist at the Sher-e-Kashmir University of Agricultural Sciences and Technology of Kashmir, says locally adapted varieties should not be overlooked. “Climate change is a reality, and farmers need to be aware of adaptation strategies,” he says.
Pressure on farmland poses another risk. In Gurez, where cultivable land is scarce, the Kishanganga hydroelectric project has affected land in the valley through acquisition and submergence. Among the areas affected is Badwan, a village known for its potatoes.
One potential route for preserving the varieties could be through using geographical indications – a designation granted by the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, and is similar to the French appellation d’origine contrôlée. It can be used on goods that have a specific origin and possess qualities or a reputation linked to this – which can help increase the market value and give them greater recognition. This, and the globally important agricultural heritage systems programme have helped areas such as the saffron-growing landscape of Pampore in Kashmir.
However, recognition alone will not preserve the varieties. They must be identified and documented before they disappear from cultivation, along with farmers’ knowledge of how to select, store and replant them.
In Chorwan, Begum unloads the last sack of potatoes into the pit and covers it, ready for another winter. Some will feed her family; the rest will be replanted in spring. Knowing which potatoes to eat and which to save as seed relies on knowledge passed down through generations.
If these varieties are not documented while they are still being cultivated, Kashmir may lose a living agricultural treasure trove before scientists can fully understand what it contains.

Oncologists have long wrestled with a conundrum. Healthy human tissue often carries mutations that can drive cancer, but the tissue itself does not develop tumours. Clearly, a genetic spark alone is not enough. At the same time, chronic inflammation from smoking profoundly damages lung tissue long before any definitive cancer-causing mutations even take root.

As polls opened for the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, a claim (archived) circulated online that U.S. President Donald Trump said, "If people ever get tired of me in the U.S., I'll move to Israel, become prime minister."
X user @MarioNafwal shared the alleged quote and wrote, "Well, I think they're already tired of you, Mr. President, but Israelis are tired of Bibi, too."
The claim also circulated on Facebook (archived).
Social media users correctly attributed the quote to Trump, who said it during a phone interview with Fox News (time code 22:20) on Tuesday.
According to a clip from Fox News' coverage that the network posted online, Trump said the following while speaking about cutting U.S. financial aid to Israel (emphasis ours):
And let me tell you something, if they do need it, if for some reason they do need it or they need help — So, I'm the number one, I was so voted, I'm at 99% approval rating in Israel, can you believe it? In fact, if people ever get tired of me in the U.S., I'll move to Israel, become prime minister. But I'm at 90 — think of it — I'm at 99%, I have the highest approval rating of anybody in history.
We contacted the White House to ask which approval polling Trump was referring to during his interview and await a reply.
Polling from the Jewish People Policy Institute, an Israel-based think tank that aims to shape strategy and policy on issues affecting Jewish people, published on Nov. 2 found that 73% of Israelis find Trump to be "a better-than-average U.S. president for Israel's interests." That polling also found that 54% of Jewish Israelis said Trump was "one of the best presidents in U.S. history in the Israeli context" and an additional 25% described him as "above average" on the same metric, according to the JPPI.
Election Day was not the first time Trump appeared to air thoughts of running for office in Israel. On May 20, Trump also claimed he had a 99% approval rating in Israel and could run for prime minister there. While speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Trump said (time code 03:44):
I'm right now at 99% in Israel. I could run for prime minister, so maybe after I do this, I'll go to Israel, run for prime minister. I had a poll this morning. I'm 99%. So that's good.
It was not clear what opinion polling Trump was referring to in his May 20 comment. At the time, the fact-checking organization Lead Stories reported that it could find "no publicly available poll showing Donald Trump with 99% support in Israel."
According to Israeli law, the country's prime minister must be eligible for election to the Israeli Parliament, which is called the Knesset. This in turn requires that a person is an Israeli national. There was no evidence at the time of this writing that Trump was an Israeli national, suggesting he was ineligible to become Israel's prime minister, even if he genuinely wanted to run for office.
For further reading, Snopes previously investigated whether Trump said Iran asked him to be the country's supreme leader.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday ruled that the constitutional mandate of producing an arrestee before a magistrate within 24 hours starts the moment one is detained for interrogation and not from the time when formal arrest is made by an investigating agency, since the liberty of a person is curtailed when one is detained.Noting that no artificial distinction should be created between detention and arrest, a bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar quashed the verdicts of high courts which had held that the 24-hour period starts only after formal arrest and not during antecedent detention necessitated by statutory procedure of seizure. Article 22(2) mandates that every person who is arrested and detained in custody has to be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of such arrest."Article 22(2) does not sanction exclusion of the time taken for enquiry and investigation before the arresting authority could effect arrest of the detainee. This is beyond the mandate of Article 22(2) of the Constitution. Article 22(2) does not sanction creation of any buffer zone where the liberty of an individual is curtailed for investigating purposes but not formally shown as arrested. Creation or contemplation of such buffer zone is unconstitutional.
.." the bench said.As it is common practice for police to record formal arrest much later, sometimes even a day after detaining a person for interrogation, Supreme Court's order would serve as a check on the police and other investigating agencies. The court also noted that its order was meant to eliminate custodial violence, which unfortunately takes place during the time when a person is under detention and not shown as formally arrested, in the process delaying production before the magistrate.

Discursive Verses: Is 'Spend Dat' the best financial indicator of America's grift economy?
After spending three hours counting the pores on Elizabeth Holmes' and Nathan Fielder's faces, I couldn't help but think how perfect Yung Miami's "Spend Dat" would've played over the closing credits. Whatever you feel about the veracity of the protagonist in the blockbuster doc You Can See Everything, there is no doubt about her innate ability to cop and blow money fast. She's probably about as familiar with Diddy's favorite City Girl as she is with Abbott & Costello. But a scammer of such ill repute deserves an apropos theme song. Hell, maybe we all do.
When people complain about hip-hop no longer being political, what they're really talking about is commercial rap's long-fizzled countercultural agenda. The politics of consumption and corruption however have never enjoyed a louder ringing endorsement. Like a billionaire hogging the bully pulpit. To that end, no song in 2026 comes closer to mimicking the feeling of being the violated and the violator. On its face, "Spend Dat" is a get-money flex dedicated to all the "scammers" and "booster b*****s." But behind that seductive veneer is the sadomasochistic loop of late-stage capitalism's long, punishing con. An inflation indicator like no other, it's easily our most American anthem of the year. And we're all transfixed, nodding along in unblinking commitment to the charade.
The video for "Spend Dat" feels like a throwback to the early 2000s, when making it rain in strip clubs was still obligatory signposting for selling the dream. It almost feels trite now that prediction markets allow us to place digital bets on democracy and buy-now, pay-later loans keep expanding on our freedom to fall deeper in debt. At least a good lap dance came with a tangible return on investment. Now we're all just being teased to death.
When India.Arie echoed the public denouncement of "Spend Dat" — which included a call for Black folk to boycott the Billboard-charting song of the summer — another film, I Love Boosters, had just hit streaming. Unlike the aforementioned documentary on the blonde-haired, blue-eyed, white-collar scammer Holmes, rapper-turned-director Boots Riley's fictional narrative centered on the supposed scourge of the hood. In it, Keke Palmer plays an illegit booster, selling high-end fenced clothing out of the abandoned fast-food chicken joint she's squatting in while harboring her own fashionable aspirations. It takes an international worker-led intervention — and a sci-fi bopgun full of Marxist intentions — for her to realize the minor disruption she and her shoplifting girlfriends are causing is but a necessary cog in the ever-churning, exploitative wheel of global capitalism.
What Riley wants us all to understand, as an avowed communist who switched his weapon of choice from fronting Bay Area rap group The Coup to writing screenplays, is that we the people are hardly the problem. Even when sufferers turn into self-styled hustlers out of desperation instead of pooling their collective power. Like WEB DuBois before him, Riley calls his art propaganda. And he's equally adamant about calling art on the other end of the spectrum of propaganda, too. "When The Coup first came out they would call us a political rap group. And we'd be like, 'No,' " he said on a recent episode of Novara Media's podcast Downstream. "Don't call us that unless you're calling everybody that. Because what it then made it seem like was as if everything else was just what it is." Rather, art magnifying the status quo is not some benign representation of a fixed reality but an uncritical regurgitation of everything indoctrinated by the moneyed elite.
When the controversy surrounding "Spend Dat" reached a fever pitch earlier this summer, it came with the usual diatribe. The song was criticized for being culturally degrading. Even India.Arie caught a bunch of flak for stating the obvious when she said, "Everything you listen to see or eat is going to influence you." I don't blame anybody Black for getting in their feelings over the seemingly negative portrayals or stereotypical depiction centered in rap. But the buck doesn't stop there. It never has. "We are bound by all sorts of customs that have come down as second-hand soul clothes of white patrons," as DuBois so eloquently stated 100 years ago this month in his essay Criteria of Negro Art. "We are ashamed of sex and we lower our eyes when people will talk of it," he says, concluding with this thought: "Our worst side has been so shamelessly emphasized that we are denying we have or ever had a worst side."
The same week "Spend Dat" went platinum, Yung Miami appeared on "The Breakfast Club" to promote the release of her solo debut, Watch Dis. When asked about the criticism the song received, she defended it as inspirational music "that builds you up to want to be somebody." Rap may have started at the bottom. But at some point the script flipped. The systems hip-hop was oriented to rebel against became the metric for its success. The victors, in this case, were found striving for the same spoils. Having finally achieved the market share and visibility we'd been denied for decades, we became centrists: a marginalized culture subsumed by the mainstream. Commercial rap made itself a useful tool of the establishment, and the perfect racially coded scapegoat.
If the American Dream really is a pyramid scheme, as commonly critiqued, all hail the original scammers who bricked up the foundation. Even with their fuzzy slave-owner math (discounting Blacks as three-fifths human) and gender restrictions on equal rights (ratified while rocking powdered wigs), the nation's so-called founders created a system even the lowest caste could be constrained and cajoled into aspiring to.
It reminds me of the funniest meme I encountered online last week: a comic strip calling cap on the promise of Black capitalism. It pictures two brothers chopping it up, with one plainly stating, "You can't buy your way out of a system that was built on selling you." Totally undeterred, the other replies back, "Well, I'm gonna try!" before invoking the Black power era's "by any means necessary" rhetoric. In the next panel, Malcolm X expresses frustration over his words being misused to validate participation in the futile American experiment.
We've been hoodwinked, indeed. Bamboozled. Led astray. Run amok and flat-out deceived like a mug.
The grift is so complete that it's almost impossible to distinguish the mark from the actual con artist. Whether it's a convicted felon hiding fraudulence behind white tears, or a ride-or-die who bossed up with the boosters and got it off the muscle. In a year when prediction markets and predatory installment loans sucked us all dry, inflation skyrocketed and tech billionaires quickened the apocalypse, an ode to America's undying hustle and flow might be the closing credits theme we all deserve.

Public records and an email first obtained by KARE 11, a Minnesota news station, indicate ICE purchased the vacant facility for $495.6 million roughly a year after private prison operator CoreCivic offered it to the Minnesota Department of Corrections for $75 million. The Department of Homeland Security and CoreCivic said the price was set through the standard federal appraisal process, which involves independent estimates of the property's value.
In late October, a claim emerged that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement paid roughly $495 million for a private prison previously offered for sale to the state of Minnesota for $75 million.
Snopes readers sent us images of Instagram (archived) and Facebook posts featuring the story, which spread amid the White House's highly-publicized attempts to portray Minnesota as an example of poor governance and a hotbed of fraud.
On X, Democratic lawmakers like U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California also shared the story.
This claim originated from a credible Oct. 29 report by KARE 11 (archived), a Minneapolis-based television station and NBC affiliate. 
In August, the Department of Homeland Security paid a private prison operator, CoreCivic, $495.6 million for a vacant facility in Appleton, a rural town in southwestern Minnesota. KARE 11's investigative report found that roughly a year before the sale to DHS, the Minnesota Department of Corrections had declined a $75 million sale offer for the same prison — Prairie Correctional Facility — from the same company. 
Snopes independently verified the facts behind the report via publicly available documentation, as well as emails shared by KARE 11's lead reporter on the story — A.J. Lagoe — and the Minnesota DOC. CoreCivic stated in its news release announcing the sale that it was under contract with ICE, which DHS oversees, to manage Prairie Correctional Facility. As such, we have rated this claim true.
It is unclear why ICE paid so much more than the previous asking price for the facility. The purchase occurred shortly before the Government Accountability Office, the nonpartisan "congressional watchdog" of the U.S. government, published a report on Sept. 24 saying ICE has "wasted" taxpayer funds "on unsuccessful detention initiatives and lacks important information about the long-term affordability of its investments" (Paragraph 2, Page 13). 
During an Oct. 30 press event, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent denied knowing anything about the overpayment for the Minnesota facility and said a question about it was a "waste of our time."
DHS emailed Snopes the same statement KARE 11 published on Nov. 2 (as an update to its Oct. 29 article), saying the department followed "the standard federal appraisal process." The statement reads, in full:
DHS acquired the Prairie Correctional Facility to strengthen America's ability to enforce its immigration laws and carry out the American people's mandate for mass deportations.
The 1,600-bed site gives ICE immediate capacity to detain and remove those who have no legal right to remain, protecting American communities and restoring the integrity of our borders without waiting years for new construction.
The purchase price was set through the standard federal appraisal process. Independent appraisers applied a replacement-cost method, current cost of equivalent secure space, adjusted for depreciation, land, and condition, including the security and fire upgrades required for ICE operations.
The $75 million figure was a preliminary, non-binding indication offered during earlier discussions with the Minnesota Department of Corrections. Those talks never advanced to formal appraisal or agreed scope. The number was not based on replacement-cost analysis and did not reflect the intervening rise in construction costs or federal operational standards. Minnesota's own estimate to replace Stillwater was roughly $1.3 billion.
(In the statement above, "Stillwater" appears to reference a Minnesota prison scheduled for closure in 2029. In May 2025, the Minnesota DOC said maintenance needs for that facility were estimated at $180 million, with full modernization or replacement of the prison estimated at $1.3 billion. It is a similar size to the vacant Prairie Correctional Facility.)
In an emailed statement to Snopes, CoreCivic echoed DHS' statement, saying the price was set by "an independent, state-certified appraisal firm engaged by the government."
Proof of sale and previous offer
In an Aug. 5 news release, CoreCivic announced that DHS purchased Prairie Correctional Facility in Minnesota for $495.6 million (emphasis ours): 
CoreCivic, Inc. (NYSE: CXW) (CoreCivic or the Company) announced today that it has completed the sales of its 1,600-bed Prairie Correctional Facility in Appleton, Minnesota and its 1,033-bed Midwest Regional Reception Center in Leavenworth, Kansas to the United States of America and its assigns, by and through the Department of Homeland Security for an aggregate gross sales price of $734.0 million, including $495.6 million for the Prairie Correctional Facility and $238.4 million for the Midwest Regional Reception Center.
In an email to Snopes, KARE 11 reporter Lagoe shared a link to the Aug. 4 purchase agreement between the U.S. government and CoreCivic on the official U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission website, which also confirms the sale price. Here is the relevant part of the agreement (emphasis theirs):
Dated as of August 4, 2026
PURCHASE AND SALE AGREEMENT
THIS PURCHASE AND SALE AGREEMENT (this "Agreement") is made as of the 4th day of August, 2026 (the "Effective Date") pursuant to 6 U.S.C. §§ 202, 251, and 551, and 8 U.S.C. §§ 1226 and 1231 by and between CoreCivic, Inc. a Maryland corporation (successor by name change to Corrections Corporation of America, a Maryland corporation) having an address of 5501 Virginia Way, Suite 110, Brentwood, Tennessee 37027 ("Seller"), and United States of America, by and through the Department of Homeland Security ("Buyer") (each of Buyer and Seller being a "Party" and collectively being the "Parties"), and is joined in for the limited purposes set forth herein by Chicago Title Insurance Company, as escrow agent (the "Escrow Agent").
[ ... ]
Purchase Price. The purchase price for the Property shall be $495,639,588.00 (the "Purchase Price") and shall be paid at the Closing (as defined in Section 12.1 below) by wire transfer or immediately available funds, subject to any prorations, adjustments, and credits made pursuant to the terms of this Agreement including without limitation Section 4 below.
Lagoe also shared a May 7, 2025, email between CoreCivic and the Minnesota DOC deputy commissioner, Safia Khan, which Lagoe said KARE 11 obtained through a public records request.
In that email, CoreCivic executive Kelly Durham said the company would sell Prairie Correctional Facility for "$75M inclusive of the upgrades CoreCivic has identified would be needed to re-activate the facility."
Minnesota DOC spokesperson, Shannon Loehrke, provided an attachment of the same email to Snopes, further confirming its legitimacy.
Loehrke also shared an Aug. 4 email from CoreCivic notifying the Minnesota DOC that the company had entered into "a 5-year contract last night with the federal government to reopen our Appleton facility." Federal spending records show the U.S. government awarded CoreCivic $18.6 million to run the prison for a year.
Response from Minnesota officials, reports of taxpayer waste, unproven fraud allegations
The New York Times reported that, according to Khan, "company officials seemed eager to get rid of the prison, at one point offering to sell it for a fraction of that price." 
Both KARE 11 and the Times said state officials declined to purchase the prison, citing a lack of funds, its remote location and staffing challenges. The two news outlets also reported that Minnesota officials said the facility's final sale price stunned them.
In reference to Prairie Correctional Facility, Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said in an Oct. 30 X post that he was calling on Congress to investigate ICE's "corrupt misuse of [the public's] tax dollars."
Even before KARE 11's story ran, U.S. Rep. Betty McCollum, a Minnesota Democrat, said in an Oct. 5 X post that DHS overpaid for the facility and questioned whether it was because "its owners are mega donors to Trump and Republicans."
According to nonprofit campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets, which aggregates Federal Election Commission data, individuals tied to CoreCivic donated $223,223 to the Republican National Committee in 2024.
CoreCivic's emailed statement to Snopes denied allegations of fraud:
To be clear, any allegation or implication of fraud, corruption or bribery related to this transaction is categorically false. The transaction followed the federal government's long-established appraisal process, conducted by independent appraisers the government engaged. These claims are not only unsupported — they are defamatory, and we take them seriously.
As of this writing, there is no evidence disputing CoreCivic's statement.

'Speedy trial is a fundamental right, can't tinker'
NEW DELHI: The Constitution will prevail over all other laws and regulations, 
Supreme Court
 said on Thursday and made it clear that in case of any contradiction or conflict between constitutional provisions and special laws like NDPS, UAPA and PMLA, it is the former which will triumph.
It reiterated that the right to speedy trial was a fundamental right and could not be violated under any law and could be the ground for bail.
The bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and A S Chandurkar faulted the apex court's earlier order, which held that under special statutes such as NDPS Act, an accused's right under Article 21 (speedy trial) must be exercised within the confines of Section 37 of the Act (stringent bail conditions) and cannot be invoked solely on the ground of prolonged delay to override Section 37.
The latest ruling comes amid sharp differences within the apex court over granting bail in PMLA, NDPS and UAPA cases on grounds of delay in trial, with the issue now before a larger bench.

CBI seeks Chandrakar’s custody to identify Chhattisgarh officials who received money
The CBI alleged that Chandrakar and associates secured the protection of police and administrative officials
Custodial interrogation of Saurabh Chandrakar, the alleged mastermind of the ₹6,000-crore Mahadev online betting syndicate, is crucial to identify police and administrative officials in Chhattisgarh who allegedly received huge amounts as money to allow the illegal operations to continue, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) told a special court.
The CBI alleged that Chandrakar, other promoters and associates of Mahadev Book secured the protection of police and administrative officials and influential politicians by regularly paying them.
The special court in Raipur on Wednesday granted the CBI eight days of custody of Chandrakar, who was extradited from Oman on November 1. It permitted the agency to take him to Delhi for interrogation.
Deep Dive
The CBI said custodial questioning was necessary to identify other masterminds and beneficiaries of the alleged fraud, trace the channels through which the proceeds were collected, layered and transferred outside India, and identify assets created from the illegal earnings.
It sought Chandrakar’s interrogation to identify public servants in Chhattisgarh, who allegedly received or were receiving illegal financial benefits in return for allowing the betting syndicate to operate.
The CBI said hawala operators were used to arrange and distribute the alleged protection money. Police officers and employees were also allegedly engaged to channel these payments to police and administrative officials.
Investigations have indicated that Chandrakar, Ravi Uppal and their associates promoted the Mahadev Book app and ran online betting operations through an extensive network of panel and branch operators, the agency said.
The promoters allegedly retained 70-80% of the illegal earnings, while the remaining amount was distributed among panel operators. The CBI claimed that Chandrakar and other promoters were generating around ₹450 crore every month through online betting since the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020.
The accused allegedly arranged hundreds of bank accounts using forged documents to facilitate transactions involving the proceeds of crime. These accounts were operated on a commission basis, while betting proceeds were transferred by panel operators to Chandrakar and other promoters in the UAE through multiple bank accounts, the agency alleged.
A substantial portion of the illegal earnings was also allegedly spent on advertising betting websites and organising lavish annual events attended by celebrities. The agency claimed that celebrities were paid from the proceeds generated through online betting.
The CBI alleged that police and administrative officials and influential political persons misused their positions to obtain illegal financial benefits and subsequently acquired assets from such proceeds.
Chandrakar and other promoters operated the Mahadev Book syndicate from Dubai, which they referred to as their head office. Several youths from Chhattisgarh were allegedly employed as managers, supervisors and other staff to run the betting operations, the agency said.
According to the CBI, Chandrakar left India in 2022 to evade the process of law and deliberately remained abroad without joining the investigation.
Following his extradition from Oman, he was brought to Raipur in a private aircraft on Tuesday evening for production before the trial court.
The Enforcement Directorate (ED) has been separately investigating the alleged money laundering in the case, which came to light during the previous Congress government led by Bhupesh Baghel in Chhattisgarh.
After the BJP government came to power, the state’s Economic Offences Wing (EOW) registered an FIR in March 2024 on the basis of an ED report, invoking charges of criminal conspiracy, cheating and provisions of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
Baghel, Mahadev app promoters Ravi Uppal, Saurabh Chandrakar, Shubham Soni and Anil Kumar Agrawal, along with 14 others, were named as accused in the EOW FIR. Baghel termed the case against him politically motivated.
In August 2024, the state government transferred cases related to the alleged betting scam registered at various police stations, along with an EOW case, to the CBI.
The ED has estimated the proceeds of crime in the alleged scam at around ₹6,000 crore and attached several properties in India and abroad linked to the syndicate.
Chandrakar and Uppal are from Bhilai in Chhattisgarh’s Durg district. Uppal was arrested in the UAE, and India is pursuing his extradition, officials said.

HT exclusive: Delhi Police informed MCD of unauthorised construction at Chawri Bazar building months ago
At least two people were killed in the Chawri Bazar building collapse on Thursday morning, officials said.
The Delhi Police had informed Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) officials about unauthorised construction at the three-storey building in Chawri Bazar that collapsed on Thursday nearly five months ago, but no action was taken by the civic body, officers aware of the matter said.
At least two people were killed and one was injured in the Chawri Bazar building collapse on Thursday morning, the latest in the series of such mishaps in the Capital. The number of people trapped under the debris was not immediately known. Track LIVE updates from Chawri Bazar building collapse rescue operation here
“After receiving complaints, we had informed MCD about unauthorised construction at 4547 Gali Sheesh Mahal, Chawri Bazar on June 15 but we are not aware of any action being taken,” a senior officer aware of the investigation told HT on condition of anonymity.
HT has reached out to MCD officials for a response. This report will be updated as and when the civic body responds.
The incident was reported at 9.50 am from Gali Sitara, near the Chawri Bazar Metro station, according to PTI news agency.
MCD suspends 2 engineers
Hours after the building collapsed, the MCD suspended assistant engineer (AE), Mohd Naeem, and junior engineer (JE) Aman Dalal on the orders of chief minister Rekha Gupta. The chief minister also ordered thorough inquiry into the incident and the registration of FIR against the contractor.
The chief minister's office (CMO) also said on X that strict directions have been issued to ensure best possible medical treatment for the injured and immediate ex-gratia assistance to the affected families.
Stringent action will be taken against those found responsible, in accordance with the law, the CMO X post stated.
A witness said about eight to ten labourers were working at the site when the building collapsed.
“…Work was underway on the lanter of the third floor. It collapsed at around 9:30 am, while approximately seven to eight labourers were working at the site,” said the witness, on condition of anonymity.
Chief minister Rekha Gupta visited the mishap site and said that overlooking safety and security measures during constructions poses a fatal risk to lives. She said, while speaking to media persons, that further investigation will reveal the exact cause of the collapse.
“Two bodies have been recovered so far, and one injured person has been rescued. The structure was a ground-plus-two-story building. Further investigation will reveal the exact cause of the collapse. In the meantime, the Municipal Corporation has suspended the concerned JE and AE, and an FIR has been registered against the contractor responsible for the construction. I must emphasise that the way people often overlook safety and security measures while constructing their homes poses a fatal risk to their own lives,” CM Gupta said.

Bengaluru-based biotechnology startup Venomics AI has raised $2.7 Mn (around ₹25.5 Cr) in a pre-seed funding round co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons, with participation from Operators Studio. The startup, spun out of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc), combines venom biology, AI and experimental screening to identify and develop venom-derived molecules into potential therapeutic leads. The fresh capital will be used to expand ‘Venom Atlas’, a molecular dataset of venom-derived compounds, and strengthen its AI and laboratory screening capabilities. The startup also plans to expand its team across venom biology, computational science and drug discovery, while supporting the validation and optimisation of promising molecules. Founded in 2026 by Kartik Sunagar and Vinay Prabhu, Venomics AI is working to tap the largely unexplored molecular diversity found in animal venoms to identify potential drug candidates. Animal venoms contain complex molecules that have evolved over millions of years to interact with specific biological targets. Some of these compounds have already inspired medicines. However, a large part of the molecular diversity across venomous species remains unexplored, presenting an opportunity for drug discovery. Venomics AI is building a platform that combines molecular sequencing and venom biology to map this diversity through its Venom Atlas. It then uses AI to prioritise promising molecular candidates and validates its predictions through functional laboratory screening. “Animal venoms represent one of nature’s richest yet least explored sources of potential medicines, and at Venomics AI, we are combining cutting-edge experimental science with artificial intelligence to unlock this extraordinary potential,” Sunagar said. India's bioeconomy is on track to reach $300 Bn by 2030, with the country's rapid emergence as a global biotechnology hub, based on IBEF data. Notably, the biotech sector in the country has been booming in recent years. The country is home to more than 11,000 biotech startups. Also, as part of the Budget 2027, finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a new ‘Biopharma SHAKTI’ scheme with an outlay of ₹10,000 Cr. Meanwhile, investor interest in this space has been gradually seeing an uptick, where earlier this year, Cellogen Therapeutics secured ₹20 Cr in funding from Kotak Alternate Asset Managers (Kotak Alts), while StrainX Bioworks has raised $13 Mn in a funding round led by Prime Venture Partners and Leo Capital.

Russell Brand is convicted of rape, and judge says he'll get a prison term
London — Russell Brand was convicted Thursday of rape and sexual assault charges involving four women on allegations dating back more than 20 years.
Judge Joel Bennathan said the British actor-comedian faces a "significant" prison term when he is sentenced Monday. Brand had been free, but the judge rejected a bail request because of the possibility he might flee and he was taken into custody.
"I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course," the judge said. "But the hardship has been caused by serious criminal offending by their father."
Brand was a ruthless, calculating, manipulative "sexual predator," prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said at trial.
Brand, 51, denied the charges and testified that he was obsessed with sex as a young man and once led a promiscuous life but had never forced anyone to do something against their will.
He was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault. He was acquitted of two rape counts and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand closed his eyes as the guilty verdict on the rape count was read but showed no emotion otherwise. When bail was denied, he gestured to his lawyers that he was OK and repeatedly said, "I'm good, I'm good, I'm good," before being taken away.
Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy of London's Metropolitan Police said the conviction was "a testament to the extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them."
"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women," he said. "As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."
The jury of eight men and four women in Southwark Crown Court deliberated more than eight hours over two days.
Known for risqué stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him to the Greek and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.
He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan he met backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.
The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.
Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party's annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men's bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.
The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.
Brand said in the witness box that the criminal case had a devastating impact on his life and family.
"My entire life has been consumed by these events, these allegations, these accusations," he said.
Brand's lawyers argued that the alleged victims were undermined by the fact that they only went to police years after the alleged assaults and following the broadcast of a 2023 documentary that contained anonymous allegations against Brand.
Brand testified that friends and colleagues had abandoned him.
His wife, Laura, who accompanied him to court, testified as a character witness in his defense, but no one with relevant evidence was willing to give evidence on his behalf, Brand said.

Members of the Sudanese diaspora and international human rights monitors have denounced the candidature of an Emirati diplomat for the top job at the UN, citing her denial of accusations that the United Arab Emirates is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.
The UAE nominated Lana Nusseibeh last week to replace the UN secretary general, António Guterres, as he finishes his second five-year term this year, upending a race that had become gridlocked.
Rights groups and others have for years documented evidence of UAE support for the RSF, which has been accused of atrocities during the course of its war against the Sudanese army, including an attack on the city of El Fasher in October 2025 that the UN said had “hallmarks of genocide”.
Nusseibeh, the UAE’s representative to the UN until 2024, has repeatedly reflected the UAE’s blanket denials of the accusations.
The Sudanese pro-democracy and women’s rights activist Hala al-Karib, the regional director of the Strategic Initiative for Women in the Horn of Africa, said Nusseibeh had “no track record of acting independently of her country’s role in Sudan” and that endorsement by the security council would amount “essentially [to] a denial of the genocidal acts committed in El Fasher by the RSF”.
There was also strong criticism of Nusseibeh’s candidature at a virtual briefing by the Avaaz human rights advocacy group on Tuesday.
Ibrahim Alduma, who grew up in El Fasher and is the co-founder of the human rights organisation Sudan Action Hub, told the briefing that success for Nusseibeh would result in people losing faith in the UN.
“If this candidate [succeeds], how would we tell people on the ground that the United Nations is not an obstruction of the [rights of] the people of Sudan?” said Alduma. “How could the people – not only in Sudan, but other victims of wars and international criminals – trust that the UN will achieve some kind of justice?”
Husam Mahjoub, a Sudanese advocate and co-founder of independent media Sudan Bukra TV, said: “Electing [the UAE’s] senior diplomat as secretary general would hand leadership of (UN) institutions to that government’s chief defender, at the very moment Sudanese civilians most need the UN to hold powerful states accountable.”
Kenneth Roth, a former executive director of Human Rights Watch, told the briefing: “She has been asked about the UAE’s role in arming and supporting the RSF, and she just blatantly denies it without regard to the facts. That is not what we need as UN secretary-general.”
On Wednesday, Bruno Stagno Ugarte, the chief advocacy officer at Human Rights Watch, said Nusseibeh’s dismissal of UN reports documenting the UAE’s links to the RSF had “seriously undermined justice and accountability for the victims”.
In a statement on Tuesday Nusseibeh said that if she got the top UN job she would support the work of UN fact-finding missions for accountability and transitional justice over the war in Sudan, and described the RSF’s crimes as “atrocious”.
She added that she had taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government to be “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would entail, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.
To become the next UN security general, a candidate must secure a minimum of nine affirmative votes out of the 15 security council members, and avoid a veto from the US, the UK, China, France or Russia, its permanent members.
An informal security council poll earlier his month had placed the former Costa Rican vice-president Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race. But she and all other candidates received two or more opposing votes from the permanent council members. The next straw poll could take place as soon as Friday, but the format and exact timing are still being negotiated by the diplomats.
At Tuesday’s briefing, Roth said: “It’s fair to say the RSF would not have been able to be nearly as successful militarily as it was and has been without that support from the UAE. And with that support, it didn’t just fight the Sudan armed forces. This wasn’t just a civil war. It committed mass atrocities.”
He added: “It amazes me that she’s being put forward. This is a completely unsuitable candidate.”
Kate Ferguson, co-founder and co-executive director of Protection Approaches, a charity working to prevent identity-based violence, said at the briefing: “There is not, as far as I have seen, sufficient evidence that this candidate is independent from the state from which she comes. And we must not be naive nor hide behind the pretence of naivety.
“This is autocratic capture of our most significant multilateral institution.”
Additional reporting by Kaamil Ahmed

When Nisha Panwar,30, was diagnosed with lupus in December 2013, she felt relieved. Before the diagnosis, she says, several doctors had told her she had no disease and that it was “all in my head” and was referred to a psychiatrist.

She developed avascular necrosis of the right hip and underwent surgery in September 2025. Her recovery was slow, she became dependent on her mother for everyday activities and had to stop working. Recurring flare-ups continue to affect her mental health.

We reached out to the Army for comment, and a spokesperson responded: "“XVIII Airborne Corps conducts rigorous training exercises to ensure constant readiness for any national mission."
Images purportedly showing U.S. soldiers practicing digging mass battlefield graves circulated on social media in late October.
According to several posts, the purpose of the supposed grave-digging rehearsal was to prepare soldiers for large-scale temporary burial until bodies could be identified and returned home in the case of mass casualties as the U.S. war on Iran stretched on.
"DISTURBING: The U.S. Army is now training soldiers to dig MASS BATTLEFIELD GRAVES for American troops as the war continues," one Facebook post read (archived).
Both the image and the claim were real. The images were originally distributed (archived) on Oct. 22 by the Department of Defense's media distribution service.
It wasn't clear precisely what the exercise was in preparation for, though it appears that conclusions drawn about an imminent or specific threat originated on social media, not the Army's report. We reached out to the Army for comment and a spokesperson responded: "XVIII Airborne Corps conducts rigorous training exercises to ensure constant readiness for any national mission."
According to the photo credit, they were taken by Capt. Thomas McCarty on Oct. 21. The caption called the operation a "simulated temporary interment trench," meaning that soldiers were practicing digging 15-foot-wide trenches for temporary burial of bodies so that they could later be identified and relocated. The full caption read:
A U.S. Army D6 bulldozer, operated by horizontal construction engineers from the 20th Engineer Brigade, backfills a simulated temporary interment trench during Phase II of Operation Dragon Covenant near the St. Mere Eglise Drop Zone, Oct. 21, 2026. The test-of-concept exercise, executed by the 3rd Corps Sustainment Command, evaluated the structural impact of heavy earthmoving equipment on remains by placing simulated skeletal models and sealed water containers inside burial bags. Operators practiced casting dirt inward from a 15-foot-wide trench to verify that the gravity fall of displaced soil preserves remains intact for future forensic identification and repatriation, while refining spatial standards for future Army fatality management doctrine. (U.S. Army photo by Capt. Thomas McCarty)
McCarty later wrote a report on the training exercise that both the Defense Department and the Army website published. (The article on the Army website appeared to no longer be available, as of this writing.)
According to McCarty, the exercise was "an operational reality the U.S. Army has not executed at scale since the Korean War."
The report detailed how in a 24-hour period of continuous operations, a crew could bury up to 2,400 bodies.
"Backfilling without desecrating the remains is where the real skill lies," one engineering officer reportedly said.

WELLINGTON – New Zealand’s party leaders made final appeals to voters on Thursday, three days before a general election that polls show is too close to call as discontent around an ailing economy continues to swell.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told reporters while campaigning in Hawke’s Bay that the election would likely go down to the wire.
“The message is pretty simple — it’s going to be tight and close,” he told reporters, “we want to encourage everybody to get out and party vote National,” urging voters to give National another three years to “complete the job.”
Polls released this week showed no clear majority for either bloc of parties, with the centrist Opportunity Party positioned as a potential kingmaker. Political commentators expect it could take weeks for New Zealand to form a government with support growing for smaller parties as voters lose confidence in the two largest ones.
Opposition leader Chris Hipkins said Labour hoped to form a Labour-led government before Christmas.
“The best way to ensure there is a change in government, and most New Zealanders are indicating to us they want a change in government, is to give your party vote to Labour so we are the biggest party,” he said.
Early voting began on Oct. 26 and, by Tuesday, 1,250,057 votes had been cast, compared with 1,007,928 at the same point in 2023, according to Electoral Commission data.
The election is largely a verdict on the government’s handling of the economy. Inflation has eased from earlier peaks, but petrol and other everyday costs have renewed pressure on households.
An Ipsos survey published this week found inflation and the cost of living remained voters’ biggest concern. Healthcare and hospitals followed at 45%, while petrol prices and fuel rose to third place at 31%, ahead of the economy at 30% and unemployment at 19%.
New Zealand has emerged only slowly from a prolonged downturn, with growth subdued, household budgets strained and unemployment rising to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest level in 11 years.
“This was very much an election about the economy, so mostly cost of living,” said Mona Krewel, a senior political science lecturer at Victoria University of Wellington. “This is the one issue that unites all voters. No matter if people are young or old, it’s actually where they come together.”
She said Labour had run a strong campaign on the cost of living, while National and other center-right parties had focused more broadly on the economy.
Krewel said ACT and New Zealand First had sought to elevate immigration as a campaign issue but had struggled to dislodge economic concerns.
