In the Israeli legislative elections held in late October 2026, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and its allies secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, falling short of the 61-seat majority required to govern. The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, alongside other opposition factions, captured 48 seats. Notably, Arab-led parties made historic gains by winning 19 seats, elevating them to a potential “kingmaker” role. Following the vote, President Isaac Herzog formally accepted the results and opened a two-day consultation window with party leaders to determine who is best positioned to assemble a stable coalition.
In this context, a video (here, here & here) is being shared on social media claiming that Muslim MPs are performing Namaz together in the Israeli parliament. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Video of Muslim MPs performing Namaz together inside the Israeli parliament.
Fact: The video shows Jordanian MPs performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the Jordanian parliament in Amman on 03 November 2026. There are no reports of Muslim MPs performing namaz in the Israeli parliament. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
First, we searched for reports of any such act happening in the Israeli Knesset recently but couldn’t find any credible reports to support it. Moreover, the parliament announced that Israel’s newly elected Knesset will hold its inaugural session on 10 November 2026, during which lawmakers will be sworn in, and the speaker will be elected.
Next, a reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to the same visuals published by BBC News Arabic and Jordanian media outlets (here, here & here). These reports state that the footage shows members of parliament performing the Dhuhr (noon) prayer inside the House of Representatives of Jordan (the Jordanian Parliament) in Amman on 03 November 2026.
The prayer was reportedly led by MP Dr. Ahmad Al-Raqab right before a scheduled legislative session to elect members of the parliament’s permanent bureau. He can be seen leading the prayer in the extended video published by some media outlets.
Furthermore, the presence of Jordan’s national emblem in the viral video, along with matching interior visuals, conclusively proves that the footage is from the Jordanian parliament and not the Israeli parliament.
To sum it up, the video from Jordan’s parliament is being falsely shared with the claim that it shows Muslim MPs performing Namaz in the Israeli parliament.

I've been stuck on a tiny Pacific island for years and can't get a transit visa to fly home
- Published
When Ruchira Ranasingha left Sri Lanka almost a decade ago, she could never have imagined she would end up stranded on a tiny archipelago in the South Pacific.
The 50-year-old has now been stuck in the Cook Islands for three years. She tells the BBC she is desperate to go back to Sri Lanka and has even offered to go "handcuffed, bound and gagged".
Ranasingha had been hoping to settle in New Zealand.
After seeking asylum there, she says she followed an immigration adviser's recommendation to temporarily exit the country to apply for a work visa. But once in the Cook Islands, her application was rejected. And by leaving New Zealand, she had breached the terms of her existing asylum-linked visa.
Now New Zealand is refusing to issue her a transit visa that would allow her to fly home to Sri Lanka.
Australia is refusing too. The only other international destinations she can fly to from the Cook Islands - Tahiti and Hawaii - require her to give biometric information in New Zealand before any visa can be processed.
As a result, she has no feasible way of leaving.
"My son - my only child - is getting married in November and I really want to be there for his wedding. My mother is so worried about what has happened to me that she is constantly in and out of hospital," she says through tears.
"I will do anything they ask of me - I just want to go home."
Ranasingha left Sri Lanka in 2018 after being forced to close her small T-shirt factory due to a loss of business. Struggling to repay loans, she moved to Hong Kong to work as a domestic caregiver looking after elderly people and children.
Her brother tells BBC Sinhala she had come under immense financial pressure. Her husband was a drug addict who died about seven years ago, he adds.
In December 2022, Ranasingha headed to New Zealand, where she says she lived with a cousin on a two-month visit visa. As it came close to expiring, she says an immigration interpreter helped her apply for asylum on the grounds she was facing threats from lenders in Sri Lanka.
She was granted an asylum seeker "open work visa", enabling her to work for almost any employer for a year. She found a job at a restaurant, she says, which ultimately agreed to sponsor an employment visa, which she believed would give her longer-term stability.
But as asylum seekers generally cannot apply for other visas while their applications are processed in New Zealand, it was declined.
That's when she got in touch with Immigration & Secretarial Services, a firm she claims told her a fresh application for an employment visa could be made from overseas. Email correspondence the BBC has seen shows its manager, Sylviane Gallant, saying she would initiate the process as soon as Ranasingha had left the country.
So she booked a short stay in the Cook Islands while the application was made.
It turned out to be a disastrous decision.
She was again refused the employment visa. And by leaving New Zealand, she had violated the terms of her existing visa. New Zealand authorities made it clear they would not grant her any future visas.
Gallant claimed to make various interventions on her behalf, including writing to politicians including Chris Penk, New Zealand's then-immigration minister. But ultimately, Ranasingha says Gallant admitted the situation was her fault and told her "there was nothing more she could do".
"She told me I was better off going home. There was nothing holding me there so I agreed to go."
But when she turned up at the airport with an Air New Zealand ticket to Sri Lanka in hand, she was told she couldn't board the flight without a New Zealand transit visa.
Three applications for a New Zealand transit visa were rejected. Authorities said they weren't convinced she would leave New Zealand. Four applications for Australian transit visas were rejected too.
In one of its rejections, New Zealand suggested she explore other routes. But both the US state of Hawaii and the French Polynesian island of Tahiti told her she would need to provide biometric information before any visa could be processed - and that could only be done in person in New Zealand.
Her latest application to New Zealand, which included all the details of the alternative routes she'd been trying, as well as her son's upcoming wedding and mother's failing health, was also rejected.
"I have lost so much money on tickets. For almost four years I have been just applying for visa after visa with nothing working out," she says, breaking down.
On a collection of islands known for their sweeping sandy beaches and rugged volcanic peaks, just four hours from Auckland, Ranasingha has been an involuntary guest.
She's luckier than others in her position, she says, with her hotel letting her stay free of charge in its staff accommodation and friendly locals providing her with food and clothing.
One of the hotel directors even gave her a sewing machine, she says, enabling her to make a small income.
"My mother always tells me I must have done something good, for me to be in a place like this where people have been so kind to me," she tells the BBC.
But it does little to ease the sense of being trapped.
Ranasingha says the stress is impacting her health. "I am scared something is going to happen to me," she says.
"I don't know what her solution is, to be honest," says Auckland-based immigration law specialist Alastair McClymont.
She had received "terrible advice" which "certainly" could not have come from a genuine immigration lawyer, he says, pointing to an industry of "so-called immigration consultants" who charge people to lodge applications without fully understanding the risks involved. Ranasingha says she has parted with thousands of New Zealand dollars in fees to Immigration & Secretarial Services.
The BBC reached out to Gallant but did not receive a response.
McClymont suggests New Zealand authorities will not grant the transit visa because, as far as they are concerned, she has no intention of returning to Sri Lanka having made an asylum claim saying her life was in danger there.
New Zealand co-ordinates with its neighbour Australia which means it won't want to let her transit either, he says, and France and the US are likely to reach similar conclusions.
To leave, "she is going to have to transit through somewhere and no-one will want to take the risk."

Immigration New Zealand told the BBC it had received multiple transit visa applications from Ranasingha - all declined "as we were not satisfied she has a genuine intention to transit through New Zealand".
When asked why one couldn't be granted even when Ranasingha had offered to be handcuffed and escorted, a representative of the immigration minister's office said those measures do not prevent individuals from making an asylum claim.
Australia's interior ministry said it would not comment on individual cases. It said any non-citizens travelling to Australia "must satisfy the requirements of the Migration Act 1958 (the Act) and the Migration Regulations 1994".
Meanwhile, Ranasingha's family have been trying to see if the Sri Lankan government can help. Her brother says they have tried "every possible avenue... but so far we haven't been able to get anywhere on this".
Sri Lanka's foreign ministry told the BBC it was "taking all necessary steps to facilitate her return to Sri Lanka from the Cook Islands. Officials of the Sri Lankan High Commission in Wellington, New Zealand, as well as the relevant New Zealand authorities, are working closely with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on this matter."
But Ranasingha's brother is deeply worried.
"Her mental state is not good," her tells BBC Sinhala.
"One of the times we spoke, she told me that if they were not willing to get her back home alive, they might at least repatriate her body."

Refugee athlete to make history for second time at Youth Olympics
- Published
When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.
"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.
In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.
Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.
Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".
Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.
Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.
Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".
"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."
Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.
He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.
"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."
The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.
After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.
It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.
One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.
Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.
"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.
As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.
"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.
"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."
Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

Delivery of various services in government hospitals and health centres across Keralam are likely to get affected in the coming days as the job contracts of 1,495 temporary staff working under the National Health Mission (NHM) have been terminated from October 31.
According to sources, those who lost their jobs include doctors, nurses, pharmacists, accountants, physiotherapists, lab technicians, and the staff who coordinate the activities of Accredited Social Health Activists. The services of special newborn units in district hospitals and activities of ‘Ashadhara’ project, the digital and decentralised healthcare initiative launched by the government through the NHM to manage haemophilia and other rare genetic bleeding and coagulation disorders, may be hit. Functioning of urban health centres and labs and pharmacies in many hospitals and other healthcare institutions too may get affected.
Leaders of the Centre of Indian Trade Unions-affiliated NHM Employees Federation say that the highest number of the affected staff are in Ernakulam and Thrissur districts, 183 and 180, respectively. Ninety-nine people have lost their jobs in Kozhikode district alone.
Assembly elections
Meera Nimeesh, State general secretary of the federation, says that the contract staff are appointed for a one-year period from April to March. However, this year, the contract was extended till May, because of the model code of conduct for the Assembly elections. After the new government assumed office, their tenure was extended twice, till October 31. Ms. Nimeesh adds that though the staff had earlier undergone one round of performance appraisal in May, they were asked to do it again in October. Following this, their services were terminated.
Ms. Nimeesh claims that even those with close to 20 years of experience, who have consistently recorded good performance, found themselves jobless one fine morning. She alleges that the government’s action is politically motivated as those who don’t align themselves with the United Democratic Front government have been singled out and terminated.
In a statement, the federation says that the services provided by NHM staff—spanning areas such as immunisation, maternal and child care, communicable disease control, management of lifestyle diseases, palliative care, laboratory services, day-to-day operations of hospitals, and field-level health activities—constitute an integral part of the healthcare system. Meanwhile, it is learnt that the Health department has issued a notification for the appointment of new staff.

Sony Group raised its profit outlook after a string of entertainment hits propelled better-than-expected results in the September quarter.
The Tokyo-based company now expects ¥1.87 trillion ($11.8 billion) in operating income for the year through March, raising its guidance by 15% on Thursday. Its operating profit in the July-September period was ¥622.3 billion, comfortably beating the average analyst expectation. Revenue was ¥3.43 trillion, also higher than estimates.
The latest entry in one of Sony’s key franchises, “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” was a major highlight in the quarter alongside Marvel’s Wolverine for the PlayStation 5. Michael Jackson’s music catalog drew strong streaming demand, helped by the film about the pop star. They showed Sony’s strategic pivot toward a more asset-light and content-focused approach paying off at a time of high component costs hampering hardware makers.
“The PS5 is already in the late stage of its life cycle, so Sony is in the fortunate position of not having to push hardware sales at any cost,” said Hideki Yasuda of Toyo Research and Advice. “Today’s results clearly show the payoff from Sony’s aggressive investment in content over the past several years, across movies, games and music. When Sony was more hardware-driven, its earnings were much more volatile.”
Sony’s shares rose 7% in Tokyo on Thursday before company released its results.
The company’s strong slate of content across genres sets it up to better navigate the challenging consumer environment. Sony sold 2.6 million units of its PlayStation 5 console in the September period, likely limited by its supply more than demand — the upcoming debut of Grand Theft Auto VI this month has sparked a jump in sales in the U.S., especially for the most capable PS5 Pro.
Wolverine was the best-selling game in the U.S. in September and delivered Sony’s biggest launch-month dollar sales since Helldivers II in February 2024, according to market researcher Circana.
Spider-Man has grossed about $2.5 billion in ticket sales worldwide, making it the third-highest grossing movie of all time, according to Sony. And streaming of Michael Jackson’s music, co-owned by Sony, surged to roughly four times the usual level following the release of the biopic “Michael.”
Sony now expects better earnings from its closely watched games division, as well as its music and pictures groups. The company’s image sensing and solutions unit is also set to improve on its profit number, according to Sony, even with smartphone shipments sinking dramatically this year.

My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.
His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.
Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.
Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.
After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.
Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.
In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.
While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.
After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

What do Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, South Carolina senator-elect Annie Andrews, Ohio governor-elect Amy Acton, and North Carolina representative-elect Jamie Ager have in common, beyond their victories in this week’s midterm elections?
Each is either a doctor or a scientist. And each had the backing of the political action committee 314 Action Fund, which focuses on electing pro-science voices to public office.
“We really benefit by having those data-driven, fact-based decisionmakers actually in a position at the governing table,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, a chemist and former congressional candidate who founded 314 Action after losing her race in 2016. This cycle, the PAC spent above $30 million donating to and supporting various campaigns, including fundraising for specific races. It raised $3.6 million for pediatrician Andrews in the fight over what had been Lindsay Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina, for example, and another $3 million for physician Acton’s campaign in the hotly contested Ohio governor race, according to Naughton.
The organization’s success rate topped 80 percent this cycle for congressional candidates, with 14 of 17 of its candidates in the US House of Representatives winning their races and hundreds of successful down-ballot candidates. Nine of these races flipped seats from Republican to Democrat. Victorious congressional candidates who flipped their districts this year include an oncology nurse-practitioner, a mathematician, a microbiologist, a nuclear engineer, and an agricultural scientist. “It did turn out to be a health care election,” Naughton says.
Richard Frank, the director of the Brookings Institute’s Center on Health Policy, notes that health care workers and scientists have always been part of the makeup of Congress, but not to this degree. “What is unusual,” he says, “is just how many came in one wave.” He sees the spike in this type of candidate as a direct result of the hostility toward medical and technical expertise from the Trump administration. “Science has been under attack,” Frank says. “It’s not surprising that scientists have recognized that, and some of them went out and ran for Congress.”
The rise of the science candidate has several causes, according to historian Kristoffer Shields, who runs Rutgers University’s Eagleton Institute of Politics. “Some of it certainly is a reaction to what's been happening at the federal level, the defunding of a lot of laboratories and scientific exploration,” he says. But he also sees this as a legacy of the pandemic, when many health care workers started thinking about how politics impacts public health.
Earlier this year, El-Sayed emphasized to WIRED that his candidacy was focused on public health, noting that the cyclospora outbreak that sickened Americans over the summer likely stemmed from the Trump administration’s choices. “We DOGE’d our whole service that keeps the lettuce safe,” he said at the time, referencing the so-called Department of Government Efficiency directing mass layoffs at the Food and Drug Administration.
In 2024, 314 Action’s past acceptance of funding from groups with ties to the pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC came under scrutiny. The organization no longer accepts AIPAC funding and supported candidates like El-Sayed who were vocally critical of the Israeli government. Unlike some other political committees that aim to put doctors in office, like the American Medical Association’s PAC, 314 Action specifically focuses on electing Democratic health and science experts; it is forthright about its opposition to the Trump administration’s approach to public health.
That so many of these politicians are advocates for the importance of public health and scientific expertise suggests that the election was, in part, a rejection of current health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s MAHA movement, which promotes medical misinformation, including anti-vaccine sentiment. Many of the winning candidates with scientific and technical backgrounds have explicitly discussed how their concerns about the state of health care policy drove them to enter the race. “I am appalled seeing infectious diseases spreading through our communities that we had once declared eradicated,” microbiologist Jasmine Clark, the incoming representative from Georgia, told The Guardian earlier this year.
Clark was first supported by 314 Action when she ran for Georgia’s House of Representatives eight years ago. “She was in the first class of scientists that we helped elect in that 2018 cycle and now has made that move up to the federal level,” says Naughton.
Shields sees the straightforward communication style favored by doctors and scientists as another asset that has made them strong candidates. Some of this year’s winners are especially direct. In recent interviews, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews has referred to RFK Jr. as her “archnemesis” and promised to hold him accountable.
314 Action has also been clear that rebuking RFK Jr.’s agenda is a core part of its goals. In 2025, it launched its Guardians of Public Health initiative to recruit health care experts to run for public office. “We thought it was important to speak directly to doctors and people in public health, like nurses, to say that we have this program and we need you to step up to run, because we have a madman running the Health and Human Services cabinet,” Naughton says.
The push for pro-science public servants isn’t over; 314 Action is starting its next recruitment round later this month.

Cosmoserve Space has raised $6 Mn in a seed funding round led by Japan-based Rebright Partners. While Aranya Holdings and Naandi Ventures also participated in the round, existing investors AUM Ventures and Shakti VC doubled down on their erstwhile bet. The startup shared plans to utilise the fresh capital to support tech demonstrations, fuel two upcoming missions, as well enhance the operations of its recently unveiled Hyderabad facility. Cosmoserve has now raised over $9 Mn since inception last year. The startup has doubled its valuation since it raised pre-seed funding in September, founder Chiranjeevi Phanindra told Inc42. The exact valuation is yet to be discerned. For context, the startup is building tech to remove defunct satellites and orbital debris from space and reduce the collision risks for operational spacecraft in a cost effective manner. It plans on optimising costs by setting up features within its craft that will allow it to refuel in-orbit and remove multiple pieces of debris in a single mission. The startup made its first tech demonstration, Mission Embrace-1, aboard Skyroot Aerospace’s Vikram-1 rocket. The mission was designed to test the startup’s soft robotic capture system that removes space debris, but the system’s robotic petals failed to deploy as intended. Cosmoserve claims to have now identified and addressed potential issues with the thermal mechanism used to release the petals and the impact of low temperatures on the system, according to Phanindra. The startup is now gearing up for Embrace-2, an upgraded version of the mission to validate its upgraded robotic capture mechanism, which is expected to launch in the coming months. It is also planning a full-scale demonstration of its debris-removal capabilities, aiming to break a world record by approaching within 10 m of a dead satellite. Phanindra, who served close to 15 years with the ISRO before setting up Cosmoserve in June 2025, believes that the startup would be able to complete all tech demos by 2027 and start commercial operations by 2028. “We have several letters of intent from satellite constellation operators – one from the US, one from Europe and two from India. They have to abide by the regulation for removing the dead satellite from space … so we are aiming to get one paid customer before actual commercial operations begin,” he added. Cosmoserve’s Base 1 Alongside the funding announcement, Cosmoserve inaugurated its new space debris removal facility in Hyderabad named Base 1 today, in an event attended by union minister of state Dr Jitendra Singh and Telangana IT Minister D Sridhar Babu. Phanindra says that Base 1 is India’s first private and the world’s sixth facility equipped with space vision effects and microgravity simulation. In simpler terms, Base 1 can recreate conditions that spacecraft and equipment encounter in space, allowing companies to test how their tech will perform before an actual mission. This includes simulating how objects behave in microgravity (near-weightlessness) and how they appear or function under space-like visual conditions. This costs around ₹6 Cr to construct, per Phanindra. Base 1 houses infrastructure for designing, building and testing satellite servicing and space debris recovery missions. This includes an orbital rendezvous and capture lab, an ISO Class 8 clean room for satellite integration, a mission control centre and a microgravity simulation platform. The facility will also support the development of in-orbit satellite repair and refuelling technologies. Besides, the startup plans to use Base 1 to develop more critical technologies in-house in order to increase its share of local manufacturing from 60% and reduce dependence on imported components such as optics, avionics and space-grade electronics. “Primarily, the core technology we are building is a soft robotic capture system. We have a space robotics innovation lab where the R&D is happening. Then the next technology we are working on is a vision-based navigation system,” the founder told Inc42.

The Maharashtra government on Thursday (November 5, 2026) approved a one-time, one-year relaxation in the upper age limit for recruitment examinations, following recommendations by a high-level committee that also proposed increasing Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) Group C vacancies to over 16,000.
The seven-member committee, headed by Additional Chief Secretary V. Radha, was constituted on September 4 to review the State’s recruitment examination system and recommend measures to improve transparency and prevent irregularities. It submitted its interim report to the government on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
According to the report, around 12 lakh candidates have applied for the MPSC Group C Combined Preliminary Examination 2026, for which more than 5,000 vacancies have been advertised. With government departments submitting requisitions for over 11,000 additional posts, the committee has recommended including these vacancies through a corrigendum.
Under a Government Resolution issued on Thursday (November 5, 2026), the age relaxation will apply to recruitment advertisements issued from January 1, 2026, where no stage of the selection process has been completed, and to fresh advertisements issued until December 31, 2027.
The relaxation also covers recruitment examinations conducted by agencies other than the MPSC. The commission has been directed to provide a special opportunity for newly eligible candidates to apply. The existing upper age limits will apply to advertisements issued from January 1, 2028.
Welcoming the recommendations, Nitin Andhale, an MPSC student movement organiser, said they addressed two major demands raised by aspirants during discussions with the government.
“We welcome the government’s decision on the age relaxation and the move towards recruiting for 16,000 posts. It is a good beginning, but the government must also fulfil its promise to restore the objective examination pattern,” he said.
Mr. Andhale criticised the descriptive pattern used for the State Services main examination, arguing that it disadvantaged candidates from rural and economically weaker backgrounds. He claimed that coaching for descriptive examinations could cost up to ₹2 lakh, forcing aspirants to relocate to cities such as Pune and Mumbai.
“The descriptive pattern is for the rich, while the objective pattern is for poor students. A student from a farming family can prepare for an objective examination while staying in their village,” he said.
Describing the descriptive format as a barrier to equal opportunity, he added, “The descriptive pattern is a ‘Dronacharya’ pattern that will exploit students like ‘Ekalavya’.”
He also questioned the MPSC’s capacity to evaluate descriptive answer sheets, citing the rechecking of main examination papers. He alleged that the commission lacked adequate arrangements for evaluating such papers and said the government should reconsider continuing with the descriptive format.
Mr. Andhale also called for the 2025 State Services examination to be brought under the scope of the separate inquiry into alleged MPSC irregularities, claiming that it had been excluded despite concerns over the examination and its evaluation process.
Referring to the government’s earlier assurance to students, he warned of renewed protests if the objective examination pattern was not restored.
“If the government does not implement the objective pattern as promised when we called off our agitation, lakhs of students across Maharashtra will take to the streets,” he said.
Meanwhile, the committee has recommended retaining the existing examination pattern and syllabus for the Group C preliminary examination, which is separate from the State Services main examination pattern opposed by Mr. Andhale. It has also recommended announcing the main examination syllabus for newly included categories of posts at the earliest.
As a precautionary measure, the committee has recommended cancelling the question-paper preparation process undertaken so far and preparing fresh papers through a secure procedure. Other proposals include stringent safeguards for printing, storing and transporting question papers and Optical Mark Recognition (OMR) answer sheets, along with police deployment, CCTV surveillance, signal jammers and trained personnel at examination centres.
While the government has approved the age relaxation, the committee’s other recommendations, including the proposed increase in Group C vacancies, remain subject to further decisions.

Drone photo award winners: Far-out landscapes. Ship recycling. Rugs, rugs rugs!
It looks like a spacecraft that settled gently onto a golden beach.
Off the coast of Bangladesh, an enormous vessel lies stranded on the mudflats, its steel hull partially dismantled as workers mill around it. This unusual aerial view of a tanker, specially designed to transport liquified natural gas used for cooking, electricity and transport, won photographer George Steinmetz the top prize — overall winner of the 2026 Siena Drone Photo Awards.
Each year, the Siena Drone Photo Awards highlight bird's-eye views of our planet, revealing landscapes, livelihoods and human stories often invisible from the ground. Here, we've selected some of this year's winning and highly commended photographs, focusing on the countries of the Global South.
In an interview with NPR, Steinmetz says he's been long fascinated by Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry, where enormous vessels from around the globe, nearing the end of their working lives, are dismantled and their materials recovered for reuse. The photograph is titled "Shipbreaking on the mudflats, Bay of Bengal." Steinmetz sent up his drone north of Chattogram (Chittagong), along this 13-mile coastal strip, offering a stark glimpse into what this industry is like.
He was exploring the relationship between human populations and the environment for a book project and saw the industry as an extraordinary example of recycling on a vast scale.
Photographing it proved surprisingly difficult. The ship breaking industry has faced criticism from environmental organizations, human rights groups, labor unions and non-governmental organizations for its unchecked pollution, the leeching of chemicals into the sea and dangerous working conditions. Shipyard owners are wary of journalists and photographers. Local photographers initially warned Steinmetz that securing access might be nearly impossible.
Undeterred, he surveyed and photographed the entire coastline north of Chattogram with his drone, searching for a vessel that would make an especially striking photograph. He eventually settled on the liquid natural gas tanker. "The trick for me was to find the right ship, that was in a really interesting state of disassembly. And these tankers are very unusual boats. It just looked weird, like some kind of a spaceship. It takes workers a long time to break it down. And then they have to wait for the tide to be right so they can pull the pieces ashore. They have big winches and boats that they use to get the stuff ashore."
He was able to convince the owner of the tanker to allow him to photograph it. The timing of the drone photo was crucial. Steinmetz wanted to capture the vessel at low tide, when the surrounding mudflats were exposed and workers could be seen moving around its enormous hull. Their tiny figures would look like ants, giving viewers a sense of the ship's mammoth scale. He spent several days photographing the vessel, returning as the tides shifted and the workers continued to take the ship apart for scrap metal.
After graduating from Stanford with a degree in geophysics in 1979, Steinmetz had first dreamed of photographing landscapes from above while hitchhiking across Africa, often traveling on the roofs of trucks.
In 1996, National Geographic agreed to finance an aerial photography project around the Sahara, for which Steinmetz learned to fly a motorized paraglider. "It was like being in a flying lawn chair or [sitting on] the front of a spoon," he says. Drones have now completely transformed aerial photography, allowing photographers to capture the world from perspectives that were once difficult, expensive or impossible to achieve, Steinmetz says.
Today, armed with a drone rather than a paraglider, he continues to explore how a view from the sky can reveal stories that remain invisible from the ground.
Southern Turkey: Carpet Fields
Why would anyone spread hundreds of beautiful carpets across open fields, leaving them exposed to a blazing Mediterranean sun for weeks or even months?
In southern Türkiye, this is part of a traditional process that gives handmade rugs their immensely sought-after, softly faded colors. Under the intense sunlight, the vibrant reds, blues and other hues gradually mellow into glowing, muted tones.
For Ankara-based documentary photographer and lawyer Dilek Yurdakul, the drone was not simply a technical choice. It was an essential storytelling tool. "I wanted to create an image that first attracts the viewer through its beauty but then invites them to look deeper, to discover the people, traditions and cultural memory behind it," she says. The photograph won first place in the contest's People section.
Yurdakul traveled six hours in blistering heat from Ankara to the Döşemealtı district of Antalya to capture this spectacle. "The first sight was astonishing. The fields were far larger than I had imagined. Thousands of carpets and kilims in different colors, sizes and patterns stretched across an enormous landscape," she says. From above, the carpets resemble a giant patchwork quilt, almost as if melded together, but her photograph captures the shadows between these slices of color.
The aerial perspective allowed her to bring together several layers of the story in a single frame, she says: the artistic richness of Anatolian craftsmanship, the scale of the landscape and the human labor that connects them.
"For me, this was a visual metaphor for the invisibility of labor. In many societies, the people whose work sustains everyday life remain largely unseen and unrecognized."
East Java, Indonesia: Tumpak Sewu's Majestic Waterfall
In this photo, highly commended in the Nature category, an imposing horseshoe-shaped waterfall spills over the cliffs of East Java, Indonesia, at sunrise. Boston-based, French-British drone photographer Colas Decloitre had hoped to capture the interesting shape of the waterfall with Mount Semeru rising behind it. What he hadn't anticipated was catching the active volcano behind the waterfall, glowing red and writhed with ash, in the middle of an eruption.
"The only way to get the right alignment of the waterfall and the volcano is with a drone, as you can only be on the side of the waterfall yourself," he says. Using his drone, he could position the waterfall against the volcano, revealing an intriguing landscape that could only be viewed from the air.
Argentine Puna: The Last Ember
It looks like the glowing eye of a fiery monster.
It's actually a volcanic cone, the pile of rock, ash and hardened lava that builds up around the mouth of the volcano over time.
The Last Ember, by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi, is an example of how a drone photo has the power to transform landscapes into a dream-like quality. It was a commended entry in the Nature category.
The photo was taken in the Argentine Puna, a vast, remote, high-altitude plateau in the Andes of northwestern Argentina: a landscape of volcanoes, ancient lava fields, salt flats and desert mountains. The cone's reddish color comes from iron-bearing minerals in the volcanic rock, while the surrounding dark terrain consists of lava that cooled and hardened long ago.
Exploring these volcanic landscapes requires careful planning, long journeys across remote terrain and constant attention to the conditions. "At high elevations, the thin air and rapidly changing weather can also make drone operations more demanding," Tabacchi says.
Her winning photo was a case of serendipity.
"I captured it during an exploratory flight, while studying the volcanic landscape and experimenting with different compositions," she says. "It wasn't even photographed during the golden hour [shortly after sunrise or before sunset] which is usually the time I prefer for landscape photography."
"When I reviewed my photographs, I found myself much more attracted to this earlier composition. There was something about the geometry of the lava field, the small red cone and the immense volcanic wilderness surrounding it that felt far more powerful to me than the warmer, more traditionally dramatic light of the other photograph."
It reminded Tabacchi of an important lesson she learned throughout her photographic career: Extraordinary landscapes don't always need extraordinary light to create a compelling image.
"Sometimes the strength of a photograph comes from the subject itself, its shapes, its geological history and the unexpected perspective from which we discover it," she says.
Lake Natron: What Lies Beneath
Another commended entry in the Nature category is Holly Kirkland's "What Lies Beneath."' At first glance, it looks like someone splashed ink over a canvas. But what seem like tiny specks of ink are actually lesser flamingos flying over Lake Natron, near the Tanzania–Kenya border. A former kindergarten teacher from Delaware, Kirkland is a self-taught photographer and plans to relocate to Kenya in the year ahead to build a larger body of aerial work.
This photo wasn't taken with a drone. (Siena does accept other aerial photography entries in the drone category). Kirkland took the shot on a Sony A1 Mark II with a 70-200mm f/2.8 lens while hovering over the landscape in a helicopter, strapped into her seat with the door flung open.
The photograph reflects the ecosystem of the Rift Valley soda lakes — highly alkaline environments where these birds thrive as the dominant species. They are called soda lakes because they contain exceptionally high concentrations of dissolved sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, the same chemical compounds found in household baking soda and washing soda.
These caustic waters would burn the skin of most other animals, but flamingos have evolved specific adaptations to turn this harsh landscape into a sanctuary. For instance, they have extra leathery, scaly skin on their legs to withstand chemical burns and specialized salt glands in their nasal cavity to filter out the excessive salt. It's an important breeding ground for these birds, Kirkland says, with an unusual landscape, like an entirely different world, with "painterly looking plumes of sediment under the surface of the lake."
"I've never seen anything like it," she says.
"I think that when you're looking down, there's just so many different layers of beauty that you see from above that you could never see from the ground," she says.
Kazakhstan: Alien Land
Another highly commended photo in the Nature category by Italy-based photographer Isabella Tabacchi, the Alien Land depicts the layers and patterns of deposited sediments, tectonic movements and erosion over millions of years — natural geological formations in Mangystau, Kazakhstan.
"My fascination with Kazakhstan began in a rather unexpected way," says Tabacchi. "I was flying from Tokyo to Rome when our plane encountered considerable turbulence while crossing Kazakhstan. I remember becoming curious about the vast country beneath us. In my imagination, it seemed like a land of remote, mysterious places, still waiting to be explored."
In 2024, she traveled there for the first time. The formation featured in Alien Land, which she nicknamed Jellyfish (their branching patterns reminded her of a jellyfish swimming through water), was the result of extensive research rather than a chance encounter.
"I spent countless hours studying satellite imagery, searching for unusual geological shapes and patterns in the Mangystau desert," she says. "Together with my guide and best friend Sav, I then explored the region in a Toyota Land Cruiser 4x4, trying to locate these formations on the ground. It was an extraordinary experience, turning shapes I'd discovered on a screen into real landscapes that I could finally photograph."
Mangystau is one of the strangest, wildest, and most mysterious places Tabacchi has ever visited. "There's something about its immense, almost empty landscapes that makes me feel completely isolated from the rest of the world, as though I'm standing at the edge of infinity," she says. "It's a feeling I find difficult to experience anywhere else: a mixture of solitude, freedom and wonder."
Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh: Rohingya Life Between Aid and Uncertainty
More than 1 million Rohingya refugees currently live in Bangladesh, primarily concentrated in congested camps around Cox's Bazar. Shahedul Islam Sadik, a student at the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Rajshahi in Bangladesh, says he has always wanted to tell their stories.
His drone shot of the settlements was commended in the Urban category . "I wanted to document how a humanitarian crisis had reshaped not only the lives of displaced people, but also [show] the natural and geographical landscape of their place of refuge. The photograph is therefore about more than population density; it also captures the visible consequences of a prolonged crisis," he says.
Sadik was struck by how densely populated and congested the settlements are. "What stayed with me most, however, was the sense that receiving assistance does not necessarily mean having the life one wants," he says. "Life in the settlements can feel confined, without the freedom they once had in their homeland."
He wanted viewers to notice not only the lack of physical space but also what it represents in the refugees' lives. "For me, the drone photograph captures more than overcrowding; it reflects a lack of personal space, freedom and room to breathe, both literally and figuratively," he says.
Bangladesh: Ferry boats, Dhaka
A burst of color and celebration fills the waterways of Dhaka, Bangladesh, as thousands of people make their way home for Eid, one of the most important festivals in the Islamic calendar.
Every year, the holiday triggers a massive exodus from the capital, as migrant workers and other residents travel to their hometowns to reunite with family. Ferries, packed with passengers and their belongings, become a vital means of transport.
For photographer George Steinmetz, the scene offered a striking contrast to his photograph of Bangladesh's shipbreaking industry. This photo was commended in the Urban category. From above, the crowded boats, their brightly colored decks and passengers' festive clothing create a vibrant patchwork against the river.
"I've never seen a ferry terminal like that," he says. Dhaka's Sadarghat Launch Terminal is widely recognized as one of the largest and busiest river ports in the world, frequented by 50,000 people every day.
"It's such a joyous scene," he says. "They have shopping bags full of gifts of food to bring to their families. When it's packed with people, I knew would be really epic. And again, it's like they look like ants."
Steinmetz captured the scene using a drone launched from the rooftop of a building overlooking the waterfront. But he almost missed the opportunity. The skies were overcast, and rain began falling shortly after his drone made the photograph. Had the rain started any earlier, he might have been unable to fly his drone.
For Steinmetz, drones offer the freedom to explore a scene from different angles, searching for the perfect composition rather than settling for the first striking view.
"I don't just want to get a picture. I want to get the best possible picture," he says.

Shari Rosenblum is departing As SVP and Head of Publicity for Disney Television Studios’ 20th Television and 20th TV Animation.
The veteran entertainment publicity and communications executive is leaving after opting for the voluntary early retirement offer that was extended by Disney to qualifying longtime employees two months ago. She is expected to take a little time off before deciding what to do next.
Rosenblum has spent more than 25 years at the company — first at 20th Century Fox and then Disney following the Fox acquisition — which translates into a 25-year service Tinker Bell statue.
For the past two decades, Rosenblum has been at 20th Television and its predecessor 20th Century Fox Television, rising to SVP in 2017 and taking over the studio’s publicity team in 2022.
Watch on Deadline
During her tenure, she has led hundreds of studio-side publicity campaigns on shows for Disney’s Disney+, Hulu, ABC, FX and Nat Geo as well as third-party platforms. She has worked on such popular series from top showrunners as Liz Meriwether’s Furious, The Dropout and New Girl; Steve Levitan and Christopher Lloyd’s Modern Family; Howard Gordon’s Homeland and The Beast in Me; Jonathan Steinberg, Dan Shotz and Craig Silverstein’s Percy Jackson and The Olympians as well as multiple The Muppets projects; Family Guy and The Simpsons and both iterations of Arrested Development.
Known for her strong relationships with talent and press, Rosenblum has stood out with her professionalism, always available and willing to handle sensitive stories not all PR executives would take on, something that has earned her respect among peers and journalists.
Her current boss Candice Ashton, EVP, Publicity, Disney Entertainment Television, touched on that in her note to staff about Rosenblum’s departure.
“Shari has led PR for Disney Television Studios’ 20th Television and 20th Television Animation with equal parts brilliance and grace,” Ashton said. “Few people have shaped the voice and reputation of our studio the way she has. Shari is a consummate pro, and an advocate and champion for so many of our teams and creative partners. She has also been a wonderful partner through every curveball along the way, and we’ve shared many laughs together that I will miss very much.”
Rosenblum started at 20th Century Fox 26 years ago working in consumer products and home entertainment before being recruited by then co-heads of 20th Century Fox Television Dana Walden and Gary Newman. Early into her tenure at the studio she also worked in talent relations, events and awards strategy.
“I’m moving on from my Disney-Fox career with nothing but extreme gratitude,” Rosenblum said. “I’m grateful to Dana and Gary for taking a chance on an ambitious young publicist over two decades ago, and to the many mentors and champions I’ve had along the way, including Shannon Ryan and Candice Ashton. It’s been a privilege to tell stories for our industry’s top storytellers, especially during this last stretch, with Karey Burke and the incredible executives at 20th TV. I feel beyond fortunate to have worked alongside the most talented and brilliant minds in our industry, and have a deep appreciation for the business of television, the people in it, the shows they make, and the journalists who report on it all.”
Rosenblum, who has mentored a slew of publicists that had started their careers as her assistants, was a member of the Local 600 International Cinematographers & Publicists Guild from 2005-2022 and was a recipient of the Maxwell Weinberg Showmanship Award for Television for her work on Homeland.

U.S. First Lady Melania Trump called for a “more enduring” ceasefire in Ukraine as she hosted a rare meeting between officials from the war-torn country and its invader Russia at the White House on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
The unprecedented meeting hoped to build on a localised six-day truce in the starvation-hit Ukrainian city of Oleshky that U.S. President Donald Trump’s wife had announced last month.
“Now we must use the courage we brought to Oleshky to find common ground through a shared concern for the suffering of innocent people,” Ms. Melania Trump told reporters.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire.”
The Slovenian-born former model said she was sending the envoys back with personal letters to Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
She urged them to use the Oleshky ceasefire — the longest truce so far in the Russian invasion that began in February 2022 — as a “spark in a world of darkness.”
“The ceasefire in Oleshky would not be possible without President Putin and President Zelenskyy. Their cooperation establishes a meaningful precedent for advancing peace throughout the region,” she added.
The rare halt in fighting, which was respected by both sides, allowed roads to be demined and residents to depart for either Ukraine or Russia.
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev said he thanked Ms. Melania Trump on Mr. Putin’s behalf for her “distinguished humanitarian role” in brokering the truce in Oleshky and for work on reuniting children separated from their families by the war.
They include children allegedly abducted by Russia.
Behind-the-scenes diplomacy
The White House meeting also reunited Russia’s human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her counterpart from Kyiv, Dmytro Lubinets, who formed an unlikely bond during the Oleshky ceasefire.
The pair were on the ground in the devastated town, addressing the media together on efforts to evacuate residents and deliver aid, in one of the most substantial instances of cooperation between the warring countries.
The U.S. first lady’s efforts come ahead of trilateral talks next week in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war — the first between Russian, Ukraine and the United States since February.
The talks have revived hopes for ending the grinding war, although a recent rapprochement between Mr. Donald Trump and Mr. Putin has raised concerns the United States could turn its back on Kyiv.
Mr. Trump had promised to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours of taking office in January 2025 but his peace efforts have been intermittent, with the Iran war taking much of his attention this year.
Mr. Zelenskyy said he had a “very detailed, hour-and-a-half-long” conversation with U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks.
The Ukrainian president awarded Ms. Melania Trump a national honor for her role in brokering the Oleshky ceasefire, which Lubinets personally presented at the White House.
“I hereby decree that the Order of Princess Olga, First Class, be awarded to Melania Trump, First Lady of the United States of America,” a decree read on the Ukrainian presidential website.
The U.S. first lady stunned the world when she announced in October 2025 that she had established a secret channel of communication with Mr. Putin in a bid to reunite war-separated children.
She has since played a growing but still behind-the-scenes diplomatic role in the Ukraine conflict — even as her husband campaigns openly to win the Nobel Peace Prize despite his own failed efforts to end the war.

It added that strong growth supports the company’s premium valuation. Equirus also raised its target to ₹874 for December 2027 from ₹698 for September 2027, retaining its ‘Long’ rating. Nomura retained a ‘Buy’ rating with a target of ₹888, implying potential upside of 21.1% from ₹733.55. It highlighted operating leverage across India and international operations, with in-house manufacturing and rent leverage supporting domestic margins. Meanwhile, CLSA maintained an ‘Outperform’ rating with a ₹773 target. It said Q2 sales growth was in line with its estimate, while EBITDA exceeded consensus estimates by 3%. Manufacturing Supports Margin Outlook HSBC retained its ‘Buy’ rating with a ₹790 target, highlighting India same-store sales growth of around 21% and international constant-currency growth of 23%. Antonelli says 2027 preparation starts now
- Published
New world champion Kimi Antonelli says he is treating the final races of the season as the beginnings of his campaign to retain the title next year.
The Mercedes driver became the youngest champion in Formula 1 history, in only his second season, when he clinched the title in Mexico City last weekend.
Antonelli, 20, has his first race since tying up the title at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix this weekend.
"I'm actually very excited to be here," he said. "It's a good opportunity for me to, first of all, you know, try to finish the season on a top, but I also feel like that my 2027 preparation starts now.
"It's going to be important to finish the season well, strong, in order to have the confidence and also to be able to get the confidence ahead of 2027."
Antonelli visited the property of the family of the late Ayrton Senna on Tuesday and sat in one of the legendary three-time champion's Lotus cars from the 1980s.
He is wearing a new helmet design paying tribute to Senna at Interlagos this weekend.
Antonelli reflected on his achievement on media day at the track on Thursday.
"I would have liked a bit more time to just even digest what happened," he said. "I had such a crazy sequence of events in these days. I won the championship, then spent time with the Senna family, which was already an incredible event. So definitely, I would have liked a bit more time to just sit down and like reflect and realise what happened."
He said the idea of being world champion "still feels surreal".
Hamilton-Verstappen picture 'already framed'
One of his most treasured moments on Sunday in Mexico was when Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen hoisted him on to their shoulders on the podium after the race.
Antonelli said: "I already framed the picture and definitely will put it on the wall because it's such a moment. Who would have said it? I wouldn't have expected to celebrate my title in that way. So definitely when they picked me up was the cherry on top of the cake.
"I will always be thankful towards them for doing that because, first of all, to receive that from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is very special.
"And also even more special because it was real. It was something that they actually wanted to do.
"So it was a very special moment and definitely I hope I can see them again to thank them properly with a bit of calm because it was just very special."

Why has Caf abandoned plans to hold Afcon every four years?
- Published
After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.
The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.
The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.
Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.
Why was the planned change controversial?
Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.
On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.
The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".
In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.
Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.
"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.
"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."
- Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn 
  - Published21 hours ago
- Afcon to be held every four years from 2028 
  - Published20 December 2025
What were the benefits of the switch?
Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.
In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".
The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.
Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.
The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.
Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.
"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.
Why the U-turn on Afcon?
The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.
"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.
"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."
Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.
Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.
He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".
How does Fifa fit in?
Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.
That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.
Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.
Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.
"He came to Cape Verde to generate support, And, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.
"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.
"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].
"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."
- Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority' 
  - Published6 days ago
- Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president? 
  - Published6 August
Why is Afcon revenue so important?
Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.
Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.
For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.
"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.
"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."
What about upcoming Afcons?
The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.
Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.
The next Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it as has decided to stick with.
An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.
Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.
The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.
Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.
While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.
It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

Bob Dylan comes knockin' on pope's door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican
VATICAN CITY — Bob Dylan came knockin' on Pope Leo XIV' s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy.
The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, "Chronicles: Volume One."
Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, "Go Away You Bomb," in his 2026 book "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift."
Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an' man-handled."
Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L'Osservatore Romano.
Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music.
He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration of Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine" for the 1967 album John Wesley Harding.
Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head.
It wasn't Dylan's first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy.
Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like "Gotta Serve Somebody" and "Saved."
In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a "religious person" who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays.
Dylan met with Leo in between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song "Tryin' to Get to Heaven" that contains the lyric, "I've been all around the world, boys/Now I'm trying to get to heaven before they close the door."

Deadly outbreaks like the Ebola epidemic raging in the Democratic Republic of Congo show the urgent need to complete an international pandemic treaty, the World Health Organization chief said Monday.
Wealthy countries and developing nations remain at loggerheads over how an agreement, adopted last year as a framework to handle future Covid-like pandemics, will work in practice.
As the ninth meeting towards finalising the deal opened in Geneva Monday, WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called on countries to "finish the job".
Pointing to several recent deadly disease outbreaks, he stressed that completing a pandemic treaty was "about protecting people".
"A pathogen threat anywhere can become a threat everywhere, to people of every country," he said, according to a written version of his statement.
"The outbreak of hantavirus earlier this year, and the ongoing Ebola epidemic in DRC remind us of this threat."
He was referring to the hantavirus outbreak that killed three people on a cruise ship in April and the latest Ebola outbreak, declared in May, which has killed nearly 5,000 people out of more than 10,000 infected mostly in the DRC.
It was vital, Tedros said, that the world learn the overarching lesson of the Covid-19 pandemic: "no country can protect itself from pandemics by acting alone".
When countries agreed in May 2025 to a Pandemic Agreement, they left out the tricky issue of how the key mechanism would operate to get the deal over the line.
The agreement's Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system covers how to share access to pathogens with pandemic potential, as well as benefits derived from them such as vaccines, tests and treatments.
"PABS is the last remaining piece of our puzzle," Tedros said.
During the Covid pandemic, he highlighted that "the world developed vaccines in record time, but too many countries were left waiting while others secured far more than they needed".
"That inequity cost lives, prolonged the pandemic and increased the risk of new variants emerging."
Completing the final piece of the pandemic treaty, he insisted, was "the key that will unlock the door to a safer future".

A video (here, here & here) of two men being paraded down the street by police is circulating on social media, with claims that it shows two men named Shehbaz Hussain and Mohammad Taufiq being arrested and paraded for harassing girls outside a school in Uttar Pradesh. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Visuals of police parading two Muslim men, identified as Shehbaz Hussain and Mohammad Taufiq, for harassing girls outside a school in Uttar Pradesh
Fact: While the video does show Uttar Pradesh police parading two men for harassment, the accused are Hindus, not Muslims. The police officially identified the arrested individuals as Subhash Pal and Daksh Pal. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes extracted from the viral video led us to media reports (here, here & here) covering this incident. According to these reports, two youths, identified as Subhash Pal and Daksh Pal, were beaten and paraded through streets by police following their arrest over accusations of harassing girls in a local market.
The two were accused of eve-teasing and committing indecent acts against women and girls at the Bhagwa Chungi intersection in the Kotwali Nagar area of Pratapgarh district. The Mission Shakti team reportedly took them into custody, after which they were made to walk through the streets while being physically assaulted by police personnel.
An FIR was initially lodged against unidentified persons for passing lewd comments under Section 296 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). Pratapgarh police subsequently arrested the accused and revealed their identities as Subhash Pal, son of Dinesh Pal, and Daksh Pal, son of Shobhnath Gaderiya. This proves that the accused are Hindus and not Muslims, as claimed in the viral post.
To sum it up, the two men seen in the viral video being paraded for harassing girls in Uttar Pradesh are not Muslims.

(Bloomberg) -- Wisconsin reported its first measles death in more than three decades on Thursday, the latest state to suffer a fatality from a virus that was long eradicated in the US but recently surged back amid a wave of anti-vaccine sentiment.
The death occurred in an infant, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said in a statement. It is the third US measles death within the last week — matching the number of deaths in all of 2025. In the preceding 25 years, the US typically had no deaths.
Across the US, measles has been spreading at an increasing rate as vaccination uptake has declined. That’s eroded the herd immunity that protects people who cannot be vaccinated like infants and the immunocompromised. At least 45 states have reported infections for a total of 4,852 people, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. 
The highly contagious virus has been spreading in the southwestern part of Wisconsin and nine people have been hospitalized in connection with the outbreak, according to the health department.
“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Wisconsin State Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. 
With the US measles case count at its highest in decades, its long-held status as a measles eliminated country is under threat. An outside group of experts is scheduled to meet next week and review the data to determine whether the US has seen continued transmission of the disease for more than 12 months. 
This week, Pennsylvania confirmed a sixth death from measles and New York reported its first. Utah, South Carolina and Texas have also seen particularly bad flareups of measles over the last year.
Wisconsin said local healthcare providers and public health staff have delivered more than 42,000 doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine since August. No vaccine is perfect, but the MMR is 97% effective after two doses. 
One to three people out of 1,000 are likely to die from measles, according to the CDC. The respiratory infection can cause flu-like symptoms and a distinct red rash across the body. Complications include brain swelling, pneumonia and death. 
The CDC has confirmed only four of the deaths this year. After Pennsylvania reported its first fatalities, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. suggested the state’s governor Josh Shapiro may have fabricated them for political gain — sparking a verbal dispute. The CDC is working on a national measles death definition with an outside group of epidemiologists.
