Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Quick Answer
Concat is a free, open-source CapCut alternative with offline AI captions, voice cloning, background removal, 100+ effects, and 4K exports. It runs locally, needs no account, and adds no watermarks. Available across major platforms, it’s promising but still in beta, with some rough edges.
When you think of video editing, CapCut is a popular name that would pop up. It has made short-form editing painless. However, it has now started to put more of its tools behind a paywall, and a few of them need an internet connection to work.
If you are looking for a way out, you have probably already seen OpenReel, the browser-based open-source editor, or gone through our list of the best free video editing software. This time we have something different. Concat takes a different route. It is a free, open-source editor that runs on your own computer and is loaded with features like captions, voiceovers, and background removal built in.
Table of Contents
What is Concat?
Concat is a video editor that is currently in beta. The idea behind its development is easy to understand: It wants to give people stuff that CapCut offers but for free, like auto-captions, text-to-speech, background removal, keyframes, effects, titles, and 4K export. Everything Concat has on offer comes without strings attached. You don’t need to sign up, no watermark stamped on your exports, and no premium tier waiting around the corner.
The other big difference is where the work happens. Concat does everything locally, on your machine. It is built on a native Rust engine with a GPU compositor, and the AI models it uses (for captions, voices, and cutouts) are downloaded once from the settings and then run offline. This means the raw footage that you upload never gets uploaded anywhere.
CapCut is still a great editor, and nobody is pretending otherwise. When we compared it with Instagram Edits, we pointed out that CapCut has the richer feature set, but also that some of its tools need a connection and that its template and music ecosystem is tied closely to TikTok, which owns it. And if you are in India, you already know CapCut is banned here. So, you have to download the modded version or depend on some ad-filled alternatives.
That is the gap Concat is trying to fill. Not a “lite” version of a big editor, but a free one that keeps the stuff you reach for every day and keeps it on your own PC.
Concat features that matter
The feature list is long. But here are the parts that stand out.
Auto-captions that work offline
Captions are quite important nowadays, as content is reaching every part of the globe. But it is a chore every Reels and Shorts editor knows too well. Concat handles them using Whisper, a speech-recognition model that runs locally. You pick a model size (you can choose larger models, which are more accurate but require a stronger machine), and styled captions appear straight on your timeline. No upload, no waiting on a server, and it keeps working without internet.
Text-to-speech and voice cloning
Concat gives you free voices for narration, which is handy for tutorials or faceless channels. You can also clone a voice from just a few seconds of recording. That’s nice to edit a flubbed line without re-recording a whole take.
Background removal
You might have removed people or objects from your images. For videos, most of the editors ask you to pay. But Concat lets you edit out people or objects from a clip for free. If the automatic cutout misses a spot, you can paint the mask manually.
Keyframes with a curve editor
With keyframes, you can animate almost anything over time: position, scale, rotation, opacity, volume, and the settings of effects. There is a built-in curve editor too. You can use this to make a zoom feel smooth instead of mechanical, something that a paid video editor offers.
100 effects, filters and transitions
Concat comes with about 100 effects, filters, and transitions. They are rendered by your GPU and show up live in the preview. This way you can see what you are doing instead of waiting for an export to find out.
Fast cutting and a proper timeline
You get everything like split, trim, ripple delete, merge, freeze frame, and speed changes. If you like clips snapping together without gaps, you can switch on a magnetic timeline. Additionally, you can stack as many tracks as you want for overlays and picture-in-picture, keep several timelines inside a single project, and use blend modes like screen, add, and multiply. Crop and flip tools are there as well.
Titles with real styling
You can change fonts, add strokes and shadows, and drop in a background plate behind the words. If you don’t have any ideas, you can start from the already available presets.
One-switch audio cleanup
If your video has bad audio because of a faulty microphone or nearby noise, it can spoil a good video more than bad lighting does. Concat has a simple toggle for noise reduction, voice enhancement, and loudness leveling. You can also change voice effects to chipmunk, robot, and telephone.
Export and performance
Now, the best part is that with Concat, there is no limitation on export. It supports H.264, HEVC, and AV1, up to 4K at 60 frames per second with 10-bit colour.
Which platforms does Concat support?
Concat is versatile and supports multiple operating systems:
- Windows
- macOS
- Linux
- Android
- iPhone and iPad
Moreover, the editor is available in 26 languages. Downloading and setting up Concat is simple. Here’s what you need to do:
- Open the official download page, which picks the right build for your device. You can also grab any version from the GitHub Releases page.
- Install it like any other app on your device.
- On Windows, your system may warn you because the builds are not code-signed yet. Click More info, then Run anyway.
- On macOS, if the system refuses to open the app, the project suggests running xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Concat.app in Terminal.
- Open Settings and download the AI models you want (captions, voices, cutout). After that, they work offline.
Concat vs CapCut
| Feature | Concat | CapCut | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | Free, no subscription | Freemium | 
| Who is behind it | Open-source project (AGPL-3.0) | ByteDance | 
| Internet needed | Only to download AI models once | Some tools need a connection | 
| Templates and music | Limited | Large library tied to TikTok | 
A few things to keep in mind
Concat is promising and has all the features you would need from a video editor that is trying to be an alternative to CapCut. But don’t forget that it is young, and there are a few caveats that you should know about.
- It is a beta. The repo had over 200 open issues at the time of writing this article. So, you may come across some rough edges. We would advise you not to trust it with a client deadline until you have tested it on your own projects.
- Unsigned Windows builds and the macOS quarantine step can feel sketchy to newcomers. But it is safe, even though they are expected for now.
- You do not get a stock library to lean on. You will need your own assets.
- iPhone users have extra work because you have to sideload it, and sideloading is not for everyone.
Once you have the clarity, you should give Concat a try and let its output help you decide if you should keep using it or not. Let us know in the comments below which editor you are currently using.

Initiative to strengthen perinatal mental healthcare to be piloted in T.N.
As a part of the initiative, Village Health Nurses and medical officers are being trained to screen pregnant women for mental health problems, particularly depression, during the antenatal and postnatal periods and facilitate timely and appropriate care
Updated - November 03, 2026 01:10 pm IST - CHENNAI
Doctors from the Institute of Mental Health said that globally, studies indicate that the prevalence of antenatal depression ranges from 10% to 20%.
| Photo Credit: Getty Images
Tamil Nadu is preparing to pilot an initiative to strengthen perinatal mental healthcare by making screening available at the primary healthcare level. As a part of the initiative, Village Health Nurses (VHNs) and medical officers are being trained to screen pregnant women for mental health problems, particularly depression, during the antenatal and postnatal periods and facilitate timely and appropriate care.
The ‘Thai Manam’ project is set to be piloted, with VHNs and medical officers in four blocks of Villupuram district — Kanai, Koliyanur, Vallam, and Mugaiyur — who are undergoing training as part of a collaborative initiative involving the Institute of Mental Health (IMH), Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Epidemiology, and the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine.

A Gujarat municipal official has been suspended for six days after 12 streetlights on a road travelled by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on October 31 were found non-functional, while several others were flickering. Mahesh Vasava, the in-charge clerk of the lighting department at Dabhoi Municipality in Vadodara district, was suspended over alleged negligence in maintaining the streetlights, despite instructions from the civic body, according to the suspension order, The Indian Express reported. The order, issued by Dabhoi Municipality Chief Officer Viraj Shah on October 31, directed Vasava to appear before the “competent authority” after the suspension period and explain the alleged negligence. The action was taken under Section 48 of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963, which provides for the imposition of penalties “for good and sufficient reasons…upon any officer or servant of a municipality”. According to the suspension order, the municipality had assigned responsibilities to various departments in view of the movement of VIPs through the area. These included “cleanliness, control of stray cattle, and maintenance of streetlights”. As the clerk in charge of the lighting department, ensuring that the streetlights were functioning properly was among Vasava’s primary responsibilities, the order stated. However, the official allegedly failed to ensure that the required repairs were completed on time, despite instructions from the municipality. “Despite being instructed by this office, you failed to ensure that the necessary repairs were carried out in a timely manner. Therefore, you are being suspended under Section 48 of the Gujarat Municipalities Act, 1963,” the suspension letter stated. The order identified the affected stretch as the road from Sinor Crossroads, through the Bhogol area, up to Sarita Bridge. It stated that 12 streetlights along the route were “not working”, while some others were flickering. Prime Minister Modi, Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel and other dignitaries were scheduled to travel by helicopter to Vadodara airport after attending the National Unity Day celebrations at the Statue of Unity in Ekta Nagar on October 31. However, as dusk had fallen, Modi and the other dignitaries travelled approximately 90 km by road to Vadodara airport instead of taking a helicopter. The highway connecting Vadodara with the Statue of Unity passes outside Dabhoi, while several key roads in the town lead to it. The suspension order directed Vasava to appear before the competent authority on November 6 at 11 am for a personal hearing and submit an explanation for failing to discharge his assigned duties. It also referred to previous repeated complaints against the official. Sources told The Indian Express that the action is being viewed as a consequence of other ongoing inquiries into certain works undertaken by Vasava. The additional charge and responsibilities assigned to him have also been withdrawn. The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats.
This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton.
After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny.
In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7:30 p.m. ET on Wednesday, the "No" vote held a strong lead.
Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country:
Reid Hoffman, LinkedIn cofounder
Reid Hoffman, the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening.
"Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote.
"This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued.
Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024.
Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right.
Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla CEO
Elon Musk, who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development.
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post.
Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX.
In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state.
Lisa Su, AMD CEO
Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
"I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added.
Dara Khosrowshahi, Uber CEO
Dara Khosrowshahi, the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC.
"I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer."
"I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out."
Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election.
Keith Rabois, Khosla Ventures managing director
Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami."
It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing.
While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted.
Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman.
Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami.
Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital CEO
Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections.
In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown."
But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade."
Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds.
The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July.
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout.
"I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
Ahead of the midterms, some in tech expressed concern that Democratic wins would mean additional scrutiny on data centers, which have faced fierce opposition in communities across the US.
Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives
Dan Ives, a veteran Wall Street analyst and AI bull, said the midterms will put the brakes on the rapid construction of data centers.
In a post on X, he said the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years."
Ives added that while some investors will prefer a slower pace, others will view it as added risk.
"We estimate 10% of data centers will not happen now," he said.
Richard Branson, founder of the Virgin Group
Richard Branson, the billionaire founder of the Virgin Group, wrote in a post on LinkedIn that the results of the midterm election are not just "a decisive repudiation of Trump" but also an encouraging sign "about the limits of money in politics."
Branson wrote, "As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on — mostly Republican — campaigns this election cycle, in an attempt to buy influence and control over public policy."
Branson added that voters looked past the "hateful and false messages" fueled by the billions spent on funding candidates, voting based on the issues that mattered to them.
"I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform," he wrote.
Patrick Collison, Stripe CEO
Patrick Collison, the CEO of Stripe, said the results were a good sign for American democracy.
"It seems to me that democracy has on the whole worked very well in America over the last decade, and perhaps better than in any other major country in the West," Collison wrote on X Wednesday. "National outcomes have repeatedly been responsive to underlying voter preferences on meaningful questions, and significant changes in policy have ensued."
He also said he'd been reading "Democracy in America" by Alexis de Tocqueville and that "it's striking how much it still rhymes nearly two centuries later."
Collison, an Irish citizen who lives in California, was among the tech leaders spending big to oppose the proposed billionaire tax in California.

Whose sight matters? How gender shapes access to eye care in India
Across their lifespans, from childhood to old age, women face disadvantages in access to eye health and care. For many, treatment depends on how their health is prioritised by the men in their household. Late care, or lack of access can leave girls and women with preventable visual impairment and loss
From families questioning the value of sight-saving treatment for girls because of concerns about marriage and appearance, to older women who receive treatment later or have poorer access to effective care, gender shapes whose vision is prioritised. File photograph used for representational purposes only
| Photo Credit: The Hindu
“I remember a patient, a little girl with retinoblastoma,” says Rohit Khanna, a community ophthalmologist and network director from L.V. Prasad Eye Institute, Hyderabad. “We told the family that the child required surgery and that the eyeball would have to be removed for her to survive. We were immediately met with resistance. The father asked, what was the point of her living if she was going to be disfigured. They would not be able to get her married later.”
Retinoblastoma is a rare, fast-growing tumour of the eye and is often seen in early childhood. It is a type of cancer, and can lead to death if not treated.

Travel-focused SaaS company RateGain reported a 46.5% increase in its consolidated net profit to ₹74.7 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27) from ₹51 Cr a year ago. Operating revenue jumped 152.6% YoY to ₹745.4 Cr, reflecting the consolidation of travel marketing platform Sojern, which RateGain acquired for $250 Mn in November last year. Sequentially, net profit declined 21.3% from ₹94.9 Cr, while operating revenue fell 5% from ₹785 Cr. RateGain reported negative other income of ₹26.2 Lakh, taking its total income to ₹745.1 Cr. Total expenses rose about 158% YoY to ₹647.7 Cr. Adjusted for deferred deal consideration related to the Sojern acquisition, RateGain said its net profit rose 78% YoY to ₹90.8 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA more than tripled to ₹169.1 Cr. For H1 FY27, operating revenue increased 169.5% YoY to ₹1,530.4 Cr from ₹568 Cr. Reported EBITDA rose 214.2% to ₹324.5 Cr, while adjusted EBITDA increased 250.9% to ₹362.5 Cr. The company said its reported H1 EBITDA had already exceeded its full-year FY26 EBITDA. Sojern Integration And Debt The Sojern acquisition expanded RateGain’s travel marketing business, particularly its presence among destination marketing organisations (DMOs), hotels, and other travel businesses. To finance the acquisition, RateGain’s UK subsidiary secured a $125 Mn debt facility from HSBC and Citibank, backed by a corporate guarantee from the Indian parent. Including a repayment of $46.3 Mn today, the subsidiary has repaid $93.8 Mn, or 75%, of the original facility. Its outstanding debt now stands at $31.3 Mn. Alongside the expansion in revenue, RateGain said the Sojern integration helped broaden its customer base. It had 14,538 customers at the end of September, about 4.5X the 3,224 customers it had at the end of FY25. Its customers include hospitality companies, online travel agencies (OTAs), airlines, car rental companies, and DMOs. Marketing Drives Business Mix RateGain operates across three verticals: data as a service (DaaS), distribution, and marketing technology. Its offerings span competitive pricing and demand intelligence, hotel distribution, digital marketing, and guest engagement. Marketing technology now accounts for 80.2% of revenue, followed by DaaS at 13.2% and distribution at 6.6%. By customer industry, hospitality contributed 48.6% of H1 revenue, followed by DMOs at 30.9%, OTAs at 7.2%, airlines at 3.7%, and car rentals at 2.3%. North America accounted for 63.7% of H1 revenue, followed by Europe at 21.5%, Asia-Pacific at 12.3%, and other markets at 2.5%. The company’s client roster includes 33 of the world’s top 40 hotel chains, four of the top five airlines, and seven of the top 10 car rental companies. RateGain also highlighted its AI products. Chairman and MD Bhanu Chopra said shifting travel demand is increasing customers’ reliance on data and AI. He said RateGain’s priorities included adding customers, increasing their use of its platform, and extending AI into more of their daily operations. In H2 FY27, the company plans to take the combined RateGain and Sojern offering to more customers. RateGain reported a total pipeline of ₹660 Cr and new contract wins worth ₹277.7 Cr. The company’s employee headcount stood at 1,244 at the end of September, up 42.8% YoY. Shares of RateGain ended today’s trading session 3.3% higher at ₹819.50 apiece on the BSE.

Cleantech startup altM has raised $10.3 Mn (₹97.5 Cr) in a Series A funding round led by new investors Rainmatter and Mela Ventures. Existing investors Omnivore, Theia Ventures, Aureolis Ventures and Spectrum Impact also participated. The Bengaluru-based startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand manufacturing, build its sales pipeline and continue investing in research and development (R&D). A large chunk of the funds will go towards setting up a 1,000-tonne-per-year commercial manufacturing facility by 2028. "We have three large focus areas for the company today. In the short term, we want to start converting revenues and building our sales pipeline from the pilot plant. From a manufacturing perspective, a large chunk of our investment will go into building the next 1,000-tonne-per-year commercial plant," cofounder and CEO Apoorv Garg told Inc42. The startup will also continue developing alternative materials and biochemicals. It plans to expand its sales team following the funding round. "The major influx will be on sales," Garg added. Founded in 2022 by former Tesla executives Garg and Yugal Raj Jain, altM develops specialty chemicals and biomaterials from agricultural residue for industrial applications. Its platform converts lignocellulosic biomass, including sugarcane bagasse, rice straw and other agricultural residues, into materials for use in beauty and personal care, textiles, industrial chemicals, construction, packaging and consumer goods. The platform uses the major fractions of biomass, including cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin, to produce multiple products from a single feedstock, offering an alternative to fossil-derived raw materials. The latest round comes nearly three years after altM raised $3.5 Mn in a seed round in 2023. Since then, the startup has built an integrated R&D and pilot manufacturing facility in Bengaluru, bringing laboratory research, demonstration manufacturing and pilot production under one roof. It has expanded its laboratory footprint nearly 5X, commissioned a demonstration manufacturing facility and advanced six molecules to the demonstration stage, with three selected for pilot production. The first products advancing towards commercialisation include a lignin-derived SPF booster for suncare, a cellulose-based rheology modifier and bio-derived ferulic acid for cosmetics and personal care formulations. The startup is currently focused on the BPC segment, while its R&D pipeline spans construction, electronics, automotive, polymers and battery materials. Garg said altM has completed the installation of its 70-tonne-per-year pilot plant in Bengaluru's Electronic City and is preparing to begin commercial production. "We have been installing it since late 2025 and finally finished the installation in 2026. It's still in pre-production, and we're getting the right certifications and validations to take it to production this month," Garg said. The startup expects to begin fulfilling purchase orders in the current quarter, with its first product launches planned for the following quarter. It currently works with nearly 30 BPC customers at different stages of product development, testing and commercialisation. Around 16-18 of them are in testing and active validation, Garg said. altM's process involves breaking down plant matter into core polymers and upgrading these fractions into chemicals. Garg said the startup has filed six patents in India covering its deconstruction technology and processes for upgrading individual molecules. It is working on a seventh patent and plans to file patents in international markets as well. The startup has carried out more than 15,000 reactions at the laboratory stage and translated over 500 reactions to the demonstration stage. It has also reduced the time taken to develop new molecules from 12-15 months to under six months, Garg said. Looking ahead, altM aims to sell out the capacity of its existing pilot plant by the first quarter of FY28. Over the next five years, it plans to expand its manufacturing capacity to 10,000 tonnes per year, with the potential to generate 100-200 Mn in annual revenue, depending on the molecules produced.

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has de-notified and withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023) where medical colleges were liable to face penalty fines for violations of educational standards and infrastructure requirements at medical colleges.
Earlier reports in The Hindu stated NMC’s withdrawal of MSMER-2023 weakens accountability in medical education by removing provisions to fine individual faculty members and administrators up to ₹5 lakh for submitting false information. Although the Medical Assessment and Rating Board (MARB) can still penalise institutions up to ₹1 crore under separate regulations, institutional penalties may be less effective in deterring individual misconduct. Misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk.

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

After Democrats' 2026 U.S. midterm election victories, in which the party gained control of the House and Senate, people claimed a screenshot showed that late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina once tweeted, "If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed.......and we will deserve it."
Numerous posts and comments about the alleged tweet specifically referenced the news Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham's sister, lost her senatorial election to Democrat Annie Andrews. Darline Graham has served as interim senator in Lindsey Graham's seat since his death in July.
(@ddiamond via X)

This woman defied lethal cancer. Can mRNA vaccines make that possible for others?
Donna Gustafson is living a cancer patient's fantasy.
At 72, the retired accountant hikes, travels, lifts weights, and exchanges adoring glances with Ed, the husband she married 50 years ago. All these moments are happening while she shows zero evidence of the Stage II pancreatic cancer that was supposed to kill her years ago.
"I have had 100% quality of life; I am back to where I was prior," Gustafson says.
"She's better than that," her husband interjects. "She's sassier, and she's in the best shape of her life — there's no question about that."
Seven years ago, Gustafson became the world's first recipient of an mRNA vaccine designed to treat pancreatic cancer, a highly lethal disease diagnosed in about 70,000 Americans every year. There are few effective treatments for the disease, but Gustafson's was a personalized version, created using samples of her tumor, aiming to reprogram her immune cells — training them, essentially, to recognize distinctive mutant proteins on cancerous cells and kill them.
mRNA vaccines having a moment
It's been a big year for cancer vaccines using mRNA, especially after drugmakers Merck and Moderna released results last month from the first major successful trial of mRNA vaccines for skin cancer, showing a 42% reduction in recurrence and death over two years.
A combination of technologies using mRNA, genomics and AI, helped create these vaccines, which are also being tested on lung, kidney, bladder and brain cancers. But researchers don't yet understand why some trials have failed, while others show eye-popping results in the form of people like Gustafson.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Gustafson, who splits her time between New Jersey and Florida, says she wasn't scared to be first to test this concept against pancreatic cancer. She credits her three grown daughters for finding and getting her into the trial. "It was a no brainer," she says. "I knew that statistically, the odds of my survival were low, and I was very happy to be offered some type of hope."
Gustafson received nine doses of the vaccine, along with surgery and chemotherapy. She was part of a small clinical trial involving 16 pancreatic cancer patients. The vaccine worked on half of the patients, and seven of those eight are still alive today.
For patients on these vaccines, treatment is also an easier option. It does not compare to chemotherapy, which requires hours of infusion and comes with after-effects that were "barbaric" for his wife, Ed Gustafson says with a shudder.
By contrast: The shots felt like nothing, Donna Gustafson says. "I had no symptoms, no side effects — to the point where I was actually worried that maybe it was not helping."
But it was. Very swiftly.
Surgeon and scientist Vinod Balachandran ran the trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City. The vaccine used in his research is made in an expansive lab made up of hallways of freezers, desks, centrifuges and cytometers. Patients' responses to the treatment are measured in the lab. The oncologists and mathematicians who work there are dedicated to decoding pancreatic cancer, then reverse engineering the mRNA necessary to fight it.
A research analyst pulls up a graph on her computer, showing dozens of superimposed green lines — each representing the number of times an immune cell reproduces, Balachandran explains.
Looking at the graph representing Donna Gustafson's immune cell count, Balachandran notes how the lines shoot up, then remain high and flat — "a 10,000-fold increase" — reflecting how her immune system mass produced cancer-attacking cells and sustained it, for years beyond her last shot. "It just tells us that this response lasts," Balachandran says.
Balachandran says it was the strength and durability of such responses in half of the patients that, for him, blew open the possibility of mRNA vaccines. "Well, if you could generate such a strong immune response in the toughest of cancers, could this similarly develop cancer vaccines for a broad array of human cancers?," he says.
Promising future
This technology is now at an inflection point — with patients, doctors, researchers and investors. The National Cancer Institute, for example, is working on a partnership with private companies to fast-track research and development of more mRNA cancer vaccines. Balachandran and Sloan Kettering are part of that, with plans to expand production of personalized vaccines for patients on site.
Donna Gustafson says she and her husband have felt overwhelmingly lucky over the past seven years.
"I saw two more grandchildren be born and grow, many birthdays, holidays and Christmases with my family," she says.
With her husband, she's created and ticked off many items off her bucket list: skydiving, summiting, celebrating their 50th anniversary with the expectation of many more to come.
"We've done so many things — we probably have done so much more," Ed Gustafson says, before his wife picks up his sentence, "...if we had not had this experience."
"We live so much more for the day now," Ed Gustafson says, looking at his wife.

A wave of Democratic candidates across the country—and notably in Texas, a national data center hotspot and home to Elon Musk’s SpaceX—won their state and congressional races on Tuesday, including many candidates who voiced opposition to the data center industry. The results have sent some corners of the tech industry looking to the heavens for answers.
In recent hours, data center enthusiasts have proclaimed on social media that they’re still “bullish” on building data centers—just not necessarily in Texas, or even on Earth at all. Instead, they say, it’s time to focus on data centers in space.
Elon Musk—who sank more than $400 million of his fortune supporting Republican candidates who all went on to lose their midterms races—has been among those leading the charge. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk posted on X in the early hours of Wednesday, after it was clear that Democrats had taken the House and Senate.
Jordan Lasker—the man behind the X account "Crémieux,” which is a popular follow in the tech world, and known for posting race-based pseudoscience—also weighed in, saying, “Data centers in space are an incredible idea and anyone who doubted them didn't think enough about tonight's election results.”
Throughout the day, Musk employees, tech investors, AI researchers, venture capitalists, and industry fans joined the chorus of support for space-based data centers. Soham Mehta, a research fellow at the techno-optimist think tank Foundation for American Innovation, argued that underwater data centers should also be considered. (In June, China began operating what it claims is the world’s first underwater data center.)
Some companies are already trying to put compute in orbit. Among them are Google, which launched a satellite that it says contains "data center class TPU,” and SpaceX, which says it aims to deploy “thousands of AI satellites starting as soon as late 2027.” Blue Origin is also in the mix, having filed for a Federal Communications Commission permit to launch 50,000 satellites that will constitute an “orbital data center system.”
There are also a few startups aiming to build data centers in space, including Starcloud, which claims to have carried "the first NVIDIA H100 GPU into orbit" in November 2025.
Despite being technically possible, the realities of in-orbit data centers are difficult. Among other things, space-based data centers are much more expensive than land-based ones, can’t grow to hyperscale size, and are subject to the risks and whims of satellite launches.
When it comes to Texas data centers, the concerns of tech bros aren’t completely unfounded. Experts tell WIRED that the change in leadership could translate to some concrete changes in the industry—albeit with limits.
Although Democrats have control of the Texas House, Republicans still have control over the state’s senate. Robert Paterson, professor of land use and environmental planning at the University of Texas at Austin, tells WIRED that the split means that some immediate attempts at change “will probably be stymied a bit.”
Adrian Shelley, director of nonprofit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen’s Texas office, tells WIRED that the legislature would be a likely place to hash out high-impact policies like the reallocation of state agency resources. However, he adds that the governor could effect more immediate changes by issuing executive orders, or requesting the resignation of politically appointed officials in state agencies.
Shelley says that these oversight agencies—such as the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the Public Utility Commission, and the Texas Water Development Board—have the authority to charge fines for breaking state law, or in extreme cases, to revoke permits for projects like data centers. But Paterson notes that Texas developers have particularly strong “vested rights,” which protects the terms of their projects from the moment their permits are approved, even if construction hasn’t begun yet.
Another medium-term route to reshaping Texas's data center industry could be giving more power to its counties. Paterson noted that nearly half of the state’s data centers exist in unincorporated territory, which puts them outside the jurisdiction of city zoning laws.
Unlike other states, Paterson says, Texas counties have relatively limited enforcement abilities. Under the state's so-called Dillon's Rule, counties only have powers that are “specifically allotted to it by the state.” So while they have authority over things like access and egress to county roads, or construction on floodplains, he says they don't have the zoning authority that would help closely regulate projects like data centers.
Paterson says that the new attorney general could theoretically adjust the terms in the state’s biannual handbook, which establishes the limits of county authority. He also argues that even in a split legislature, especially since anti-data center sentiment crosses party lines, state lawmakers could propose a viable bill giving counties “limited zoning authority over data centers."
Shelley tells WIRED that since “data centers were a decisive factor in this blue wave,” the upcoming legislative season will be “very interesting.”
“I will say the data center industry hasn't shown a lot of interest in working with state lawmakers or local leaders,” Shelley says, “and I will be interested to see if that changes.”
If not, there’s always low-Earth orbit.

TL;DR: Rice prices have risen substantially over the past few months, with sharp increases in several southern states during the second half of 2026. Prices also vary widely across states. These increases have occurred alongside growth in national production, supported by higher yields and an expansion in cultivated area.
Context
Rice is a staple in meals across India, making changes in its price a concern for household budgets. Even a small increase in the price per kilogram can add to monthly food expenditure, particularly for families that depend on rice for their daily meals.
Recent increases have brought rice back into discussions on food inflation, alongside concerns about lower paddy acreage and the outlook for the coming harvest. According to the report of the Department of Consumer Affairs’, the all-India average wholesale price of rice reached ₹4,380.49 per quintal on 2 November 2026, up 16.9% from ₹3,747.44 a year earlier. It was also 6.7% higher than the previous month, indicating a recent acceleration in prices. The all-India average retail price of rice stood at ₹48.64 per kilogram on the same day.
These concerns come against a backdrop of growth in India’s rice production and yields. Examining production alongside wholesale and retail prices provides a broader view of how the rice market has evolved and how price trends differ across states.
Who compiles this data?
The Department of Consumer Affairs, under the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution, compiles daily retail and wholesale prices of essential commodities, including rice, through its Price Monitoring System. The production and yield figures used in this article come from the Ministry of Agriculture & Farmers Welfare’s Agricultural Statistics at a Glance.
Where can I download clean & structured data related to it?
Cleaned, structured, and ready-to-use datasets on daily prices of essential commodities at state-level can be downloaded from Dataful. Datasets on agriculture area, production, and yield of crops are also available on Dataful.
Key Insights
- Average reported retail rice prices have risen substantially over the past decade, although the extent of the increase differs across states.
- In Telangana, the average rose from ₹27 per kilogram in 2014 to ₹54.7 in 2025 and ₹56.2 during 2026, an increase of about 108% over this period. Data for 2026 covers the period from 1 January to 1 November. Andhra Pradesh recorded a similar rise, from ₹25.5 to ₹51.4 per kilogram, while Tamil Nadu’s average increased from ₹31.1 to ₹57.5, or about 85%.
- The increases were smaller in some other states. Bihar’s average retail price rose from ₹29.1 per kilogram in 2014 to ₹38 in 2026, while Himachal Pradesh’s increased from ₹30.5 to ₹39.1. Both recorded increases of around 30%.
- In 2026, monthly average retail prices show a clear shift in Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. Prices were relatively stable or declined during the early months, before increasing in the second half of the year.
- Karnataka recorded the sharpest increase from January to October among these states. Its monthly average rose from around ₹48 per kilogram to nearly ₹69, with the highest reported daily price reaching ₹74.4 on 31 October. Telangana’s prices initially declined before climbing from June onwards. Its daily average peaked at ₹79 per kilogram on 20 and 21 October.
- Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu also saw successive increases from the middle of the year, with both recording their highest daily prices of the period from January to October on 31 October. Across these four states, October monthly averages were substantially higher than a year earlier.
- The trend was less pronounced elsewhere. Assam and Mizoram recorded relatively stable monthly averages. Gujarat, meanwhile, saw prices rise gradually despite its average for the full January to October period remaining slightly below the corresponding 2025 level.
As of 31 October 2026, Karnataka reported the highest retail rice price among states and UTs with available data, at ₹74.4 per kilogram, followed by Telangana at ₹73.9 and Tamil Nadu at ₹68.9. Meghalaya reported the lowest price at ₹36.4, making Karnataka’s price more than twice as high.
- India’s rice output has increased by about 42%, from 105.48 million tonnes in 2014-15 to 150.18 million tonnes in 2024-25. The long-term price, as noted in this piece, therefore occurred alongside an expansion in production.
- Both higher yields and an expansion in cultivated area contributed to this production growth. Average yield increased by about 23% over the decade, while the area under rice cultivation expanded by 16%.
Why Does It Matter?
The longer-term growth in India’s rice output and rising consumer prices show why food availability and affordability need to be examined together. Higher production strengthens supply, but it does not automatically protect households from price increases. The sharp rise in several states during the second half of 2026 also shows how annual averages can conceal emerging pressures.
The recent increases appear linked to concerns about the coming harvest. CRISIL’s October assessment links rising rice prices to expectations of lower paddy production because of reduced acreage and weaker yields. Concerns about possible El Niño conditions add uncertainty to the outlook, particularly if rainfall and water availability are affected in subsequent growing seasons. The Agriculture Ministry has also reviewed possible El Niño conditions as part of its crop monitoring. These apprehensions could keep prices under pressure, although further increases are not inevitable. The eventual harvest, fresh market arrivals and availability of stocks will influence whether prices remain elevated or ease.
Key numbers
- Telangana’s average retail rice price (₹/kg): ₹27 → ₹56.2, 2014 → 2026 (+108%).
- Karnataka’s monthly average retail rice price (₹/kg): ₹48.1 → ₹68.9, January → October 2026 (+42.6%).
- Highest and lowest reported retail rice prices, 31 October 2026: Karnataka ₹74.4/kg; Meghalaya ₹36.4/kg.
- India’s rice production (million tonnes): 105.48 → 150.18, 2014-15 → 2024-25 (+42.4%).
- India’s rice yield (kg/hectare): 2,391 → 2,929, 2014-15 → 2024-25 (+22.5%).

Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
- Published
An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.
Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.
A spokesman for Nepal's Civil Aviation Authority, Gyanendra Bhul, said: "It appears the accident happened when two helicopters... attempted to land at the same spot."
In the video footage of the incident, the weather conditions look clear and no strong wind effects are visible. One helicopter appears to be making a more rapid descent than the other.
Helicopters are widely used for transport in the Himalayan nation due to its challenging terrain. But its rapidly changing weather conditions and high altitude often make aviation operations hazardous.
The village of Pheriche, located on the trekking route to the summit of the world's tallest mountain, Mount Everest, is just over 4,000m (13,120ft) above sea level.
Climbing expeditions to Everest and Ama Dablam mountain are currently under way in the region, as autumn is a popular climbing season.

With an eye on reducing dependence on imported critical minerals, the Union Cabinet has approved a scheme to set up domestic lithium and nickel processing facilities in the country. Called the Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing, the programme has been approved with a financial outlay of ₹2,814 Cr over a period of five years from FY27 to FY31. The outlay will pave the way for setting up four plants, two each for lithium and nickel processing. In a statement, the government said that the units will process lithium and nickel ores or intermediary products into high-purity compounds. Cobalt is also expected to be recovered as a by-product of nickel production. Under the scheme, beneficiaries will receive milestone-linked capital subsidies covering 30% of their eligible investment, subject to certain thresholds. For lithium processing, support will be capped at ₹500 Cr per beneficiary. However, each of the two proposed lithium plants should have a minimum capacity of 30 kilo-tonnes. For nickel processing, the maximum support will be ₹900 Cr per beneficiary, with each plant required to have a minimum capacity of 50 kilo-tonnes. The scheme focuses on processing, rather than mining alone. This strategy aims to retain more value within India by converting raw materials into compounds, which are required by downstream industries. The government said that the resulting capacity would support use cases across electric mobility, battery energy storage systems (BESS), electronics, defence and speciality steel. “The scheme aims to develop domestic processing capabilities in India to support value addition within the country, reduce import dependence, and develop (the) value chain… This will support critical sectors such as electric mobility, BESS, electronics, defence, speciality steel etc,” read an official statement. The government also said that the applicants will be selected through a two-stage process. The first stage will assess technical qualifications, followed by financial bidding. The beneficiaries will be selected based on the least-cost criterion, meaning qualified seeking the lowest capital expenditure support will be chosen. Afterwards, incentives will be disbursed in three tranches linked to specified milestones. With this, the government aims to tie payments to progress rather than providing the entire subsidy upfront. Reducing India’s Export Exposure Citing its rationale for approving the scheme, the government said that critical mineral processing remains concentrated in a small number of global locations. This, as per the Centre, has left supply chains exposed to geopolitical disruptions, price volatility and potential restrictions. As of now, India remains 100% import-dependent for raw and refined forms of many critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt and nickel. These minerals are critical components for India’s clean energy transition, electric vehicles, electronics, and advanced manufacturing sectors. As such, the scheme intends to strengthen domestic value chains, curb imports and support decarbonisation initiatives. But the road ahead will be tricky and will also require beneficiaries to secure raw materials and processing capabilities. This is the second such scheme approved by the Union Cabinet in the past year. In December 2025, the cabinet also cleared a ₹1,500 Cr incentive scheme to develop at least 270 kilotons of annual recycling capacity for critical minerals.

- The claim that a poll worker in Rogers, Minnesota, was photographed dressed in a novelty T-shirt intended to mock the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk is unproven.
- The rumor stemmed from social media posts sharing a photo on Election Day 2026 of a woman wearing a white tee imprinted with the phrase "Problem Solved" against a blood-spattered background.
- The photograph was authentic, meaning we found no evidence it was digitally manipulated or created using artificial intelligence, but neither was there evidence the poll worker wore it intentionally to mock Kirk's death. City and county officials said the worker claimed she wore the T-shirt as Halloween attire, with no political message intended, and city officials noted she was a Republican election judge.
- The "Problem Solved" T-shirt design has been available for purchase on Amazon since at least 2024, a year before Kirk was killed.
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces.
The allegation that an authentic snapshot of a Minnesota poll worker depicted her wearing a T-shirt that some observers interpreted as an offensive reference to the Sept. 10, 2025, murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk circulated on Election Day 2026.
People on social media shared what was alleged to be a candid photo of a woman working at an early polling station on Halloween in Rogers, Minnesota, wearing a novelty T-shirt imprinted with the phrase "Problem Solved" against a blood-spattered background.
(X user @lizcollin)
The photo was allegedly taken in the community room inside the Rogers Fire Department in Hennepin County, which was on Minnesota's list of early polling places. The image was authentic, but according to city officials, the poll worker intend for it to be taken not as a political statement but as a Halloween fashion statement.
The image itself showed no obvious signs of digital editing or use of generative artificial intelligence. Snopes put the image through Pangram, an AI-detection platform, which showed a high probability that it was not made with AI (it's worth noting that such platforms are not always reliable and ought not be used as the sole determinant of an image's authenticity).
(Pangram)
City officials posted a statement to Facebook on Nov. 3 that said:
The City has been made aware of attire worn by an election judge/volunteer on Halloween that some have taken as a political statement. We have spoken with the judge/volunteer in question who has assured us that there was absolutely no political message or intent behind the shirt, that it was worn as Halloween attire, and that they would never be supportive of the apparent message that others have tied to it. The election judge in question has given the City permission to note that they are a Republican judge pursuant to the requirement to maintain party balance per Minnesota Statute.
While the shirt in question did not meet the statutory definition regarding prohibitions against political party or campaign messaging at polling places per Minnesota Statute 211B.11, the City of Rogers takes the responsibility of maintaining a safe and inviting polling location very seriously. Had the perceived political connection of this shirt been known at the time, the election worker would have been asked to remove or cover up.
We reached out to Hennepin County's public relations office, Hennepin County election officials and the Rogers Fire Department for further comment.
The public relations office pointed Snopes to the city's statement and said the complaint had been forwarded to the city clerk for review and cited it as a possible violation of Minnesota Statutes 211B.11, which states:
A person must not:
(1) ask, solicit, or in any manner try to induce or persuade a voter to vote for or refrain from voting for a candidate or ballot question; or
(2) wear, exhibit, or distribute any item that displays:
(i) the name, likeness, logo, or slogan of a candidate who appears on the ballot;
(ii) the number, title, subject, slogan, or logo of a ballot question that appears on the ballot; or
(iii) the name, logo, or slogan of a political party represented by a candidate on the ballot.
According to the state, violating the statute is considered a petty misdemeanor, but as noted in the city's statement, that did not apply to this particular case.
The county told Snopes that "most workers at polling places in Hennepin County are election judges hired by the municipality" and stated "Hennepin County expects polling places to be welcoming and free from intimidation, harassment, or disruption for voters and election workers alike. Anyone with concerns about conduct at a polling place should bring them to the attention of the head election judge or city clerk's office."
The claim that the poll worker intentionally wore the shirt to mock Kirk's death remains unproven.
A similar claim was made in 2025 against teachers in an Arizona school who wore the same shirt and were accused of mocking Kirk, despite evidence the teachers had also worn the shirts the year prior, before Kirk was assassinated.
While it could be argued that the intention of the wearers in both cases was to mock Kirk, the T-shirt design in question predates the death of Charlie Kirk, and was not conceived as a reference to him or the manner of his death.
In fact, versions of the shirt have been available for purchase on Amazon since at least July 14, 2024, according to its product page, with reviews of the product dating as far back as Aug. 12, 2024, more than a year before Kirk's death.
A search for "problem solved bloody t-shirt" on Amazon returned a variety of results for sale. A look at the Amazon reviews for the shirt show some negative comments prior to Sept. 10, 2025, primarily related to the shirt's quality. It's only after that date that some reviews object to it as offensive.

Here is a thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular Indian epic melodrama from director Nitesh Tiwari, with music by Hans Zimmer and AR Rahman, based on the ancient classical poem about Rama, the avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu. It has often been adapted for live-action and animated movies in the past, though surely not on this scale, the current three-hour blockbuster being only the first half. (There are no musical numbers though.) The idea of aristocrats submitting stoically and yet playfully to exile in the forest has something Shakespearean about it, and if you are suffering from Homer-withdrawal after Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, a story about the noble Prince Rama finally vowing to wage war on a distant city where his wife has been abducted might just fit the bill.
Ranbir Kapoor plays the mythical Rama, a noble warrior and statesman who has been brought into being in the city state of Ayodhya as a bodily representative of Vishnu, and from the first his sense of destiny is overwhelming. But what exactly is that destiny? In broad terms, his fate is to face off with Ravana (Naveen “Yash” Kumar), king of far-off Lanka, a figure whose former slave status once triggered in him such a cosmically intense prayer for justice that Lord Brahma offered him the superpower of athletic strength and indifference to pain.
In Ayodhya, Rama marries the sweetly devoted Sita (Sai Pallavi), he enjoys an intense bond of comradeship with his brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey), and is the apple of his father’s eye; this is King Dasharatha (Arun Govil) who, careworn by affairs of state, is about cede the throne to Rama. But Rama’s stepmother Kaikeyi (Lara Dutta) furiously reminds Dasharatha that he promised the crown to Bharata (Adinath Kothare), the son they had together. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana are banished to the forest.
Over in Lanka, a toxic stew of plotting against Ravana is being stirred by his slippery, smirking brother-in-law Vidyutjihva (played by Bollywood veteran Vivek Oberoi), whom Ravana ruthlessly slays in single combat; this man’s widow Shurpanakha (Rakul Preet Singh), who is Ravana’s sister, is banished to the same forest where Rama is humbly eking out his civilian existence. She falls in love with Rama, using her witchy wiles to trick and bamboozle the happily married man, and this is to lead to a cataclysmic confrontation between Rama and Ravana.
With its giant canvas and some truly beautiful sunset skyscapes, this very enjoyable film has a little of Peter Jackson’s Lord of the Rings and even Disney’s The Lion King (the latter surely influenced the animal-kingdom tableaux). The bizarre flying machine piloted by Ravana (who does not have the ability to fly as such) has something engagingly Gilliamesque about it. As so often with Indian cinema, this movie reminds you of the forthright, unselfconscious storytelling energy that popular Hollywood films had in the 1950s and 60s, the era of sword-and-sandal. It’s a rather amazing adventure.

Cristiano Ronaldo announced on Thursday that he is retiring from international football. Here are five moments from his Portugal career, beginning with the match in which it started.
1. A debut against Kazakhstan
Date: 20 August 2003
Venue: Estadio Municipal de Chaves, Chaves, Portugal
The 18-year-old came on for Rui Costa at half-time in a friendly against Kazakhstan. Portugal won 1-0 through a Simao Sabrosa goal; Ronaldo’s first appearance came just days after his move to Manchester United.
2. Portugal wins Euro 2016
Date: 10 July 2016
Venue: Stade de France, Saint-Denis, France
Ronaldo’s final against host France lasted only 25 minutes before an injury forced him off. He watched from the touchline as Eder scored in extra time to give Portugal a 1-0 win and its first major international trophy.
3. A first Nations League title
Date: 9 June 2019
Venue: Estadio do Dragao, Porto, Portugal
Ronaldo captained Portugal against the Netherlands in the inaugural Nations League final. Gonçalo Guedes scored the only goal on the hour, adding a second international trophy to the one Portugal had won in France three years earlier.
4. The international goals record
Date: 1 September 2021
Venue: Estadio do Algarve, Faro-Loule, Portugal
With Portugal trailing the Republic of Ireland in a World Cup qualifier, Ronaldo scored twice late on to secure a 2-1 win. His first goal took him past Ali Daei’s record for goals in men’s international football; the second brought his Portugal tally to 111.
5. Portugal wins the Nations League second time
Date: 8 June 2025
Venue: Munich Football Arena (Allianz Arena), Munich, Germany
Ronaldo volleyed in a 61st-minute equaliser against Spain to make it 2-2. The score held through extra time, and Portugal won 5-3 on penalties to become the first country to claim two Nations League titles.
