Anthropic is using existing AI models to train future AI models at a dizzying pace. It's also stockpiling unreleased models.
That's according to a new report from third-party safety researchers embedded at the company's San Francisco headquarters released on Thursday — a report the researchers cautioned was heavily redacted at Anthropic's insistence.
"While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions," METR said in its report.
To craft their report, researchers from METR, a research group perhaps best known for its report on OpenAI's Hugging Face agent breach, said they received "unprecedented access" inside the company for nearly three months.
The group of six researchers interviewed employees, monitored internal Slack channels, and examined unreleased AI models using company hardware.
Here are four takeaways from their report.
Anthropic recently finished 3 new models it hasn't yet released
Anthropic workers are using better AI models than the rest of us.
In fact, METR's report says that over the last six months, the company has finished training three models that aren't yet available to the public.
METR found that Anthropic's internal-only models include one from 2022, as well as models finished this July, sometime in August or September, and sometime in September or October.
Those internal-only models are helping Anthropic improve its AI capabilities even faster, according to METR's estimates. The disclosure points to one of the AI industry's high-wire acts.
Anthropic and OpenAI make money by selling the most advanced AI models to the public. Keeping state-of-the-art models private, however, also gives the companies' product and research teams a competitive advantage.
Executives could keep models private for longer due to safety concerns. Anthropic and OpenAI's batches of highly capable internal models are part of why METR Ajeya Cotra told Business Insider earlier this year that she expects AI safety's "most serious incidents" to happen at the two companies.
Anthropic staff say their productivity is skyrocketing
Anthropic turned over internal Slack poll data showing that the AI giant's staffers are reporting major productivity gains.
METR wrote that the average self-reported increase was roughly 12x "for the most capable internal model" as of October. METR cautioned that it considers Slack polls weak evidence because they may not represent all Anthropic employees. The research group also cautioned that respondents may not have given their answers much thought.
When METR interviewed Anthropic researchers about their experiences, many spoke about how Claude has significantly boosted their work.
"Now only bottlenecked on ideas & compute, no longer bottlenecked on code," one researcher told METR, agreeing with the idea that Claude has at least doubled their productivity.
More striking is that METR didn't see "observed bottlenecks" that would prevent acceleration from increasing further over the next year.
"The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks," METR wrote.
Recursive self-improvement is fueling rapid development
Anthropic engineers are increasingly delegating more oversight and training responsibilities to other AI models, a risky process known as recursive self-improvement.
The method is paying off in terms of speed.
METR found that Anthropic has made "roughly two years of historical progress over the last year."
The researchers said they were told that research and development acceleration was accomplished "primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions."
"But there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon," METR said.
Jacob Coxon, the ex-Anthropic researcher who quit the company in September, pointed to recursive self-improvement as a factor that could cause AI systems to get out of hand.
"They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives," he said of OpenAI and Anthropic.

The world is reacting to the Democrats' midterm elections victory
One color dominates international headlines about the U.S. midterm election results. French newspaper Libération called the Democrats' win "une vague bleue," or blue wave, Britain's Daily Mail dubbed it a "historic blue tsunami," and The Times of India's headline ran "midterm blues for Trump."
Countries at war were also watching closely, with Ukrainian newspaper The Kyiv Independent's online headline hopeful: "Democrats seize control of Congress in blow to Trump, potential boost for Ukraine."
Russia had a different take. Rossiyskaya Gazeta, the state-run daily newspaper, suggested the results would in fact be a blow to Ukraine, which has firm support from the European Union. "Brussels, brace yourself. After the Republicans' defeat, Trump's wrath will fall on Europe," read the headline.
In the Middle East, the Tehran Times put the Republicans' resounding defeat down to President Trump's decision to attack Iran earlier this year.
"The Iran war comes home to hit Trump at the ballot box," its headline read. The war, which Trump promised would be over quickly, has dragged on, sent oil prices soaring, and affected many Americans' daily lives with the affordability crisis.
And in Israel, which just held its own seismic elections last week, headlines focused on what the Democrats' victory means for the U.S. support of the Jewish state and its war in Gaza.
The Times of Israel ran a headline focusing on Democrat, and Muslim, candidate Abdul El-Sayed's triumph in the Michigan Senate race, saying "Anti-Israel El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, pledges no money for 'apartheid, genocide.'" The headline in Israel's other daily Haaretz read: "Abdul El-Sayed Shows Opposition to Israel Is No Barrier to Winning Battleground States."
The Toronto Star in Canada, which is in the midst of a contentious trade war with the U.S., called the results a "rebuke" to Trump. Across the southern border in Mexico, El Universal newspaper's headline was similar, reading simply: "Setback for Trump."
Some foreign politicians celebrate, others silent
Many foreign leaders shied away from commenting directly on the results, as unlike a U.S. presidential election where they politely congratulate the winner, they see midterms as a domestic American issue.
However Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has an acrimonious relationship with Trump, was forthright on X.
"Yesterday, American society voted against policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites," Sánchez said.
In South Africa, where diplomatic relations with the U.S. are at an all-time low after Trump falsely accused the government of persecuting its white minority, President Cyril Ramaphosa said "The people of America have spoken."
Ramaphosa made the comments as he cast his own ballot in South Africa's municipal elections Wednesday, adding: "I do think that this is going to introduce a new era in world relations…. We're hoping that on a bilateral basis there will be a coming together of minds."
A senior Russia diplomat suggested the Democratic Party's return to power in both houses of Congress bode ill for U.S.-Russian relations. "The approach of the activist wing of the Democratic Party towards Russia is extremely negative. There's nothing new in that," said Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov in an interview with the state RIA-Novosti news service. Ryabkov also signaled there would be no grand shifts in Russian foreign policy as a result.
In Germany, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated Democrats on an "historic victory," adding that Berlin's commitment to cooperating with the administration in Washington remains unchanged. He stressed that Berlin will be reaching out to both Democrats and Republicans.
Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere said the results are a "powerful political signal about a change of course among American voters." Speaking to Reuters, Stoere said "voices are now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."
There was no immediate reaction from UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, but London Mayor Sadiq Khan, who Trump has frequently sparred with, said on X: "Congratulations to Democrats on a huge victory last night. With a focus on hope, unity and supporting families with the cost of living - their campaign was a true rejection of the damaging and divisive politics of Donald Trump."
A spokeswoman for China's foreign ministry told a daily press conference that the midterm elections "are an internal affair of the United States." She added that "China is willing to continue working with the U.S. to…strengthen communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive, strategically stable China-U.S. relationship based on the principles of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."
Japan's top government spokesman, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press conference that Japan's alliance with the U.S. remains essential for global peace and stability, regardless of the outcome of midterm elections.
The alliance "remains the cornerstone of Japan's foreign and security policy" and is crucial to "maximizing its national interests" amid an increasingly volatile and uncertain global situation," he added.
Middle East reacts
Iran's Parliament Speaker and top negotiator Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf commented on X: "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare."
For Israel, the US midterm results fall during a time of political uncertainty, amid coalition-building talks after Trump's ally, incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, lost his parliamentary majority in Oct. 27 Israeli elections. "In some ways Netanyahu lost two elections in the last week," said Israel-American analyst Mairav Zonstein.
Netanyahu's rivals seized on the midterm results. One Israeli opposition leader, Yair Golan, said the U.S. results reveal "just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans." Another, Yair Lapid, said the U.S. results "eliminate any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu."
Additional reporting by Charles Maynes in Moscow, Esme Nicholson in Berlin, Lauren Frayer in Tel Aviv, Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Istanbul, Anthony Kuhn in Seoul.

India’s Tanvi Patri settled for the silver medal in the women’s singles badminton final at the Youth Olympic Games 2026 in Dakar, on Thursday, after losing to China’s reigning World Junior champion Zhang Yi Xin.
The Indian shuttler took some time to settle in the opening game before reeling off seven consecutive points to move from 3-5 to 10-5. With her punch tosses creating plenty of openings and her net play under excellent control, she went on to take the first game in 25 minutes.
She started the second game with a 4-0 lead, but the drift from behind began to affect Tanvi’s control on her clears, and Zhang seized command after the mid-game interval to force a deciding game.
Zhang then asserted herself early in the decider with her trademark cross-court drops to build a 19-10 advantage. Tanvi battled back to cut the deficit to four at 19-15, but a cross-court smash error from the Indian gave her opponent five match points.
Tanvi saved all five and even created three chances to close out the gold medal. However, Zhang’s superior experience ultimately proved decisive.
Tanvi became the first Indian woman to win a badminton medal at the Youth Olympics, having defeated Japan’s Yuzuno Watanabe 21-14, 11-21, 21-19 in the semifinals.
Watanabe finished with the bronze medal.
Tanvi’s silver added to India’s previous Youth Olympics badminton medals won by H.S. Prannoy in 2010 and Lakshya Sen in 2018, both in men’s singles.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago, to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

Budget 2026: Poilievre, May express disappointment in Liberal government's plan for Canada's economy
The Latest
- The Liberal government's latest budget doubles down on Ottawa's strategy to strengthen the Canadian economy at home by attracting worldwide business investors and building major projects faster, reducing the nation's reliance on the United States.
- The government's second budget under Prime Minister Mark Carney details nearly $142 billion in new spending over five years.
- The budget sets aside a one-time top-up for the federal grocery and essentials benefit, one of several measures to help Canadians struggling to make ends meet.
- Sovereignty is also a key theme, with investments for security and Canadian arts and culture.
- Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and Green Leader Elizabeth May both criticized the budget, as did a representative for small businesses nationwide.
Updates
- November 5 Budget should 'have been about real people with real problems': Poilievre Catharine Tunney It's not surprising, but the leader of the Opposition has come out swinging against the budget. Speaking in the House of Commons, Poilievre zeroed in on the interest on the country's roughly $1.3-trillion national debt, which, as we've previously outlined, will jump to $85.5 billion in 2030-31. "Seniors, single moms and small businesses will now have to spend about $60 billion every year on interest to bankers and bondholders," said Poilievre. "This budget should have been about real people with real problems in the real world." With a majority, the Liberals don't need any of the opposition parties to support their budget to get it passed in the House.
- May slams budget for lack of action on climate change Sarah Petz Green Party Leader Elizabeth May says the 2026 budget fails to address the 'fiscal' or 'ecological' deficits that Canada is facing. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she was also "profoundly disappointed" in the budget. She said it "does not meet the moment" and fails on many fronts — particularly in addressing climate change. May said the budget not only fails to address the country's fiscal deficit, but also the "ecological deficit," saying it "explicitly rejects the concept of targets for climate action." Those targets are important because under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, they are legally binding, she added.
- Budget 'a big let-down' for small businesses, advocacy group says Jillian Kestler-D'Amours The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) says the budget is "a big let-down" for the small- and medium-sized businesses the group supports. "If you are a small-business owner struggling to keep your business going in the face of rapidly rising costs and a trade war, the budget will provide you with no help whatsoever," CFIB president Dan Kelly said in a written statement. Kelly said such enterprises were looking for tax reductions and relief from the Trump administration's tariffs on Canadian goods, but "the budget provides neither." "I find it appalling that, a year-and-a-half into the trade war, the government hasn't even bothered to fix the failing tariff-relief measures," he said. The CFIB acknowledged that some elements of the budget would help, such as tax simplification measures. "The new Canadian Growth Incentive contains a promising $15 million capital gains exemption, which, if properly designed, could be a significant catalyst for investments in small businesses," the group also said.
- Cost of stamps is going up Catharine Tunney If you still use stamps to send letters or holiday cards, you're going to be spending more next year. As part of the government's plans to modernize Canada Post, prices rise to $2.00 for single stamps and will increase by seven per cent per year after that. The budget document argued it will only cost approximately $6 per year for consumers and $9 per year for small businesses.
- Immigration targets roughly staying the same Benjamin Lopez Steven Asked about some Albertans voting in favour of immigration reforms for Canada, Prime Minister Mark Carney says reductions in the numbers of asylum seekers, temporary foreign workers and foreign students show Ottawa is moving toward a 'more sustainable pace' on immigration. Carney also said he's open to finding 'more solutions' with provinces. As expected, the budget includes the federal government's annual immigration levels update — and it appears Ottawa is staying the course. The new plan sets targets of 370,000 new temporary resident arrivals and 380,000 permanent resident admissions in 2027, 2028 and 2029. That's almost identical to the last plan, which said Ottawa would admit 380,000 permanent residentials annually between 2026 and 2028. The last plan also said Ottawa would bring in 385,000 temporary residents in 2026, then scale that down to 370,000 in 2027 and 2028. So, not much change. That may come as a surprise to some after Carney told the New York Times in September that immigration is back under control and the question now is whether Canada should begin a "controlled increase" in population. Other notable tidbits from the levels plan: Ottawa says up to 200,000 temporary residents already in Canada would have the opportunity to become permanent residents by the end of 2027. Plus, the federal government will "reform the Temporary Foreign Worker Program to better align with regional labour market needs, in collaboration with provinces and territories, while improving processing time and strengthening employer compliance."
- Investments in arts and culture Catharine Tunney This year's budget promises "more than five times last budget's record levels" in Canadian arts and culture. Budget 2026 proposes creating the "Canada Creative Credit," which would make up to $45,000 of artistic earnings tax free "Canadian painters, sculptors, ceramicists, writers, musicians, actors are our storytellers. They are how we see ourselves and how the world comes to know us," said the budget. The government also plans to renew the Canada Strong Pass. Introduced last year, it offered free admission to Parks Canada sites and participating museums and galleries, and saw about 15 per cent uptake. The budget says it's renewing the pass for summer 2027 and making it permanently free for young Canadians under 25 to visit national museums year-round. There's also a commitment to promoting the French language, especially on social media and in the age of AI. If the budget passes, CBC/Radio-Canada will receive $300 million over two years.
- Poilievre says budget should really be called 'Mastered by Debt' Jillian Kestler-D'Amours Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has hit out at the budget in a brief post on X. Dubbing it "Carney's Costly Credit Card budget," Poilievre said it will lead to "higher inflation and interest today and higher taxes tomorrow." "Canadians will pay more for food, fuel and homes," he wrote, adding that the budget should really be named "Mastered by Debt."
- Champagne says budget is next step to building 'stronger, sovereign Canada' Sarah Petz Speaking in the House of Commons shortly after tabling the documents, Champagne said the budget will help unlock Canada's "full growth potential" and become "masters of our destiny" — a nod to the budget's title. Responding to heckling from opposition MPs, Champagne said: "They're so excited about the budget, they're already commenting." With measures that will encourage solid revenue growth and attract investment, the budget puts Canada "in a position to transform our economy toward stronger growth and productivity," the finance minister said. "Budget 2026 is the next step in our ambitious plan to help businesses of all sizes invest and grow, to help Canadians get ahead and build a stronger, sovereign Canada."
- $11B committed to try to end homelessness in Canada Catharine Tunney One of the biggest line items in this year's budget is the $11.2 billion dedicated to putting Canada "on a path to end homelessness over the next decade." Ottawa said it will make a "historic, multi-billion-dollar investment" to build transitional and permanent housing. It's also promising to build the facilities needed to care for and support the most vulnerable in our society. "With an estimated 65,000 homeless Canadians, ending homelessness must become a national initiative," the budget said, saying it will also need help from provinces, municipalities and philanthropy groups. "Canadians take care of each other and ending homelessness will also make entire communities better and safer."
- Will this budget help your wallet? Abby Hughes Gas, groceries and rent all come up in this budget. As well as the top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, a program to support low-wage workers is also being expanded. The minimum amount a worker had to make to qualify for the refundable tax credit known as the Canada Workers Benefit used to be $3,000; that will go down to $500 under the renamed Build Canada Workers Benefit. The amount workers can get also increases slightly. As already announced, Canadians will keep paying a bit less for gas until March 2027 due to the fuel excise tax suspension, which is costing the government $5.3 billion. Aside from those measures — some of which are short-term — the financial plan is light on direct support for Canadians and instead focuses on drawing investment. "It's not a bad budget for [investment] but they've left out the people," economist Armine Yalnizyan said. "It's not like they're doing nothing. But compared to the big picture of what this budget is about, affordability is not topical."

Erstwhile real money gaming (RMG) giant Dream11’s cofounder and CEO Harsh Jain has hinted at plans to launch a revamped version of the platform by 2026-end. In a post on social media platform X, Jain said that the “brand new Dream11” would be built by sports fans and for sports fans. He did not disclose the upcoming platform’s features, commercial model or a specific launch date. “A brand new Dream11 is launching (at the) end of Dec - by sports fans, for sports fans. Stay tuned…,” said Jain in his post. The move signals Dream11’s next phase of evolution after the ban on online real-money gaming last year disrupted the platform’s paid fantasy sports business. While the teaser points to a product overhaul, it remains unclear how substantially the new offering will differ from its existing services. This comes more than a year after the Parliament passed the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Bill, 2025, which prohibited online real money games and restricted their promotion and advertising. Following the legislation, Dream11 discontinued paid contests and pivoted to a watch-along platform where users can follow gameplays of prominent content creators. It has also been exploring alternative ways to engage sports fans. Last year, parent Dream Sports forayed into the wealth tech space under Dream Money and began offering mutual funds, digital gold, fixed deposits, and loans. It later also forayed into stockbroking with DreamStreet and forayed into the SaaS space with Dream Horizon. However, it has been rethinking many of its newer bets. The startup shut down Dream Money in June this year. Dream Sports also quietly shut FanCode’s sports merchandise business earlier this year amid persistent issues with commercial viability. It also shut down its AI-powered sports performance analytics app Dream Play in June this year. Nevertheless, the startup’s portfolio still remains substantial. FanCode continues to operate as a sports streaming platform, while DreamCricket represents its push into AAA gaming. It also has its investment platform DreamStreet. Beyond the business challenges, Dream Sports is also facing GST dues of more than ₹20,000 Cr. In a blow to the company, the Supreme Court (SC), earlier this year, also upheld the tax authorities’ move to impose a 28% retrospective GST on real money online gaming companies over the full face value of bets placed through their platforms.

Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong is sentenced to 10 more years in prison
HONG KONG — A Hong Kong court sentenced prominent activist Joshua Wong to 10 more years in prison Thursday under a Beijing-imposed national security law, in a case that critics say underscores the crackdown on the city's once-thriving pro-democracy movement.
Wong, 30, first led student protests as a teenager and engaged in international advocacy efforts for Hong Kong's democracy movement. He was already serving a four-year, eight-month prison term after pleading guilty in the city's biggest national security case, and had been due to be freed in January.
But he was further charged in 2025 with conspiracy to collude with foreign forces to endanger national security, an offense under the security law imposed by Beijing in 2020.
Judge William Tam said Wong and fellow activist Nathan Law colluded with foreign officials and other foreign actors and sought measures against China and Hong Kong.
The judge pointed to the U.S. revocation of the city's preferential treatment as a special administrative region and U.S. sanctions imposed on Chinese and Hong Kong officials, saying these were the kinds of sanctions or hostile measures Wong and Law had called for.
"The punishment must fit the gravity of the crime committed," Tam wrote. "It is also necessary for this court to express the community's abhorrence of the defendant's scheme and acts together with others to collude with foreign forces."
The United States strongly condemned the sentencing and called for Wong's immediate release.
The U.S. Consulate in Hong Kong said in a statement that Wong has been "unjustly imprisoned" since late 2020, showing that "Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong."
Wong pleaded guilty to the offense earlier this year. Tam said he considered a 13-year prison sentence as a starting point but reduced it because of Wong's guilty plea and mitigation.
Tam said Wong would serve the remaining two months of the sentence for his first national security conviction concurrently with the new sentence.
Wong looked calm during sentencing
Ahead of the hearing, Wong, who appeared at the High Court in a dark shirt, nodded to his supporters and pro-democracy activists in the public gallery.
He appeared serious but calm as the judge read out his sentencing remarks. "Thank you all," he told supporters before leaving the courtroom.
Tiffany Chin, a former member of the now-disbanded Scholarism movement once led by Wong, was in tears after the sentence was delivered.
With limited seating available, some took turns entering the courtroom. Dozens had lined up outside the court to secure a seat in the public gallery, some as early as Tuesday. One resident, ET Wong, said Wong walked a difficult path for Hong Kong's future, human rights and the student movement. "He should not have spent a single day in wrongful imprisonment," she said.
In a statement written in prison, Wong said he thought he was acting within the law and was not directly advocating for sanctions when he reposted others' social media posts or called on foreign companies to consider ceasing business with the Hong Kong police. He said he later realized his judgment was wrong.
He said during his nearly six years in prison, he enrolled in university courses and read many books. He said he devoted himself to becoming a better person, and hoped he would regard the experience as having helped forge his character when he looks back one day.
Wong's convictions seen as discouraging dissent
Hong Kong once had a freewheeling civil society. But after huge anti-government protests rocked the city in 2019, authorities reduced public choice in elections and arrested many leading activists. Some news outlets known for reporting critical of the government shut down and dozens of civil society groups dissolved.
Observers say Wong's sentencing shows authorities' determination to keep prominent activists in prison for as long as possible.
Eric Lai, a senior fellow at the Georgetown Center for Asian Law, said most of the alleged activities after the security law took effect were purely online expressions and public information transmission, which would not be seen as a great threat to national security in liberal countries.
Law, who is wanted by the Hong Kong authorities, said in a statement that it was incredibly sad to see his friend suffer further sentencing over his peaceful advocacy work.
Beijing views Wong as an anti-China figure supporting Hong Kong independence, a stance that crosses its red line. Hong Kong authorities argue the security law is crucial for the city's stability following the 2019 protests, maintaining that the city's law enforcement actions were evidence-based.
Prosecution highlights Wong's lobbying and advocacy efforts
The prosecution alleged that Wong and Law had agreed in or around 2016 to lobby internationally to achieve their goal of democratic self-determination.
After the security law was enacted, Law, who left for the U.K., and others advanced their work abroad by meeting foreign politicians and launching petition drives, it said. Wong supported the effort from Hong Kong through foreign media outlets and social media to draw international attention and bolster the request for sanctions, a blockade or other hostile measures against China and Hong Kong, it said.
Wong's lawyer Derek Chan had urged the court to impose a sentence that would give his client some hope, adding that Wong wishes to take care of his parents after his release.
Chinese and Hong Kong authorities defend the ruling
Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters in Beijing that Wong had pleaded guilty in the face of overwhelming facts and evidence and that the central government supports Hong Kong in upholding national security.
Hong Kong leader John Lee said Wong, Law and their accomplices are among the "primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong's prosperity and stability."
Steve Li, chief superintendent of the police's national security department, welcomed the court's ruling and said he hoped Wong would reflect on his wrongdoing.
The U.K. Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said the sentencing is a clear example of how the security law is being used to target individuals for political expression and participation.
To his supporters, Wong is a political star representing a younger generation born in the final years of Hong Kong's British colonial rule before the city's return to China in 1997.
Though he's held behind bars, Wong's influence appears to have remained a concern for the pro-Beijing camp.
In September, a pro-Beijing newspaper report criticized a 2017 documentary about Wong on Netflix for "beautifying" his crimes. The city's security bureau told local media the government was taking follow-up action.
The documentary then topped Netflix's most-watched list in Hong Kong.

Amagi posted a consolidated net profit of ₹74.8 Cr in Q2 FY27, up nearly 30X from ₹2.5 Cr a year ago, while operating revenue rose 27%
Revenue growth outpaced the 9% increase in total expenses, helping the media SaaS company sharply expand profitability
Net profit more than doubled sequentially, while the board approved the appointments of Bhaskar Ghosh as an independent director and CTO Srividhya Srinivasan as a whole-time director
Listed media SaaS company Amagi reported a nearly 30X YoY jump in its consolidated net profit to ₹74.8 Cr in the September quarter (Q2 FY27), as revenue growth outpaced expenses.
The company had posted a net profit of ₹2.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Sequentially, profit rose 120.7% from ₹33.9 Cr.
Operating revenue increased 27% to ₹475.8 Cr from ₹374.8 Cr in Q2 FY26. It grew 8.9% from ₹436.9 Cr in the preceding quarter.
Amagi provides cloud software that helps media companies produce, distribute, and monetise television and streaming content.
Including other income, its total income stood at ₹501.9 Cr in Q2 FY27 as against ₹389.6 Cr a year ago and ₹454.5 Cr in Q1 FY27.
Amagi’s total expenses increased 9% to ₹419.3 Cr from ₹384.5 Cr. Alongside the results, Amagi’s board approved the appointment of former Accenture chief strategy and innovation officer Bhaskar Ghosh as an additional non-executive independent director for three years.
It also approved the appointment of promoter and CTO Srividhya Srinivasan as a whole-time director for five years. She will retain her CTO designation. (The story will be updated soon)

- A rumor circulated in October that some popular chocolate brands have switched to using lab-grown chocolate, also referred to as cell-based chocolate or cultured chocolate.
- The rumor stems from information published by a variety of unreliable outlets that cite no sources, such as investment firms giving advice on investing in lab-grown cocoa, holistic food blogs or alternative lifestyle blogs.
- Snopes bases its ratings on direct and verifiable primary evidence. In the absence of such evidence in this instance, we've left this claim unrated. Most of the companies named in examples of the claim have denied using lab-grown cocoa in current products. One has admitted to investing in the research of lab-grown cocoa but not actively using it in products. Another has a product with a sunflower-seed-based cocoa alternative that is different from cultured chocolate. One of the companies has not responded as of this writing.
Ahead of the candy-fueled Halloween season in October, a rumor spread that some popular chocolate brands have switched to using lab-grown chocolate, also referred to as cell-based chocolate or cultured chocolate.
Cell-based chocolate has been billed as a possible sustainability solution for harvesting cocoa, an industry faced with supply, environmental and labor issues.
Essentially, the goal of cell-based chocolate is to create an environmentally and ethically sustainable alternative to farming cocoa beans, the fermented seed of the cacao tree that is the basis of making chocolate.
Critics of such technology claim some of the leading chocolate brands are "quietly pulling off a massive corporate bait-and-switch ... to flood retail shelves with lab-grown chocolate alternatives." One popular social media video asserts that specific brands are "spending billions of dollars into biotech startups that are making the switch from real cocoa to lab-grown," including:
- Kinder (a brand of Ferrero)
- Lindt & Sprüngli
- Snickers & M&Ms (brands of Mars)
- Kit Kat (a brand of Nestlé)
- Hershey
- Cadbury (a brand of Hershey)
The rumor appears to stem from a variety of unreliable outlets — such as investment firms giving advice on investing in lab-grown cocoa, holistic food blogs or alternative lifestyle blogs — the latter of which claims "climate change is a hoax" and therefore people should not "let corporations replace real chocolate with lab experiments."
Crucially, none of these outlets provide sources when making iterations of this claim. We reached out to each outlet, asking for any evidence they have to support their claims and if they would share their sources. We will update this article if we receive responses.
As Snopes bases its ratings on direct and verifiable evidence, we have left this claim unrated. It is important to note that most of the companies named in examples of the claim have denied using lab-grown cocoa, while one admitted to investing in researching lab-grown cocoa but not actively using it in products. Two have not responded as of this writing.
The Hershey Company and Cadbury
A Hershey spokesperson said via email, "Hershey has no active research and development or product commercialization work on cocoa substitutes, such as lab-grown cocoa or alternatives, underway or planned in the future."
Hershey's FAQ section on its ingredients webpage directly addresses the question of using lab-grown chocolate, using identical language to the above statement.
The company's sustainability webpage says it made a $500 million investment in Cocoa For Good, a strategy aiming to "improve farmer livelihoods, support children's well-being [and] protect the environments in which cocoa grows."
The company also notes the struggles within the cocoa industry, such as child labor, and points to Cocoa for Good as a way of "contributing to a cocoa supply chain where farmers and their families can prosper."
Further, Hershey's website notes that it has produced the Cadbury brand in the U.S. since 1988.
In February 2026, a descendent of the inventor of Reese's Peanut Butter Cups, a brand Hershey's now owns, reportedly accused the company of cutting corners and using inferior ingredients, but did not mention lab-grown chocolate.
Nestlé and Kit Kat
A Nestlé spokesperson said via email, "We are not developing lab-grown chocolate."'
They added, "While we keep an eye on emerging technologies and ingredient innovations, our primary focus remains on cocoa. It is at the heart of our confectionery business and will continue to be the core ingredient in our chocolate portfolio."
Nestlé's corporate website highlights The Nestlé Cocoa Plan, an initiative launched in 2009 and billed as an effort to help its farmers and improve the quality of ingredients.
The spokesperson focused on those efforts in their email:
Our research efforts concentrate on strengthening the resilience and sustainability of cocoa production, including supporting the development of climate-resilient cocoa varieties.
At the same time, we remain strongly committed to supporting cocoa-farming communities through initiatives such as the Nestlé Cocoa Plan and our Nestlé Income Accelerator Program, which aim to improve farmer livelihoods and strengthen the long-term sustainability of the cocoa supply chain (for example through cash incentives, training or agroforestry support that promote good farming practices and help reach higher crop productivity).
In 2025, the company announced that its research and development division had devised a "novel technique that uses up to 30% more of the cocoa fruit."
Nestlé does produce a product in Europe called Choco Crossies that is made with ChoViva, a chocolate alternative made from sunflower seeds — a different process to cultured chocolate — that German company Planet A Foods produces.
Planet A Foods describes ChoViva as a "cocoa-free chocolate alternative [proving] that chocolatey indulgence doesn't have to depend on cocoa: it can be produced at scale from an independent supply chain."
Lindt & Sprüngli
Best known for its Lindt brand of chocolates, as well as owning the Russell Stover and Ghirardelli brands, a Lindt & Sprüngli spokesperson said via email that claims the company is "using 'lab‑grown' or 'artificial' cocoa in its products are not correct." They added: "All Lindt chocolates available on the market today are made with cocoa beans sourced in the traditional way. All ingredients are clearly labeled on the packaging."
The company's sustainability webpage, like Hershey's and Nestlé's, cites similar issues in the cocoa industry, including child labor practices and forest conservation.
However, the Lindt & Sprüngli spokesperson said the company "continuously explores innovation in cocoa cultivation and chocolate production as part of its long‑term commitment to quality and sustainability," and, as a result, "made an investment in Food Brewer, a Swiss company researching cocoa ingredients based on natural cocoa plant cell cultures. "
The company added: "This collaboration is research‑focused and at an early stage ... Lindt & Sprüngli remains fully committed to exceptional quality and taste. Traditional chocolate made from natural cocoa beans will always remain at the heart of our portfolio."
Food Brewer posted about Lindt & Sprüngli's investment via LinkedIn, saying, "The profound knowledge of this global chocolate player will help us in accelerating our go-to-market strategy and further develop our delicious cocoa products."
Other brands in the claim
A spokesperson for Ferrero, which operates the Kinder brand, said via email that the company "does not use 'lab-grown' cocoa in any of our products," but added that it does "work with a number of partners to understand how a range of new technologies may someday affect the market, but don't necessarily plan to use these in our products."
The spokesperson did not answer whether or not the company is financially invested in cultured chocolate.
Snopes also contacted Mars (which operates the Snickers and M&M's brands) but we had not received a response prior to publication. Both Mars and Ferrero have sustainability webpages similar to the other companies mentioned in the claim.
Ferrero's website says its goals involve "protecting the environment and sourcing ingredients sustainably," as well as "promoting responsible consumption and empowering people."
For its part, Mars describes its sustainability program as "transforming the way we work – from how we source raw materials like palm oil and cocoa, to how we fish the oceans for our pet food ingredients – to ensure every part of our operations and extended supply chains help people and the planet thrive."
We will update this article if we receive further comment from Mars or the outlets that reported their alleged investments.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales
Abdul El-Sayed says his win is a mandate to take on affordability and Trumpism
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, defeating Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate as his party reclaimed control of Congress.
The 42-year-old former public health official campaigned on lowering costs, Medicare for All and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers, backed by President Trump, repeatedly attacked El-Sayed over his Muslim faith and opposition to U.S. military aid to Israel.
But Israel and the war in Gaza became a defining fault line in the race. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers just days before the election amid a bitter dispute over Israel.
After a campaign marked by heated disagreements over Israel, El-Sayed now finds himself on the same side of an issue as Trump.
The president announced plans to end roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year, though he offered no details on how the cuts would work.
Speaking to Morning Edition after his victory, El-Sayed welcomed the proposal.
"I think the president is actually right on this policy," he said. "I'd also like to see us stop selling weaponry that gets used to do the worst things, including genocide and apartheid, to Israel."
The U.S. provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual military aid under an agreement that runs through 2028.
His argument goes beyond Israel. El-Sayed also questioned U.S. military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Pakistan, saying American tax dollars should be spent at home.
Winning Michigan's Senate seat, however, doesn't mean every division within his party has disappeared.
During a visit to Michigan before the election, NPR's Michel Martin heard concerns about El-Sayed from some Jewish and Black voters. Asked whether he still had work to do to win their support, El-Sayed said the election results challenged that narrative.
"There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.

In early November, an image circulated online purportedly showing Pope Leo XIV meeting with American folk singer Bob Dylan, 85, who was dressed in a black hoodie.
"What's the deal with the hoodie? Why is he wearing it all the time?" one Reddit user commented on a post. Other people wanted to know if the image was created using generative AI.
The image was authentic. The Vatican's official social media pages posted the image (archived) of the two men, who both hail from the American Midwest.
"Pope Leo XIV met with American singer-songwriter Bob Dylan in a private audience on Wednesday, November 4," the photo's caption read.
Writer Salvatore Cernuzio contributed a story (archived) to the Vatican News about the meeting that read, in part:
The meeting between Pope Leo and Dylan—who wore a black hooded sweatshirt—was brief, consisting of greetings and a few lighthearted exchanges. The Holy Father presented the singer with a rosary, while Dylan reciprocated with a book: Chronicles: Volume One, his autobiography, which has been published in the United States and other countries around the world.
It wasn't the first time Dylan made a public appearance in a black hoodie, nor was it his first time meeting a pope (he also met Pope John Paul II in 1997). Though the singer was born and raised Jewish, he converted to Christianity in the 1970s.
Antonio Spadaro, an Italian priest who arranges meetings with public figures for the pope, formerly known as Robert Prevost, wrote in an Instagram post: "Born in Chicago in 1955, Prevost grew up with the American music of the era" (translation via a native speaker).
For further reading about Leo, we've previously verified an image showing him wearing Nike sneakers with his vestments.

Disgruntled National Conference legislators have held another huddle at a senior MLA's residence to finalise their demands ahead of a meeting with party patron Farooq Abdullah and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. The rebel legislators have refused to meet at the party headquarters or Farooq Abdullah's residence, insisting on a neutral venue. The internal mutiny escalated following Omar Abdullah's public remarks during the cabinet reshuffle stating no posts remained vacant. Claiming unity after two years of simmering grievances, the MLAs seek concrete action rather than mere assurances to resolve the ongoing crisis.
A ground report from Chennai highlights how political hoardings and banner culture continue to encroach upon pedestrian walkways, putting public safety at risk. Near a political party office, banners extend onto the road and block footpaths for 30 to 40 feet, leaving no walking space for pedestrians despite the presence of police and civic officials. The report emphasizes that such illegal structures have previously caused fatal accidents in the city. With both sides of the busy road obstructed by supporting beams and hoardings, questions are raised over who grants permission for these hazards and whether politicians consider themselves above the law.
A panel debate moderated by Preeti Choudhry examines the controversy surrounding the Election Commission of India, electoral roll manipulation allegations, and administrative revisions concerning Form 6. Congress spokesperson Salman Soz criticized the poll panel, alleging widespread voter disenfranchisement, pointing to reported institutional dissent, and demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. In response, Bharatiya Janata Party national spokesperson Dr. Syed Zafar Islam defended the constitutional body, stating that electoral concerns should be debated inside Parliament rather than through public demonstrations. Political analyst Sanjay Jha called for institutional transparency regarding internal deliberations among election commissioners, while commentator Rajat Sethi highlighted judicial scrutiny at the Supreme Court, voter infiltration issues in border states, and discussions regarding a National Register of Citizens. The discussion centers on poll body accountability, administrative course corrections, and whether the Election Commission should hold direct press conferences to address questions regarding electoral integrity.
A Republican setback in the US midterm elections has exposed a divide within Donald Trump's camp. Vice President JD Vance attributed the electoral defeat to the ongoing war in Iran, rising living costs, and voter dissatisfaction. While acknowledging that the conflict drove up short-term gasoline prices and affected poll outcomes, Trump maintained he would strike Iran again to prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons. Meanwhile, Democrats, having secured control of Congress, have pledged to challenge the administration's agenda and focus on making life more affordable for everyday Americans, leaving questions over whether Trump will reconsider his military policy or escalate action.
A 308-metre bridge constructed at a cost of 8 crore 86 lakh rupees over the Dudhi River in Madhya Pradesh's Narmadapuram district has remained disused for three years due to the absence of an approach road. The structure was planned to link between 40 and 50 villages across Narmadapuram and Narsinghpur districts. Instead, commuters, farmers, and patients are forced to travel through mud, waterlogging, and potholes. While local residents expressed frustration over official apathy, the district bridge construction department stated that it completed its assigned contract of the bridge and immediate approach stretches, leaving further road connectivity decisions to the state administration.

How sporting events are being impacted by Middle East conflict

The 2027 Asian Cup is just the latest event to be postponed in the Middle East amid concerns about missile attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement.
The 24-team tournament - Asia's version of the Euros - was scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia from 7 January to 5 February next year.
The Asian Cup has now been delayed by almost a year, and will be held between 23 December, 2027 and 21 January, 2028.
Sport in the region had already been heavily affected by the US-Iran conflict, which led to the cancellation of the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Formula 1 Grand Prix weekends in April this year.
Now the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi at the end of the year are also in doubt due to that ongoing situation and the current conflict involving the Houthis. If they are cancelled, F1 would have lost four of its 24 events this year.
It is not just football and F1 that have been forced to cancel, reschedule or move high-profile events, and many more remain under threat.
BBC Sport takes a look at the situation across the sports.
Football
The Saudi Pro League has, for the most part, managed to carry on as usual.
Several domestic league games had to be postponed, including three fixtures last month as the situation escalated.
The games were moved in the immediate aftermath of the attack on a major airport in Riyadh - though the SPL said they were switched "as a result of mandatory minimum rest periods between matches and to accommodate logistical requirements".
Following the postponement of the Asian Cup, this weekend's full round of Saudi Pro League has been called off.
The league once again has not attributed this to conflict in the region, instead saying the calendar would be recalibrated after the cancellation of the Asian Cup to achieve "a more balanced distribution of fixtures".
The AFC Champions League has been affected as well.
Cristiano Ronaldo and Kingsley Coman were among Al-Nassr's star players who did not to fly to Uzbekistan this week "given the pressure of matches and the amount of travel involved".
Al-Wasl of the United Arab Emirates also opted not to fly to Saudi Arabia to play Al-Nassr, and the match will be rearranged.
Meanwhile, the wife of Ollie Watkins, who plays for Riyadh-based Al-Hilal, posted on TikTok that she would be staying in the UK with their two children "until it calms down".
"We've had a bit of a plot twist," said Ellie Watkins. "I have come back to the UK for a little bit.
"There's just a little bit of conflict and things going on over in Saudi and we basically decided just to stay here.
"I felt like I needed to do that for the kids so there is some form of normality until we can get back out there and all be together."
Other well-known stars playing in the country include Gabriel Martinelli, Tijjani Reijnders, Darwin Nunez, Ivan Toney, Alexandre Lacazette, Ruben Neves, Sadio Mane and Joao Felix.
Formula 1
Andrew Benson, F1 Correspondent
Formula 1 has a major dilemma about racing in the Middle East both at the end of this season and the beginning of next.
Most pressingly, the 2026 season is due to end with races in Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.
As things stand, the sport is pressing ahead with plans to go to those races after being given security reassurances from various governmental sources that it should be safe.
There are, though, many people within the sport with misgivings about going.
Should the situation in the Middle East deteriorate in the next week or so, they could be called off and replaced with a single event in Imola in Italy on the Abu Dhabi weekend.
The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, with Saudi Arabia hosting on the following weekend.
But as things stand between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthi separatists, that race could not go ahead, and is likely to be cancelled if nothing changes by December.
Bahrain and Saudi Arabia are linked by a causeway, at the Saudi end of which is a facility belonging to state oil company Aramco, which has been targeted by the Houthis, while it joins Bahrain close to the F1 track.
So Bahrain is also be in jeopardy.
One option being discussed is to hold that race in Malaysia, as was done in October this year.
Other motorsport
The Dakar Rally was due to take place in Saudi Arabia in January but has been moved "following recent developments in the region".
Now the 2027 edition will begin in Loule-Faro in Portugal and end in Marrakech in Morocco.
Saudi Arabia had hosted the previous seven editions of Dakar, and the intention is to return in 2028.
Rally Saudi Arabia, part of the 2026 FIA World Rally Championship, which was scheduled for 12–15 November, has been cancelled.
But MotoGP will still take place this weekend at the Lusail International Circuit in Doha, Qatar, with three races left in the season.
It will go ahead without the Yamaha team, which has been advised against travelling from Japan.
Tennis
The Six Kings Slam, which should have begun on Saturday in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been postponed by two months.
It is now scheduled to run from 27 December to 30 December at the ANB Arena, located about 31km away from the King Khalid International Airport, which was the target of an attack on 10 October that killed 13 people and injured 308 others.
Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Alex de Minaur, Taylor Fritz and Learner Tien are due to compete.
But the 2026 WTA Finals, this weekend's season-ending championship of the women's tour, will not take place in Saudi Arabia.
A mutual agreement was reached to terminate a hosting agreement early, and it will instead take place at Indian Wells in the United States.
Boxing
Saudi Arabia regularly hosts title fights and high-profile bouts.
Only last week, Mexican legend Canelo Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super middleweight championship against Christian Mbilli.
But the whole of the card did not survive as Lindolfo Delgado withdrew from his IBF lightweight title fight against Arthur Biyarslanov over safety concerns.
Next on the schedule is the Zuffa Boxing event, which will feature Carlos Adames against Welshman Gerome Warburton in Riyadh Season 13, on 14 November.
WWE
The WWE Crown Jewel 2026 event will still take place this weekend, but at a new venue.
It was originally scheduled for the Kingdom Arena, before being switched to the ANB arena.
The reigning men's and women's world champions of WWE's Raw and SmackDown face each other.
Roman Reigns, Sami Zayn, Liv Morgan, Chelsea Green, Bron Breakker, Austin Theory, Penta, Je'Von Evans, Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton are on the bill.
Other sports impacted
The FIFAe Finals, an esports tournament series organised by Fifa, should have taken place in Jeddah last month but was cancelled.
This week's UCI Urban Cycling World Championships, for the world's leading riders in trials and BMX Freestyle, in Riyadh was called off too, with a decision due "on the sporting consequences of this announcement".
The PIF Saudi International event, the season finale of the Asian Tour, will not be held between 18-21 November at Riyadh Golf Club.
After "an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament" the decision was taken to call it off.
And on Tuesday, the Professional Triathletes Organisation said it was moving the Saudi Arabia T100 and World Triathlon Cup, in Jeddah, from the end of this month to 16-17 April.

Man arrested with Rs 1.4 crore unaccounted cash at Kharagpur railway station
Railway police arrested Rahul Soni after finding Rs 1.40 crore in his luggage at Kharagpur station. He could not provide documents proving the cash's legitimate source.
Police have arrested a 36-year-old man after recovering Rs 1.40 crore in cash from his bags at Kharagpur Railway Station in West Bengal's Paschim Medinipur district. The man, identified as Rahul Soni, was unable to produce valid documents to establish the source of the money, following which the police seized the entire amount.
The recovery was made on Wednesday at Platform 7 after railway police personnel noticed Soni behaving suspiciously and stopped him for questioning. He was carrying two handbags and a blue backpack.
A search of his luggage led to the discovery of bundles of Rs 500 notes packed inside the bags. The cash was subsequently counted using a currency-counting machine, which confirmed the total amount at Rs 1.40 crore, comprising 280 bundles of Rs 500 notes.
MAN CLAIMED CASH WAS BEING TAKEN FROM TATANAGAR TO HOWRAH
During questioning, Soni, a resident of Howrah, reportedly told the police that he was transporting the cash from Tatanagar to Howrah.
The search was conducted in the presence of Kharagpur Government Railway Police Station (GRPS) Officer-in-Charge Abhijit Chatterjee and independent witnesses. The entire operation was videographed using the e-Sakshya system.
As Soni failed to provide documents establishing the legitimate source of the money, the police seized the cash and arrested him following the prescribed legal procedures.
CASE REGISTERED UNDER BNS SECTIONS
The arrest was made under Sections 47 and 48(1) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), following procedures outlined under Supreme Court and National Human Rights Commission guidelines, according to the police.
Based on a written complaint filed by Sub-Inspector Tarun Kishore Jena, Kharagpur GRPS registered Case No. 167/26 under Sections 317(2), 317(5) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).
The investigation has been handed over to Sub-Inspector Swapan Kumar Bhuiya.

Kolkata witnessed an unusual procession on Saturday, October 31, as thousands of book lovers took to the streets carrying books instead of political flags. Called “Let’s Walk for Books”, the march was organised in protest against the alleged vandalism of Left-affiliated bookstalls by BJP workers and police during Durga Puja festivities across West Bengal.
The procession began at College Square, the hub of Kolkata’s literary and academic life as well as the publishing industry, following an appeal circulated on social media over several days. Among those who urged people to join were prominent academics, writers and public figures, including Pabitra Sarkar, Shamik Bandyopadhyay, Jawhar Sircar, Kumar Rana, Malini Bhattacharya, Ziad Ali, Paranjoy Guha Thakurta and Shobhanlal Dasgupta.
The appeal, which urged participants to carry a book each, said books were facing a ‘barbaric’ attack across the state.
Bookstalls have long been part of Durga Puja festivities in Bengal, along side fairs, music, theatre and poetry events.
This year, however, several bookstalls were allegedly vandalised, their organisers assaulted, and books thrown onto the streets and trampled underfoot, the appeal noted. In Jadavpur, an attempt was allegedly made to demolish bookstalls with the help of central forces. A Kolkata Municipal Corporation garbage truck was also brought in to remove newly printed books.
The appeal described the incidents as an assault on Bengal’s cultural traditions and warned that continued attacks on books could damage the state’s reputation and values. It called on writers, artists, students, teachers, publishers, booksellers and others to assemble in front of the Vidyasagar statue at College Square, carrying a book of their choice as a symbol of resistance.
The Rally
Responding to the appeal, people began gathering around College Street from 3 pm. Students from colleges and universities joined participants across generations, from middle-aged people to the elderly. Almost everyone carried a book.
The collection reflected a wide range of political, literary and religious traditions. Participants carried works by Rabindranath Tagore, Karl Marx, Bhagat Singh, Sukanta Bhattacharya and Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, alongside books by contemporary writers such as Arundhati Roy. Some carried works by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, while others held copies of the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and books on Swami Vivekananda.
Scheduled to begin at 3.30 pm, the march started around 3.45 pm, with several thousand people taking part. In a city accustomed to processions marked by political flags, banners and party slogans, this one stood out. Participants carried books and sang songs.
They sang the Bengali translation of Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet’s song “They Don’t Let Us Sing”, as well as Rabindranath Tagore’s “Bnadh Bhenga Dao”. International protest songs, including “We Shall Overcome” and its Bengali version, “Amra Korbo Joy”, also featured in the procession.
Large banners, or tifos, carried messages such as “Don’t Burn Books, Read Them” and “Books versus Bulldozer”.
The procession also offered glimpses of solidarity among participants. An elderly newspaper vendor distributed candies to those taking part. In a video shared on social media, he said he had joined the march because of his love for books. Although financial difficulties had prevented him from completing his education, he said, he had always loved reading and ensured that his daughter completed her education.
Starting in front of College Square and Calcutta University, the march passed the National Book Agency and the iconic sweet shops, Putiram and Mouchaak, on Surya Sen Street, before entering Bankim Chatterjee Street. It then proceeded past the College Street Coffee House and Presidency University before returning to College Square.
Several videos shared on social media showed people standing on balconies and outside shops, recording the procession on their smartphones. Marchers waved at onlookers along the route.
Left leaders Mohammed Salim, Sujan Chakraborty and Biman Basu also joined the procession, walking at the back.
After the march, the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA) organised a brief cultural programme in front of the College Square gate. Activists performed songs including “Tu Zinda Hai”, Paul Robeson’s “Ol’ Man River” and Bhupen Hazarika’s Bengali adaptation, “O Ganga Boichho Keno”.
Addressing the gathering, senior Left leader Biman Basu said people who believed in reading books had come together for the march. He added that efforts to promote reading must continue whenever books come under attack.
Participants said the protest was not about defending any particular political ideology. A book, they said, was neither Left-wing nor Right-wing; it was simply a book. Some described the attacks during Durga Puja as an assault on education, free thought and rationalism, and said they had joined the march to collectively resist such incidents in the future.
SFI central executive committee member Shuvajit Sarkar (in blue shirt in photo below), who participated in the march, said, “Fascists and communal forces oppose books because books promote rationality and reject blind subordination. We will defend books and continue the struggle against the divisive politics of the RSS and BJP until we defeat it.”

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
