Jammu, Nov 05: Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Thursday called for a shift in the education system from rote learning and memorisation towards independent thinking, ethical conduct and the development of well-rounded citizens, saying academic excellence alone cannot define the purpose of education.
In his address as the chief guest at the Diocese of Jammu-Srinagar Education Society (DJSES) Awards 2026 at the Government Convention Centre here, Omar Abdullah said that education is the foundation of what we will go on to become but it was not everything.
He emphasised the need to look beyond examination results he said while securing marks required for admission to colleges was important, educational institutions must also focus on creating responsible citizens capable of thinking and acting independently.
He said that the education system had, for a long time, remained centred around repetition and the ability of students to reproduce what they were taught, leaving little scope for independent thought.
“Children have to learn to think for themselves. Children have to learn to act for themselves. But children also have to be able to learn to distinguish between what is right and what is wrong,” he added.
CM Omar said the younger generation was facing challenges that previous generations had not encountered, particularly in an era dominated by digital platforms, social media and rapidly evolving technology.
Drawing a comparison with his childhood, when television offered limited entertainment options, he said holding the attention of students had become increasingly difficult amid hundreds of television channels and platforms such as YouTube, Instagram and Snapchat.
He also highlighted the challenges posed by artificial intelligence (AI) in the education sector, saying the focus should be on teaching students to use the technology ethically and as a learning tool rather than a means of avoiding academic work.
“How do we get children to use Artificial Intelligence correctly, ethically? How do we get them to learn from it, not cheat from it?” he said.
He said students should not outsource their homework and essays to AI tools, stressing the need to ensure that technological advancements do not undermine their ability to think and learn independently.
The Chief Minister also expressed concern over the declining habit of reading among youngsters, saying students must develop an interest in books beyond their prescribed syllabus.
He said that reading played an important role in developing intellectual abilities and encouraged students to cultivate the habit of reading.
He further highlighted the contribution of the Diocese and its educational institutions to Jammu and Kashmir, saying the society was running 24 schools across Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, educating around 28,000 students annually and employing nearly 1,600 people.
He said these institutions had produced civil servants, police officers, doctors and business leaders, but their most significant contribution was the creation of individuals who remained good human beings.
The Chief Minister urged students not to hesitate in asking questions, saying questioning was essential for developing an informed and accountable society.
“There are no stupid questions. There are only stupid answers,” he said and encouraged the youngsters to question existing practices and seek explanations about what was happening around them.
He said a generation willing to ask questions would also make those in positions of responsibility answerable, ultimately contributing to a better Jammu and Kashmir.
“We must create a generation that is happy to ask what is happening, why it is happening and what we can do to make it better,” Omar said.
He congratulated the students who had excelled in examinations and employees completing 25 years of service in the society's schools.
He said educational institutions must strive to produce well-rounded individuals rather than focus exclusively on academic achievements.
Omar also recalled his personal association with the Diocese and its schools, saying his education briefly began at Presentation Convent in Srinagar before he moved to Burn Hall School, where he studied until Class 5.
Recalling his childhood memories at Burn Hall, he spoke about Christmas celebrations, nativity plays and his repeated role as Angel Gabriel in the school's annual performances.
He said the memories had remained close to his heart and reflected the longstanding personal connection he shared with the institution.
CM Omar also urged youngsters to focus on becoming good human beings, saying values, mutual respect and compassion were as important as academic and professional success.

Windows 11 is testing eight upgrades in Insider builds to reduce daily friction. Key updates include flexible taskbar positioning, faster Windows Search with inline actions, a Battery Status widget, phone-to-PC integration, per-app privacy controls, smarter Windows Hello, anti-glare tools, and enhanced File Explorer previews.
I can’t count how many times I’ve had to drag the window to full size, squint at a bright screen, or open Settings just to turn on dark mode. Each one takes a few seconds, but you repeat them all day. Thankfully, Windows 11 is about to trim a lot of that. Microsoft seems to have noticed, and over the past few months, it has been stacking up small but genuinely useful changes for Windows 11. The best part is that all these features are coming with future updates.
With new optimized features, Windows now feels up to 20% more responsive, with the gains showing up in Start, File Explorer, Search, and more. With the latest Windows Insider release notes, you are in for a eight-feature treat you should know about. One heads-up before we start: not everything is available to everyone yet. Many of these are still being tested in the Windows Insider Experimental channel, so I’ll tell you where each one stands.
Table of Contents
Taskbar customization
For years, the Windows 11 taskbar has been stuck to the bottom of the screen. There was no way to change its position. That is finally changing. Microsoft’s Windows Insider blog confirms that, with the current insider update, users can now park the taskbar on the top, bottom, left, or right edge. Here’s what you can do:
- You can choose icon alignment for every position. On the sides, icons can be top-aligned or centered. On the top or bottom, they can be left-aligned or centered.
- Start, Search, and other flyouts follow the taskbar. Meaning, if you put the taskbar at the top, Start opens from the top.
- On a vertical taskbar, when you choose “Never combine” and turn on labels, every app window gets its own labeled button, so you can see all your windows at a glance.
Moving the taskbar to the side can give you vertical space, handy for developers who want to see more code. To tweak the taskbar, you need to navigate to Settings > Personalization > Taskbar > Taskbar behaviors. You can also choose to make the taskbar smaller, optimal for small screens. Simply choose the “Show smaller taskbar” option to Always, and you get smaller icons and a shorter bar. No restart or sign-out needed.
Things may not work perfectly, though. Auto-hide and the tablet-optimized taskbar don’t work in the new positions, touch gestures are still in progress, and the search box shows up as a plain search icon for now. Aside from this, the Recommended section is getting renamed to Recent, and you can hide your name and profile picture. There are also separate toggles to show or hide Pinned, Recent, and All.
Smarter Windows Search
This one might be the biggest everyday upgrade. Microsoft has confirmed that a new search built on WinUI 3 is incoming and says it makes it faster and lighter on resources. Windows Search also understands you better. Typos and synonyms are matched more intelligently, so a sloppy query is more likely to give you the right result.
The main highlight is inline actions. So, instead of finding a setting and then opening Settings to change it, you can enable/disable a setting from search. This means you’ll be able to:
- Switch to dark mode, turn on night light, or turn on Bluetooth
- Dim your screen or mute your PC
- Minimize all your windows or arrange windows on screen
Phone actions are coming soon too, allowing you to quickly do things like sending a text through a Phone Link-connected device. Search is soon expected to get inline previews of files, richer file details, web answers (think weather or “how tall is the Eiffel Tower”) and filters. This new experience is also expected to arrive for the Start menu, but only next year. Other features are expected for broader availability later this year.
Battery status widget
This is not a big update, per se, but if you want to know what the battery level is on your wireless mouse? Your headphones? Your laptop? Or any other connected device, usually you’d have to hunt through different menus for each answer.
With the Windows 11 26340.9616 release, Microsoft introduced a Battery Status widget that shows the battery levels of your PC and your peripheral devices in one view. To get it, you need to open the Widgets board > Add widgets > Battery Status. It is rolling out to Insiders on newer builds. Widgets are also getting lighter. Microsoft says on PCs with 8GB of memory or less, Widgets now load only when you open them. This helps free up more than 200 MB for your apps.
Phone to PC continuity
Microsoft seems to be making sure that your phone and PC act like one setup. With the upcoming updates, Windows 11 could allow users to reply to messages, answer calls, and open phone apps without picking up their phone. Here are all the features, reportedly available in the insider build:
- Messages and notifications: You will be able to preview them from your Android phone or iPhone right in Start. When you want to reply, you can open a window focused on that chat.
- Quick Settings: Put your phone in silent mode or ring a misplaced phone right from your PC.
- Phone apps on your desktop: Supported Android phones can open phone apps in separate, resizable windows.
- Files: You will be able to browse your phone’s files in File Explorer.
- Photos: You can snap a picture on your phone, and your PC shows a notification that you can open with one click.
- Resume: Pick up supported activities where you left off when you switch devices.
One thing to note is that this requires a compatible Android phone or iPhone, and features vary by platform. The rollout date, similar to other features, isn’t confirmed, but it may arrive by next year.
Better privacy controls
Until now, regular desktop apps were controlled by a single device-wide switch for things like your camera, microphone, and location. That was not something one would want, especially when you want to have granular controls. According to the 28120.3302 release notes, Insiders can now allow or deny access for each desktop app individually. For that, you need to head to Settings > Privacy & security, then open Camera, Microphone, or Location.
The rollout is gentle on your existing setup. All the apps that were granted access will continue to keep it, and apps that were denied stay denied. Nothing will reset. Apps that haven’t asked yet will prompt you the first time they request access.
Smarter Windows Hello
According to Microsoft, with the latest insider builds, it has introduced faster Windows Hello sign-ins, made them easier, and more reliable, with improvements to both face and fingerprint recognition. There’s also a very practical new trick for face sign-in. If you’ve ever tried to unlock your laptop in a dim room, you know the struggle. You have to turn on the light so that your face is detected correctly.
The 26340.9750 release notes say Windows Hello facial recognition can temporarily brighten your screen to help you sign in when the lighting is poor. To use it, go to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Facial recognition (Windows Hello) and turn on Automatically adjust screen brightness during face recognition. This one is currently in the Experimental channel.
Anti-glare mode
Although Microsoft doesn’t use the name “anti-glare mode,” that’s exactly what the newly added option does. Notably, it’s a contrast theme toggle inside Magnifier, as mentioned in the 28120.3302 release notes. While many people use Night light or color inversion to calm a bright screen, but the downside of using is that it flips everything, including photos, charts, and videos.
With the new toggle, it will recolor the interface only. This way, your images keep their real colors. The dark theme is the default, and you can pick a different contrast theme under Settings > Accessibility > Magnifier. You still get the “Color inversion” option, and it isn’t going anywhere if you prefer it.
Magnifier also learned some multi-monitor tricks:
- Zoom per display: With your monitors set to Extend, each screen can have its own zoom level. So, one screen where you are writing can sit at 300% while your reference screen stays at 150%.
- View locking: Press Ctrl + Windows + K while pointing at a screen to hold its view in place, then press Windows + Esc to release all locks.
If you just want a softer tint, Windows 11 is also testing a “Screen Tint,” which lets you pick a color overlay and adjust its strength.
File Explorer previews
You might already be using third-party software for file previews inside File Explorer, but wait. Microsoft is also cooking the same feature, and it may arrive very soon for Windows 11. A couple of preview-related changes are incoming:
- Thumbnails in the Recommended section on File Explorer’s Home page are sharper, so they’re crisper and easier to read without needing you to open them.
- You can now preview and install fonts from File Explorer and desktop right-click menus.
If you work with fonts, that second one saves a few steps. For everyone else, it’s a polish update, and it’s good to see File Explorer getting some attention.
Can everyone try these features?
Unfortunately, these features aren’t available for everyone, for now. Most of the features above live in Windows Insider builds. If you’re comfortable with a few bugs, you can join through Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program. You will see most features in builds 26340.9616, 26340.9750 and 28120.3302 in the Experimental channels.
These builds can be unstable, and features in them might change, be removed, or never ship. Many are also rolled out gradually to a subset of Insiders first, so you may not see everything right away. For those who are using Windows 11 on their primary device, you should probably wait.

- Xbox is also rolling out the refreshed design and navigation to cloud gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets.
Following reports of a new Xbox PC app update with console-like features in early October 2026, Microsoft has officially announced the overhaul, bringing faster launch times, simpler navigation, and a cleaner interface. The updated app is now available to Xbox Insiders, starting November 5, 2026.
According to Xbox Wire’s latest blog, the updated Xbox PC app launches up to 60% faster, with Home, Store, and Xbox Game Pass pages loading up to 50% faster and in-app windows opening up to 65% faster. Not just that, Microsoft has made it a lot simpler to navigate the app for PC users.
The new Xbox PC app makes it easier to find the best Xbox games with simpler library navigation, updated filters, and more ways to organize your collection. Microsoft has also brought friends and social features into the main navigation, making it easier to see what friends are playing, chat, and join parties.
Furthermore, the improved search brings together results for games, installed titles, add-ons, and people in one place, so you can find games on the Xbox Store or on Xbox Game Pass more quickly. Lastly, Microsoft has also given a cleaner look with the Xbox PC app overhaul, with refreshed game cards, Home, Settings, and animations.
The updates don’t end here, as Microsoft is bringing a refreshed Xbox Cloud Gaming experience with the Xbox PC app overhaul, which introduces a new Library tab that brings together owned and Game Pass cloud games, with options to browse, sort, and filter by recently played titles, genre, and input type.
Additionally, desktop mode uses larger screens better, while new dark and light themes and five high-contrast options let players customize the experience to their preferences. After Xbox revealed new cloud gaming prices, it is now rolling out the updated design and navigation to cloud gaming apps on supported TVs and VR headsets.

A mother is dead and her daughter is missing in western Canada after a suspected grizzly bear attack in the same community where a bear attacked a group of schoolchildren earlier in the year.
On Tuesday, the British Columbia conservation officer service said in a social media post that it had launched a search for the two missing people on the weekend, and that during the search on Sunday an officer found the mother’s body. The search for her 19-year-old daughter is ongoing.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre said in a video posted online.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (4.97 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast. Its remote location and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
“While the full circumstances are still unfolding, we understand first-hand the trauma this incident will inflict upon the victims’ family members, the victims of last year’s attack and the community at large,” said Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, on Tuesday. “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.”
Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

A video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov is being circulated on social media. In the video, Lavrov allegedly describes India as merely a trading partner, stating that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries (here, here, here). Let us verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov stated that India is neither a Russian ally nor a superpower and has no right to interfere in or advise Russia on its foreign policy decisions concerning Russia, Ukraine, the United States, or other countries.
Fact: The viral clip has been digitally manipulated by altering the original footage and adding fabricated statements about India’s relations with Russia. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A keyword search related to the viral claim led to no credible reports confirming that Sergey Lavrov made such statements.
Further, we conducted a search using the ‘M World’ logo visible at the top of the viral clip. This led us to the M World News Instagram page, where we found the original video featuring Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov. The video was posted with the caption, “Lavrov Fires Back Over Claims Putin Refuses to Meet Zelensky.”
Based on this clue, we found in the original footage that Lavrov dismisses claims that Russian President Vladimir Putin is refusing to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He emphasises that any potential negotiations must address the underlying issues. During the briefing, he discussed US-Russia relations, possible peace talks on Ukraine, and international diplomatic responses (here, here).
Upon closer examination of the video, we noticed certain inconsistencies, particularly that Lavrov’s lip movements do not appear to be properly synchronised with the audio.
To further verify the video’s authenticity, we analysed it using multiple AI detection tools. Hive Moderation’s AI-generated content detector gave an aggregate score of 99.4%, indicating that the media likely contained AI-generated or deepfake content. Similarly, NVIDIA’s Synthetic Video Detector classified the footage as synthetic media.
To sum up, this Video of Sergey Lavrov making derogatory remarks about India is digitally manipulated.

Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.
One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.
In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.
Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race that Axios reported would fundamentally scramble the math on Trump’s AI buildout. According to Bloomberg, Hinojosa’s election has developers facing down the “worst-case scenario.” Texas is the epicenter of the AI boom, Axios noted, and was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028.
Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects as long as it takes to pass laws “tackling impacts on water, electricity, air, and property rights.” Approximately “13 gigawatts of data center capacity” is now exposed, Bloomberg reported. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research warned in a note that Texas projects with “power, permits and steel keep going,” but “those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months,” Bloomberg reported. Some projects may leave the state entirely, perhaps moving to Louisiana or Georgia—or perhaps going nowhere.
“She would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for data centers,” Johnson’s note said. “The question now is how long the pause lasts.” As PIMCO head of public policy Libby Cantrill similarly warned, “even if statewide moratoria do not result, we expect to see a lot more sand in the gears of the AI buildout regardless—with more time required to secure permits and other approvals, as well as more concessions that data center developers will have to make.”

“If the public is drifting away from government hospitals and being pushed into the clutches of the corporate healthcare system, it is undeniably because politicians and governments lack genuine sincerity,” said 115 citizens and activists in an open letter to Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy and Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha.
The letter accused successive governments of failing to strengthen public healthcare, alleging that the lack of basic amenities in government hospitals is driving patients towards private healthcare.
Gaps in basic facilities
The letter highlights concerns over drinking water facilities, toilets, sanitation and the maintenance of infrastructure at major government hospitals in Hyderabad, including Osmania General Hospital, Gandhi Hospital, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Niloufer Hospital and Petlaburj Maternity Hospital.
The signatories — comprising social activists, academics, writers, journalists, teachers and other citizens — questioned whether the government’s promises to improve public healthcare translated into better conditions for patients.
Is the problem a lack of medical expertise or basic facilities?
The signatories argued that the challenges confronting government hospitals cannot be viewed solely through the lens of shortages of doctors and other medical personnel. The signatories acknowledged that healthcare workers were already working under considerable pressure, but said the absence of basic amenities was adding to the difficulties faced by patients.
“Government hospitals have experienced doctors, medical staff and research capabilities, but inadequate facilities are undermining the healthcare experience,” they added.
Referring to Osmania, Gandhi, NIMS, Niloufer and Petlaburj hospitals, the signatories questioned why patients should have to endure difficult conditions to access treatment when the institutions were expected to provide essential public healthcare services.
When basic amenities become a question of dignity
They have identified clean drinking water, functional toilets and proper sanitation as among the most pressing requirements in public hospitals. Questioning the government’s responsibility for maintaining these facilities, the signatories asked whether patients should be held responsible for unhygienic conditions and unpleasant odours in hospital toilets, arguing that the responsibility for maintenance rested with the authorities.
They said patients who could afford private healthcare might choose to seek treatment elsewhere, but those unable to bear the additional expense were left with fewer options.
Should hospital maintenance be handed over to private entities?
The signatories also cautioned the government against transferring responsibility for maintaining basic hospital amenities to corporate entities under the banner of public participation as doing so would impose an additional financial burden on patients. They called for the government to take responsibility for improving existing infrastructure and ensuring that essential facilities were properly maintained.
They further questioned the emphasis placed on changing photographs on walls and ambulances after a government assumes office, arguing that the same attention should be directed towards providing basic amenities in hospitals.
A call for a Right to Health law
Beyond immediate improvements to hospital infrastructure, the signatories urged the Telangana government to introduce a strong Right to Health law through consultations with people’s organisations and public. They called for a broader effort to strengthen the public health and medical system so that ordinary citizens would not be compelled to abandon government hospitals because of inadequate facilities.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

Vance walks Trump tightrope with scathing election critique blaming Iran war
- Published
Vice-President JD Vance sent shockwaves through Washington on Wednesday by blaming his party's midterm defeat squarely on the Iran war, in what was widely interpreted as an effort to distance himself from President Donald Trump ahead of a potential 2028 White House run.
In a carefully calibrated, 600-word statement on X, the vice-president acknowledged that Trump's 2024 voters had deserted Republicans in the midterm election.
"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."
In interviews late Tuesday night and Wednesday, Trump had defended the war but acknowledged that it played a factor in Democrats flipping control of the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Vance's view on the war in Iran is an open secret in Washington. While he has repeatedly backed the conflict since the US and Israel attacked Tehran in February, he has reportedly expressed opposition in private meetings with administration officials.
But those disagreements had been kept out of the public eye - until now.
Hours after Trump and the party were handed a bruising election defeat, Vance made clear that he felt the decision to go to war was a clear political mistake.
"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest," Vance said.
It was a striking statement, and one with no recent precedent: it's hard to recall a similar moment in recent US political history when a sitting vice-president has so sharply broken with the president on a signature foreign policy issue.
Then came an arguably even greater surprise: Trump - who typically demands steadfast loyalty from his senior advisers - agreed with Vance that the midterms were "largely" decided by the war. He added that he would "do it again" if given the same choices.
- LIVE: Follow latest updates
- BOWEN: Trump's loss limits powers at home, but it will likely be different abroad
- THE BIG MOMENTS: Ecstatic scenes that greeted key results
- ZURCHER: Midterm carnage weakens Trump but he still wields power for now
- 'A DISASTER': Angry Republicans blame Trump for midterms defeat
It was an early sign that Trump - who has prized loyalty from his advisers - may give Vance a wide berth should he choose to launch a presidential campaign.
"I know how he feels about it. I think it was -- I think it was fine," Trump told reporters when asked about Vance's post blaming the war. "I knew that when I went in, and we stopped them from having a nuclear weapon, and they will never have a nuclear weapon."
Vance's statement seemed like "a way of separating himself from Trump," said Daniel Byman, a foreign policy expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Drawing contrasts with Trump will be a delicate balancing act if Vance seeks the presidency, Byman added.
That balance was on display in Vance's post. The vice president didn't mention Trump by name and attributed much of his election results analysis to unnamed pollsters.
Vance "put his toe in the water to see what he's going to do," Ashley Davis, a Republican strategist, told the BBC.
Beyond the Iran war criticism, Vance also offered a political roadmap that could preview a possible presidential campaign. He distilled the party's strategy to win back voters into a neat four-point gameplan: "1) End the war 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation 3) Put America First 4) Change our relationship to Israel."
The list encapsulated much of Vance's worldview since bursting onto the national political scene, and read like the core argument in a future stump speech.
The BBC has contacted Vance's office for comment.
Of course, the next presidential election is still two years away. Vance is expected to run but hasn't made an official decision, and aides insist that he's still mulling it over.
It's also up for debate exactly how much Vance broke from Trump. Vance showed the message to Trump before posting it online, according to The New York Times.
Trump, for his part, could change his mind and make clear he'll brook no dissent from Vance or anyone else.
The president has been circumspect about who he'd support to succeed him as the 2028 Republican presidential nominee. Trump has praised Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio on several occasions, but hasn't said when - or if – he'd make an endorsement.
The president appears to relish the guessing game of who he'd back to carry on his political movement, even in the past floating the idea that he'd continue to a third term (which is barred by the US Constitution).
Vance's midterms missive might not be that significant in the end. Or it could have been the starting gun for the 2028 race and the battle for the post-Trump Republican Party.
Nardine Saad contributed reporting.

The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.
@zoo_bear @DelhiPolice Tweet Deleted Now ?
Daro Mat 😂😂 https://t.co/q51PIYEFZG
— 𝐉𝐄𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐒𝐇 𝐀𝐑𝐘𝐀 🇮🇳 (@jeevansharya) October 25, 2026
After the post was deleted, many social media users posted that they expected something like this to happen.
Like most of us predicted, tweet deleted by @DelhiPolice
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) October 25, 2026
The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing side effects of cancer treatment in children. Preventing them is essential not only to improve quality of life, but also to help patients complete treatment. Yet the medicines used to prevent vomiting can themselves cause adverse effects, making the search for safe alternatives an important challenge in paediatric oncology.
An Indian multicentre clinical trial suggests that olanzapine may offer an alternative to dexamethasone, a corticosteroid routinely used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy — treatment with a high risk of inducing vomiting. The current regimen using dexamethasone is a guideline that is used regularly, but dexamethasone is a corticosteroid. The study was aimed at finding a comparable, non-corticosteroid option.

Leh, Nov 5: Ladakh administration on Thursday notified the delimitation of 100 constituencies of the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (LAHDC) in eight districts, specifying the panchayat halqas and villages or wards falling under each constituency.
The move paves the way for elections in the region.
The delimitation was notified through an order issued by the revenue department, in accordance with the final recommendations of the State Election Commission, Ladakh, dated November 5, 2026.
The exercise covers the districts of Leh, Sham, Changthang, Zanskar, Nubra, Kargil, Drass and Sankoo.
"In exercise of the powers conferred under Section 5(1) of the LAHDC Act and in pursuance of the final recommendations of the State Election Commission, the administration of the Union Territory of Ladakh hereby determines and notifies the delimitation of constituencies of the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils, comprising the districts of Leh, Sham, Changthang, Zanskar, Nubra, Kargil, Drass and Sankoo," the notification said.
As per the notification issued by Commissioner-Secretary Shurbir Singh, Leh district has 22 constituencies, Sham 9, Changthang 10, Zanskar 9, Nubra 9, Kargil 21, Drass 7 and Sankoo 13.

- The claim that the U.S. and Israel would carry out a nuclear strike on Iran after the 2026 midterm elections is unproven.
- The rumor stems from an X post by the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson, who claimed on Nov. 1 that Trump could decide to carry out the alleged strike as early as next Nov. 7. Carlson claimed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was attempting to push Trump and his administration to use nuclear weaponry in the war in Iran.
- At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed whether the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran. Experts warned that doing so would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region and could start a global nuclear arms race.
- A White House spokesperson told Snopes that Carlson had "no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking" but that Trump would "do what is right to keep the American people safe."
- Snopes will update this report if, or when, additional information surfaces. We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Sunday.
On Nov. 1, two days before the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, the conservative political commentator Tucker Carlson posted (archived) on X that "the Trump administration may be within days of launching a nuclear strike on Iran."
In a more than 700-word post, Carlson claimed that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was seeking to pressure U.S. President Donald Trump, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and U.S. Central Command head Brad Cooper to take out Iran's Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected key location in Iran's nuclear program, using a nuclear bomb.
According to Carlson's "informed observer," Trump could make a decision on whether to carry out a nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain as soon as Nov. 7.
Carlson's post also circulated on Facebook and Bluesky (archived, archived). Snopes readers contacted us about Carlson's claim.
At the time of this writing, neither the Trump administration nor the Pentagon had confirmed that the president was considering using nuclear force against Iran.
The U.S. has not used nuclear power in warfare since dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, a move that forced a Japanese surrender and led to the end of World War II. Over the past month, Trump has given mixed signals in media interviews about his plans for ending the war in Iran, but has not suggested he was considering using nuclear force.
Experts warned that using nuclear force against Iran would have a devastating impact on the entire Middle East region, could inspire existing nuclear powers like Russia or China to use their arsenal in conflicts in Ukraine and elsewhere and would lead to a nuclear arms race.
A White House spokesperson said in an email to Snopes on Nov. 5:
President Trump has a wide range of options available regarding Iran, and he will do what is right to keep the American people safe. Tucker Carlson lost his way long ago due to a debilitating case of Trump Derangement Syndrome, and he has no insight into military planning or the Commander-in-Chief's thinking.
We contacted the Department of Defense to ask whether Carlson's post was true. We also contacted Carlson to ask about the credibility of his anonymous source and any updates he had gotten on the situation since publishing his initial post on Nov. 1. We await replies to our queries.
Why is Pickaxe Mountain important?
Though there was no proof that the Trump administration would use nuclear power to do so, Trump has been considering striking Pickaxe Mountain — the target Carlson claimed would require nuclear force — since at least July. For example, on July 21, Trump told reporters at the White House (time code 26:34), "We'll be hitting that area pretty soon and very heavily."
In September, the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a bipartisan think tank, wrote that Israeli intelligence reportedly indicated that Iranian authorities moved "uranium centrifuges and centrifuge parts," which are necessary to enrich uranium for commercial or combat use, to Pickaxe Mountain, which is near the Natanz nuclear facility.
At the time, the think tank wrote that Pickaxe Mountain would be "difficult" to destroy "even with the heaviest non-nuclear U.S. munitions." The facility is reportedly buried deep in a granite mountain and the U.S. does not have access to blueprints that would give away its size and shape, or whether it has weak points like the ventilation shafts the U.S. targeted at the Fordo nuclear facility during Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025.
Trump has repeatedly said since the start of the war in Iran that his and Netanyahu's primary goal is that Iran does not get access to enough enriched uranium to obtain a nuclear weapon. To achieve this aim, the U.S. and Israel would need to curtail Iran's nuclear material and capabilities like the site at Pickaxe Mountain through either force or diplomacy.
Carlson's post suggested without proof that the Trump administration was weighing up using its ultimate military power to achieve its aims in Iran.
Mixed signals about Trump's next steps in Iran
Trump has given mixed signals about how he wants to approach his and Netanyahu's goals in Iran. By October, Trump was still saying that he wanted to strike Pickaxe Mountain, though no reports suggested such a strike had taken place.
For example, Trump told Newsmax on Oct. 15, "We're looking at Pickaxe Mountain. We may have to go there. We'll take a shot at that one. We'll knock it out fast."
Starting after Oct. 20, several U.S. news outlets reported that the Trump administration was drawing up plans for strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3. These reports did not say that Trump was considering using nuclear force.
In fact, Trump said on Oct. 15, in response to a question about whether he would use tactical nuclear weapons in Iran, "No, I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to."
This remark could suggest that the U.S. had non-nuclear ways of destroying Pickaxe Mountain or that Trump wanted to allow time for diplomatic negotiations to take place.
However, by the start of November, PBS reported that negotiations between Washington and Tehran on a deal to end the war were "tense." According to the report, Washington wanted early assurances that Iran would not develop a nuclear weapon, while Tehran wanted to defer the issue for later talks.
On Nov. 2, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi appeared to signal that the ball was in the U.S.'s court. He reportedly said:
We have put forward our conditions and proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political judgement. If it opts for sincere diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if it intends to resort to deception or military action, it will face a response more bitter and more severe than before.
Carlson published his post alleging that the U.S. was considering a nuclear resolution to the war in Iran that same day.
By Nov. 3, despite the October reports that the U.S. was planning strikes on Iran after the midterm elections, Trump reportedly told the Financial Times that the U.S. seemed to be "getting everything we want" in diplomatic negotiations and had no plans for immediate strikes.
However, that same day, Trump also told Fox News (time code 13:57) the U.S. had to "do something large" in the war with Iran. He did not specify whether "something large" was in reference to diplomacy or military attacks, but did add, "A lot of people would like to do the heavy hitting."
Trump must balance input from Tel Aviv and Washington
It was unclear from Trump's Election Day interview with Fox News who "a lot of people" were, or who exactly the president was taking advice from on the war in Iran.
On Oct. 28, news broke that U.S. Vice President JD Vance reportedly sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's top security body, in a bid to restart peace talks. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vance sent the letter at Trump's request, though Trump himself appeared to suggest it was Vance's idea. Either way, the letter suggested the U.S. had not given up on the idea of a diplomatic solution to the war in Iran.
On Nov. 1, Carlson claimed that Netanyahu had pressured both Trump and other officials, including Hegseth, to use nuclear power in Iran. PBS reported that there had been "growing fears" that Netanyahu could be pushing Trump to escalate the conflict in Iran.
Netanyahu, whose coalition failed to secure a majority in Israel's October elections, will lose his position as prime minister if he cannot form a 61-seat majority in the Knesset. PBS reported that Netanyahu could be, "pushing for new strikes against Iran in an effort to stay in power in an emergency government during renewed war." Snopes has not independently verified this claim.
Trump reportedly spoke to Netanyahu on Oct. 31, the day before Carlson's post, though the details of that call were unclear. However, the Telegraph newspaper reported it was unlikely Netanyahu would have pushed for a nuclear strike on Iran, writing that if Israel "were seen to be involved in any way in breaking the taboo on the use of nuclear weapons, it could rebound horribly. It would take only one strike on Israel to make it unliveable, given that it is such a tiny country."
Therefore, while Netanyahu might have reason to encourage refreshed strikes on Iran, it's unlikely he would push for those strikes to use nuclear weapons.
Ultimately, the mixed reporting throughout October and November and Araghchi's statement on Nov. 2 suggested the U.S. and Iran were preparing for both a diplomatic and a military resolution to the war, potentially developing at the same time. The available evidence did not suggest that the Trump administration, regardless of input from Netanyahu or anyone else, was planning a U.S. nuclear strike on Iran, something that could set off further strikes in the Middle East and Europe and lead to a nuclear arms race.
For further reading, follow Snopes' coverage of the war in Iran.

Head of Justice Department office on Civil Rights resigns
The head of the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, Harmeet Dhillon, is out after 18 tumultuous months in charge, during which she radically reshaped the unit's mission, oversaw the mass exodus of career staff, and aggressively pursued President Trump's agenda.
Dhillon is the first senior department official to depart the Trump administration since Democrats retook control of the House and Senate in midterm elections.
Attorney General Todd Blanche, in a statement on X, announced Dhillon's resignation and thanked her for her service.
"She has defended the civil liberties of every American and enforced the law without fear or favor," he wrote. "The Department is grateful for her dedicated public service, and we wish her every success in her future endeavors."
In her own statement, Dhillon said the job had been "the honor of a lifetime."
"We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women in girls' sports, and so much more," she added.
During her tenure, Dhillon implemented dramatic changes in the Civil Rights Division, pushing out roughly 300 career attorneys, hiring inexperienced ideological allies to replace them, and using the division's enforcement powers to advance Trump's MAGA policies.
The changes marked a dramatic shift for the division, which was created some 70 years ago during the civil rights movement to end racial segregation in the U.S. For decades, it fought to protect the constitutional rights of all Americans across all aspects of life, from housing and employment to education and policing.
Dhillon, a conservative attorney and Trump loyalist, came into office with a different view. In her eyes, the division had narrowed its mission in recent decades to only protecting the rights of people of color, and she promptly shifted to aggressively pursuing conservative priorities.
"We don't just slow down the woke," she said at a Federalist Society event in 2025. "We take up the cause to achieve the executive branch's goals."
Under her leadership, the division redirected its energies to enforce Trump's executive orders, including ending the alleged radical indoctrination in schools, defending women from "gender ideology extremism," and combatting antisemitism and purported anti-Christian bias.
In the run-up to the midterm elections, the Civil Rights Division sued dozens of states demanding they turn over voter information — in furtherance of Trump's allegations of voter fraud.
Election officials pushed back, and courts tossed the department's lawsuits.
The division also accused numerous universities and law schools of discriminating against white and Asian students, and sued UCLA and Harvard for allegedly allowing antisemitism to flourish on campus.
In an email to division staff, Dhillon said she informed Trump in early October that she planned to return to private practice after the midterms, and now is the time to do so.
"I'm proud of all we've accomplished during this time to ensure our nation's civil rights laws protect every American," she wrote in the email, a copy of which was obtained by NPR. "I'm also grateful for the hard work of the dedicated employees within the Division and the rest of the Department of Justice."
For many division veterans who were highly critical of Dhillon's treatment of career staff and her enforcement goals, her departure was a welcome development.
"Harmeet Dhillon has been the most destructive, lawless, and hateful head of the Civil Rights Division in DOJ history," said Stacey Young, a former division attorney. "Dhillon wielded the enormous power of the Justice Department to threaten universities, state and local officials, and election workers in spurious cases that rarely won in court."
"Americans' civil rights don't enforce themselves. For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Young, who now heads who Justice Connection, a group of department alumni that provides support to DOJ employees.

Crocodile bites Karnataka woman who jumped into river to kill self, screams lead to her rescue
A woman who jumped into Karnataka's Kumaradhara river in an alleged suicide bid was bitten by a crocodile, whose attack triggered screams that alerted rescuers. Police and local residents pulled her out of the water. She suffered minor injuries, received first aid and was later sent home with her family.
Call it a bizarre twist of fate or divine intervention. A woman who plunged into Karnataka's Kumaradhara river in an alleged suicide bid was bitten by a crocodile, an attack that inadvertently saved her life. Her screams for help alerted police personnel and local residents, who rushed to her rescue and pulled her out of the water, police said.
The incident took place near the Kumaradhara bridge at Kukke Subrahmanya on Wednesday night, reported news agency PTI. The woman suffered minor injuries and received first aid at a local hospital before being counselled and sent home with her family, according to police.
Police said the woman was distressed over personal matters when she entered the river intending to end her life. A crocodile bit her while she was in the water, prompting her to cry out for help, a senior police officer said.
Staff members at a nearby lodge heard her screams and informed the Subrahmanya police. Police personnel reached the location and, with help from local residents, pulled her from the river and brought her to safety.
She was then taken to a local hospital, where she was given first aid for her injuries. Police subsequently contacted her relatives and counselled her before allowing her to leave with them.
No complaint has been registered in connection with the incident. Police said the woman's identity had been withheld at her family's request.

FIFA has joined forces with the United Nations (UN) and the World Health Organization (WHO) in supporting the #BeActive campaign launched on the UN International Day of Sport for Development and Peace to encourage people to be #HealthyAtHome as the world comes together in the fight against COVID-19, today and every day.
WHO recommends all healthy adults do at least 30 minutes a day of physical activity and children at least 60 minutes per day. As part of this, #BeActive and remain #HealthyAtHome include the following suggestions along with any other form of recreation to stay healthy at home:
- Taking some online exercise classes,
- Dancing,
- Playing active video games,
- Jumping rope, and
- Practising muscle strength and balance training.
“We are delighted that football is strongly supporting the International Day of Sport for Development and Peace by asking everyone to #BeActive and to remain healthy at home during this difficult time,” said António Guterres Secretary-General of the United Nations. “FIFA has asked the football community, from member associations and clubs, to players and fans, to show their support, to put their rivalries aside and to show a new solidarity so we can overcome the coronavirus. This is an important lesson not only for today, but for every day.”
“More than ever, especially now, one thing must be clear to everyone, health comes first,” said FIFA President Gianni Infantino. “FIFA is delighted to support both the United Nations and the World Health Organization in amplifying the #BeActive campaign today, and we are encouraged that the football community is also playing an active role in ensuring the message understood globally. For the first time ever, we are all on the same team and together, with team spirit and positive energy, we will win.”
“WHO is proud to collaborate as part of the UN family with FIFA and football lovers worldwide to promote the importance of being active for both physical and mental health,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “The #BeActive campaign supports WHO’s drive to help people be healthy at home.”
The campaign kicks off with Real Madrid CF, FC Barcelona, Liverpool FC and Manchester United FC asking football fans to set aside their rivalries and to come together to #BeActive in order to defeat the coronavirus. Other clubs, including Club América, CD Guadalajara, Beijing Guoan FC, Shanghai Shenhua FC, Mohun Bagan AC, East Bengal FC, Melbourne City FC, Sydney FC, Auckland City FC, Team Wellington FC, CA River Plate, Olympique de Marseille, TP Mazembe, CR Flamengo and SE Palmeiras will also join the initiative in the coming days.
As part of the campaign, world-famous players share the following message: “At this time, even rivals need to stick together. We have to keep our distance, but we do not lose our focus. We can show solidarity by being active, and active means following the guidelines from the WHO.”
The video campaign will be published on various FIFA digital channels, with regular subsequent updates from clubs and players across the world during subsequent days. #BeActive is also being supported with graphics toolkits for the 211 FIFA member associations and various media agencies to facilitate additional localisation and to further amplify the message.
WHO, the UN’s specialized health agency, and FIFA, football’s world governing body, collaborate closely to promote healthy lifestyles through football globally and launched the “ Pass the message to kick out coronavirus” campaign last month to share advice effective measures to protect people from COVID-19.

Srinagar, Nov 05: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has questioned the Ladakh administration's reported move against the Himalayan Institute of Alternatives, Ladakh (HIAL), alleging that the institution is being targeted despite receiving national and international recognition.
In a statement, Wangchuk described the administration's action as a “shahi farmaan” against the school, sarcastically questioning the decision with the remark, “Close schools and open liquor bars.”
“There is a lot of raita spread on the internet and news about our school,” Wangchuk said, adding that India's Parliamentary Committee on Education had recommended replicating HIAL across the country.
He further claimed that the institution had received international recognition, including a permanent display at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and a feature in TIME magazine's list of 100 climate solutions.
“ And yet... They want it closed!” he said.
The controversy stems from a notice issued by the Office of the Tehsildar, Leh, directing HIAL, co-founded by Wangchuk and Gitanjali J Angmo, to refrain from undertaking any further activities at the school until the court delivers its verdict or issues fresh directions.
As per reports, the administration cited the commencement of classes and other activities without obtaining the requisite consent, clearances or approvals from the competent authorities. The notice also referred to a representation submitted by Angmo to the Deputy Commissioner, Leh, on September 22, seeking a no-objection certificate (NOC) or clearance for the proposed members of the school's managing committee.

Warning: this article contains discussion of eating disorders
"If you keep this up, you'll be in a wheelchair at 30."
That is what doctors told British long-distance runner Jake Smith four years ago.
From the outside looking in, his career was flying.
By the age of 23, he had signed a professional contract with Nike and represented Great Britain on the global stage.
But at the same time, his body was deteriorating - enduring a relentless pattern of race, illness, injury, repeat.
Balancing an intense training regime with disordered eating meant the 28-year-old returned from a running camp in Uganda weighing just eight stone (51kg) at 5ft 5in (1.7m). He had such brittle bones that he was told his career could be over.
After suffering two stress fractures in the space of four months, Smith sought professional help and was diagnosed with REDs – relative energy deficiency in sport.
It is a syndrome that can affect anyone and if left undiagnosed or untreated, can have an impact on performance and cause serious, long-lasting health problems.
The symptoms are slightly better documented in women - just last month, tennis player Emma Navarro revealed her diagnosis and subsequent decision to step away from competition until 2027.
But men are just as susceptible and due to stigma and lack of obvious warning signs, it can go undetected for longer and means many, like Smith, suffer in silence.
BBC Sport explains what the condition is, how it affects men and women and why, despite its prevalence and severity, REDs remains a relatively under-reported and overlooked area of sports science.
REDs can cause bone stress injuries, disrupted sleep, fatigue and low mood. Left untreated, the condition can lead to serious long-term health problems, including osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and fertility issues.
Dr Nicky Keay, an expert in hormone health, says many of these symptoms stem from hormonal disruption caused by insufficient energy intake.
"Hormones go to every single bit in your body. So, if your hormones are not working well for you, you're going to feel it in all sorts of different areas," she says.
"In order to have healthy hormones, they need to be fed regularly. If you're not doing that and there's an energy deficit, often some of those hormone systems will slow down or shut down completely."
Women have a monthly barometer of their hormone health with the menstrual cycle, described by Keay as a "free monthly medical check".
Put simply, she says, a woman suffering from REDs has her periods "switched off".
For men, it is more subtle – testosterone levels will drop, resulting in a reduced libido and fatigue.
The impact on a woman's period is why the condition was first referred to in the early 1990s as the "female athlete triad".
But it was renamed by the International Olympic Committee in 2014 to acknowledge the broader range of symptoms of energy deficiency and that it also harms male athletes.
"We realised we were ignoring the other half of the population," Keay says.
"It's a strange situation because normally it's women's health that is the one being ignored but, in this situation, it's the men who weren't being recognised or represented."
Twelve years later that decision appears to be vindicated, with recent research highlighting the prevalence in men.
Meta-analysis published in Australian journal Sports Medicine last year, following a study involving thousands of elite and amateur athletes around the world, indicated 44.2% of female athletes and 49.4% of male athletes had low energy availability.
So why is REDs so common?
One of the answers lies in the phrase 'lighter is faster'.
For decades, it had been an accepted wisdom in sports like endurance running, cycling, climbing, horse riding, dancing and aesthetic sports like diving and gymnastics.
And for athletes like Smith, it is how his problems started.
"I believed it for years. I thought that was the way forward," he says.
"I started thinking 'how do I improve my half marathon by 10 seconds? Is it a drop in weight?'. And that's when my head completely went."
Initially, the strategy can work.
When it comes to choosing energy to cover training demand or energy to stay healthy, the body has learned through evolution and threat of predators to always prioritise movement.
It means that athletes can drop weight and still train and exercise and achieve good results.
But eventually, the luck runs out.
Described by Keay as "fool's gold", the body will adjust to the energy deficit and cause a drop in performance and high risk of injuries.
Olympic and world champion Jonny Brownlee acknowledges under-fuelling mistakes he made in his triathlon career contributed to serious injuries.
"I didn't see the importance of it. Training came first and I think we weren't educated enough in how important fuelling was," he tells BBC Sport.
"You were seen, culturally, as a bit weak if you were fuelling on the bike. And the impact of that was definitely injuries - probably not recovering from my training quite as well as I should have done, stress responses, stress fractures. So there's that side of it and probably underperformance in races as well."
Brownlee, who recently announced his retirement, believes the culture of not fuelling on the bike has now changed but a stigma lingers around REDs and the perception that it is a "female issue".
"In females, there are more obvious signs but in males it can go under the radar a little bit and then it hits you by a really serious injury," he says.
"I think there's a stigma attached in there, or it's not looked at as the obvious answer to some of your problems, it's found later down the line. Men also don't like to talk about under-fuelling because it's just seen as 'you probably should feel better and you should be on top of that'."
It is those attitudes among male athletes that prompted Keay to conduct an experiment in 2019.
Assessing 50 male competitive cyclists, Keay found in her initial screenings that nearly half had poor bone health and 25% were suffering from REDs.
The cyclists were then split into two groups and across a six-month period, one half continued their training and fuelling habits as before while the others were tutored by Keay and offered nutrition and training advice.
"The group that I left to their own devices unfortunately went on the default and they lost even more bone mineral density, similar to an astronaut in space… And they performed OK, but relative to their functional threshold power, they didn't get the race results that you would have expected.
"For the group I took under my wing, there was an improvement in their bone health and really good race results.
"So, I had evidence that REDs definitely does exist quite extensively in my group of the male cyclists and you're going to underperform if you don't fuel sufficiently. The good news is that REDs is reversible. But if you don't take action, it's a decline."
As the syndrome and its symptoms are still not commonly known, it is often difficult to know where to find help.
After former GB runner Pippa Woolven's struggles with the condition, she set up a website called Project REDs which offers information and practical resources for athletes, coaches, parents and healthcare professionals.
Keay also helps people competing at all levels to recover from REDs. Most of her patients are women, but she is starting to see more men reach out for help who, she says, are often in "bad shape".
"I think the men are maybe more reluctant than the women, or maybe they don't realise they've got it. Sometimes they might use a different word for it, they say burnout," Keay says.
"I don't mind that though because there is definitely a psychological aspect to REDs. Why are you doing this? Why are you not eating the carbohydrates?"
Sometimes, it's hard to answer those questions because the under-fuelling is unintentional, either from not understanding or underestimating energy requirements or failing to match an increase in the intensity or duration of exercise with higher calorie or carbohydrate intake.
For others, former British cycling champion Brian Smith among them, the answer comes from intention.
Competing in the road race for Great Britain at the 1996 Olympics should have been the highlight of his career but, behind the scenes of the success, Smith was suffering with an eating disorder and serious mental health condition called bulimia – something he believes he developed from his sport's obsession with weight.
"I always felt like I was overweight. Everybody was under pressure regarding weight, but nobody really spoke about it," he says.
"I'm just under six foot and I've got large glutes and thigh muscles. As a road cyclist, I used to race at 68kg and for my height and build, that's quite skinny. I even got down to about 66kg and when I got down to that, I felt underpowered, I felt bad."
Smith, now 59, only discovered he had been suffering from REDs during his career when he started running eight years ago and developed three severe stress fractures, including one in his femur.
Such has been the toll on his body that Smith says he would now never encourage anyone to pursue a career as a professional cyclist.
"It really is not healthy," he says. "If you want to go to the highest levels of the sport, you will suffer later on in life. You're destroying your body.
"Sporting teams don't care - all they're worried about is performance. So they will nurture a rider, they will feed a rider, they'll get a rider to be a certain weight. They don't care about what happens to them later in life.
"I'm suffering now and I've so many regrets. I just wish I'd known more about this."
While Smith believes his sport has a long way to go in changing attitudes, British Cycling says a lot of progress has been made through education that starts at academy level and annual physical and psychological screenings.
"One of the big things we've done in the past 10 years is try and turn this into a performance-related conversation," Dr Nigel Jones, British Cycling chief medical officer, tells BBC Sport.
"Now, we couch the conversation with an athlete around 'if you under-fuel, you will not be able to perform at your best', whereas previously, conversations in power-to-weight ratio sports might have been 'you need to be lighter'.
"I think it would be naive to say REDs is never going to be an issue. But I would like to believe that its prevalence will reduce with the work that we're doing," he adds.
British Cycling is not alone in this approach, with World Climbing taking things a step further two years ago with the introduction of mandatory health checks on athletes.
Using a combination of pre-season questionnaires and 'random and targeted' screenings at competitions - similar to the way doping tests are enforced – climbers at World Championship or World Cup-level competitions are monitored for any indicators of low energy availability or REDs and could be prevented from competing if they are not deemed to be healthy.
The policy was drawn up by expert Professor Naama Constantini, who says she is "proud" of the move by World Climbing and believes other federations should follow suit.
"We are trying to educate and prevent. I'm not a policeman and we're not looking for cheaters. I'm a medical doctor and we want to make sure our athletes are healthy," she says.
"Prevention is the best medicine you can give. We want athletes and coaches to understand that it's not about weight. It's about strength, it's about performance and fuelling the body and you pay a price if you lose weight in an unhealthy way."
With more awareness and education, it is hoped the tide can be turned on REDs.
But many still suffer in ignorance, as well as silence. That is what motivates Jake Smith to keep sharing his recovery on social media, with hundreds of men and women messaging him for advice and support.
Smith has managed to reverse his condition and is now racing better than ever, recently completing the Berlin marathon in a personal-best time of two hours, nine minutes and 24 seconds.
The big goal is the 2028 Olympics, but he is adamant that the priority is making sure he stands on every start line as healthy as possible.
"I'd never want to see an athlete go through the years I've had. I'm 10-15 kilos heavier than I've ever been and the biggest thing I can say is I've never been so happy. You need a healthy body to do everything else.
"I'm heavier, I'm faster, I'm happier."
