The Supreme Court on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) held that laws penalising having more than two children have lost their relevance due to the falling fertility rate in India.
“We are of the strong opinion that laws that penalise having more than two children have lost their relevance. The foundation of such laws, that is, the fear of overpopulation, has crumbled due to demographic changes in the past few decades,” a Bench headed by Justice P.S. Narasimha observed in a 37-page judgment.
The court said its 2003 judgment (in Javed versus State of Haryana) which upheld such penal laws, needed a revisit by a larger Bench. India’s Total Fertility Rate (TFR) had fallen from 3.02 to 1.9. A TFR of 2.1, known as the replacement rate, would allow one generation to completely replace itself.
“Even though India’s population is not yet declining, the TFR falling below the replacement rate will soon result in a demographic transition towards an older population with a declining share of the working-age population. Therefore, laws aimed at limiting population growth have now lost their significance,” Justice Narasimha observed.
The 2003 judgment in the Javed case had referred to the situation that existed in China as of 2000 and drew inspiration from the measures that it had undertaken to control the population.
Justice Narasimha said the decades-old view that population explosion was an impediment for progress was outdated.
Healthy growth
“The earlier perception that population harms development does not hold water anymore. Rather than society and the courts being concerned about the negative consequences of high population, it should instead focus on the need to encourage a healthy growth of population,” the judgment, by a Bench comprising Justice Alok Aradhe, said.
The judgment pointed out that the share of persons aged 60 and above had already risen from about 8.3% in 2014 to 9.7% in 2024, and government projections place that share at nearly 15% by 2036.
India’s falling fertility rate, the court said, would necessarily mean a smaller proportion of younger persons in the future, and, correspondingly, a larger ageing population. It said the issue had been of significant concern in recent years.
The court said the failure to take notice of demographic changes would lead to only serious consequences for India. Failure to adapt not only produced injustice, but was also an abuse of power.
The judgment was based on a petition filed by Mangala Bhimrao Ingle, whose election as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat in Maharashtra was set aside on the ground that she had more than two children. The lower courts and State authorities found that she had given birth to a third child in 2014, but still contested and won the panchayat elections in 2022. They had held that she acted in violation of Section 14(1)(j-1) of the Maharashtra Village Panchayats Act, 1959, which upheld the two-child norm.
Justice Narasimha found such laws linking motherhood to political representation a violation of Article 21 (right to life) under the Constitution.
“Allowing such laws to stand excludes an entire class of citizens from political representation on grounds bearing little rational connection to their capacity to hold public office. It compels an unconscionable choice between bearing children and democratic participation, impinging on the right to reproductive autonomy under Article 21,” Justice Narasimha observed.
Seeking an immediate re-visitation of the Javed judgment of 2003, the court permitted the appellant to continue in her elected position as Sarpanch of the Kakoda gram panchayat while staying any proceedings against her.

Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.
The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."
Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.
Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:
B – BALANCE loss
Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.
E – EYE changes
Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.
F – FACE drooping
Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.
A – ARM weakness
Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?
S – SPEECH difficulty
Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?
T – TIME to call 911
If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.
A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.
Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.
Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

Haitian police say they found vehicle of 4 missing Salvadorans as search continues
Haiti’s National Police agency has found the charred remains of a vehicle used by four missing Salvadoran aviation technicians
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Haiti’s National Police agency says it has found the charred remains of a vehicle that four Salvadoran aviation technicians were traveling in when they were attacked more than two weeks ago deep in gang-controlled territory, but no sign of the missing men.
The attack on Oct. 18 prompted Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele to send more than 2,000 troops to Haiti to help find the missing technicians. That deployment has raised questions about who is in charge of the soldiers as they work alongside an international effort to quell the gangs terrorizing the Caribbean nation.
Haitian authorities said late Tuesday that they found the vehicle on the outskirts of the capital in the neighborhood of Santo in the Croix-des-Bouquets community, which has been under the control of violent gangs, though police said they met no resistance there.
Authorities posted pictures of the charred vehicle and said the operation that took place early Monday was carried out by Haitian police, the U.N.-backed gang suppression force and Salvadoran troops.
The U.N. has said that the Salvadoran troops are operating outside of the framework of the U.N. gang suppression force and stressed that they should follow international law. Haiti's prime minister has said foreign forces are under Haitian command, but Bukele has not confirmed that for the Salvadoran soldiers.
In a statement late Tuesday on X, Bukele invoked Haitian hero Jean-Jacques Dessalines and said that those who betrayed the liberator “still exist in Haiti.”
“Some are gang members, others finance the gangs or supply them with weapons, and some among them are doing everything they can to prevent the Haitian people from gaining their freedom,” Bukele wrote.
He posted hours after Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé spoke publicly for the first time since the attack, saying that Haiti is in charge of any foreign forces in the country and that they are not replacing the state.
Bukele promised to rid Haiti of its “traitors.”
“We can help you defeat them, but we are not your enemies,” he wrote. “We are people with the same courage as you. We must stand up, take back control of our communities, and put under our control those who are making us endure all this pain, all this suffering.”
As Haitian police and soldiers, along with foreign forces, battle gangs in Port-au-Prince and beyond, one gang leader called for dialogue.
Wilson Joseph, best known as Lanmò Sanjou and leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, told The Associated Press on Monday that he wrote the U.N. secretary-general and requested that the organization deploy a delegation to Haiti for dialogue.
Joseph said he was concerned about the killing of civilians given the surge in fighting.

Typhoons batter East Asia as El Niño makes Pacific 'burn with fever'
- Published
Wild weather is a way of life for people living along the coast in the Philippines, Taiwan, China and Japan. But the last few months have been extraordinary.
A wave of intense and, at times, unpredictable storms exacerbated by the El Niño weather pattern has killed dozens, shuttered major airports and wiped out crops and infrastructure across a swathe of East Asia.
In October, nearly all of Taiwan shut down as a monster storm big enough to engulf the island of 23 million roared towards its north-eastern coast. Equivalent to a category five hurricane, Typhoon Champi's 295km/h (193mph) winds had the power to flatten homes and whip up destructive waves.
Thankfully it did not make landfall in Taiwan, skirting past the island while dousing it in rain. But it had far-reaching impacts: hundreds of flights were cancelled in Hong Kong, Taiwan and Japan. In the Philippines' Batanes archipelago, seaside highways shut as huge waves crashed onto the shore, and in southern Japan's Okinawa islands, power was cut to 15,000 homes.
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon in which warm waters pooling in the eastern Pacific and altered wind patterns drive extreme weather events around the world.
It happens around every two to seven years, lasting for around a year. This year's El Niño, which the UK Met Office has forecast to be the "strongest in living memory", is likely to last until February or March.
In June, Japan watched two storms - Typhoon Mekkhala and Severe Tropical Storm Higos - race towards its eastern coast simultaneously, forcing one million people to evacuate. In July, Tropical Storm Narra grazed China's southern coast along Guangxi, submerging villages and displacing tens of thousands.
August brought Super Typhoon Dolphin, which churned across the Pacific for 16 days - before slamming into eastern China, triggering heavy floods and dozens of casualties.
Later that month Typhoon Saudel made landfall in three south-eastern Chinese cities over one week, shutting transport networks and forcing thousands to evacuate.
'Burning with fever'
The Pacific Ocean, heated to record levels by El Niño, is now brimming with typhoon energy, according to the Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) metric which measures the total intensity of a season's storms. This year, the ACE reading for South East and East Asia is forecast to be nearly double the 30-year average.
El Niño also affects wind patterns and in this case, that means typhoons are tending to form further east than usual. They are also becoming stronger as they remain over warm waters for longer.
The Pacific can be likened to someone "burning with fever", says Ana Liza Solis, head of climatology at the Philippines' national weather bureau. "It can go into convulsions soon," she said at a press briefing in Manila in September.
Forecasts suggest the worst may not be over. Last month, sea surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific - the area monitored by the Japan Meteorological Agency for its El Niño predictions - soared to 4C above normal, the highest since records began in 1949. The previous record - 3.6C - was set in December 1997.
China's climate agency has warned of sea surface temperatures continuing to rise over the next three months because of the El Niño.
Despite typhoon season usually peaking around September to October, this is likely to raise concerns across a region that has already been battered by back-to-back storms.
'Very, very scary' simulations
In August, Typhoon Chan-Hom baffled storm watchers in Japan by crossing the country from east to west, as opposed to the usual south-to-north trajectory. Japan's well-resourced and prepared authorities were able to evacuate people swiftly, but this would be far more challenging in some neighbouring countries.
To get a better picture of how rising temperatures could amplify the risks, Manila-based climatologist Rafaela Jane Delfino and colleagues simulated the effects of warmer conditions on the Philippines' most recent monster storms, including 2013's Super Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) which killed more than 6,000 people.
They arrived at what she describes as "very, very scary findings": higher temperatures increased total accumulated rainfall by 26%. It's a devastating prospect in a country where flooding from monsoon rains and some 20 tropical storms per year has emerged as one of the main disaster risks.
In recent years, floods have paralysed entire cities for days, and tired of the annual ordeal, Filipinos have taken to the streets to protest against corruption which they say is gnawing away at millions of dollars from flood-control projects.
Delfino, in an article on the University of the Philippines website, insists leaders and officials must gain a better understanding of climate hazards if communities are to be better prepared.
Preparing for the onslaught
Countries are bracing for the immediate impact. Japan has urged citizens to stockpile food and essentials for the typhoon season, and to secure outdoor furniture that could become deadly projectiles when typhoon winds hit. China has asked local officials to identify vulnerable areas and is upgrading its warning and monitoring systems.
The Philippines and its South East Asian neighbours are preparing for disruptions to food production, especially rice, and have increased support for famers, including the provision of fertilisers.
But what happens in the long term is less clear. The window for governments to act on El Niño is "closing", the United Nations Development Programme in Asia and the Pacific said recently.
"How severely a community experiences an El Niño is decided years in advance, by where roads and settlements are built, how water is managed, who is covered by social protection and whether public budgets have room to absorb a shock.
"Every El Niño tests the resilience we have built; this one should also drive us to build more," it added.

No change in IT chief's supervision: EC official after work order revision
The EC has clarified that DG (IT) Seema Khanna continued under a senior deputy election commissioner's supervision after the deputy election commissioner's transfer. The senior DEC, designated as the latter's link officer, took over his allocated responsibilities. A July 28 order directing Khanna to report directly to the EC was never implemented.
A senior Election Commission official on Thursday said that there had been no change in the supervisory structure for its director general of information technology, a day after the poll authority revised its work allocation order, reported news agency PTI.
Under the order issued on Wednesday, DG (IT) Seema Khanna will be supervised by newly appointed deputy election commissioner Prakash Raj Purohit instead of senior deputy election commissioner Manish Garg. Khanna, an NIC officer, is also at the centre of a controversy over the alleged centralisation of digital electoral roll infrastructure and restrictions built into election software systems.
The clarification came in response to a question on whether Khanna had reported directly to the Commission, comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and the two Election Commissioners, between July 28 and November 4 without the additional supervisory layer of a deputy election commissioner.
The issue arose after Garg issued an order on July 28 directing Khanna to report directly to the Commission. He issued the order after deputy election commissioner Sanjay Kumar, to whom Khanna had been reporting, was transferred to the Delhi government.
Election Commissioners SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi objected to the order, following which it was kept in abeyance.
In a press note issued following The Indian Express's report, the poll body said, "The work redistribution orders issued by the concerned officer were not actually implemented following the orders of the two Commissioners, and oversight of the IT division by the DEC was never actually withdrawn."
“Since the order was not implemented, Khanna was supervised by Garg after Sanjay Kumar moved out of the EC. Now, she will report to Raj Purohit, who joined as deputy EC a few days ago,” the official told PTI.
Garg was designated as the “link officer” for Sanjay Kumar, meaning that Kumar's allocated responsibilities passed to Garg after Kumar left the Election Commission.
The Commission's position is that Khanna continued to work under Garg's supervision after Kumar's departure and will now report to Purohit under the revised allocation of duties.

Digital traffic simulation model, road safety audit for 2,205km of Delhi roads
Traffic congestion in Delhi has been increasing, with even stretches that earlier experienced smooth traffic movement now witnessing frequent bottlenecks
Under spotlight for congestion on Delhi’s arterial road network and worsening traffic congestion, the Public Works Department (PWD) has decided to undertake a comprehensive traffic simulation study and road safety audit covering 2,205.68km of roads across its South, North and East zones in Delhi. The ₹11.17-crore exercise will use digital models to study traffic movement on individual road stretches and test possible solutions to congestion before implementing them on the ground.
Roads and Zones Covered
The study, which is expected to be completed within three months, will cover 1,796 roads across the three zones. These include 270 roads spanning 426.28 km in the South Zone, 1,137 roads covering 1,374.76 km in the North Zone, and 389 roads stretching across 404.64 km in the East Zone. PWD oversees arterial road networks with width more than 60ft while smaller roads are overseen by the Municipal Corporation of Delhi.
Why the Study Is Needed
According to the project report, traffic congestion has been increasing across the city, with even stretches that earlier experienced relatively smooth traffic movement now witnessing frequent bottlenecks, particularly during peak hours. Rising vehicle numbers, inadequate road capacity, poorly designed intersections, on-street parking and conflicting traffic movements have added to the problem. The increasing incidence of road accidents has also highlighted the need for a scientific assessment of the city’s road infrastructure.

Traffic Data and Digital Models
As part of the exercise, the department will collect detailed data on traffic volumes, turning movements at intersections, vehicle speeds during peak hours, travel times, road geometry and pedestrian movement. Surveys will also cover public transport operations, parking demand and other factors influencing traffic movement.
“The collected data will be fed into specialised traffic simulation software to create virtual models of individual roads and intersections. These models will allow engineers and traffic planners to recreate existing traffic conditions and test different scenarios to identify the most effective solutions and recommend infrastructure changes and development of new flyovers and underpasses,” official said.
For instance, authorities will be able to assess whether changing traffic signal timings, opening or closing U-turns, introducing dedicated turning lanes, modifying lane markings or changing traffic circulation patterns can reduce congestion. The models will also help evaluate the impact of proposed road widening, flyovers, underpasses and other infrastructure projects before they are taken up.
The three month long study will also examine major junctions to identify locations where traffic signals, road geometry and intersection designs are contributing to delays. Possible interventions such as intersection redesign, pedestrian crossings, refuge islands, traffic calming and improved bus facilities will be assessed, officials added.

Road Safety Audit and Possible Interventions
In the second phase, a road safety audit will be conducted alongside the traffic simulation exercise, with particular attention to accident-prone stretches and vulnerable road users, including pedestrians and cyclists. The audit will assess existing road designs, visibility, signage, street lighting, road dividers, footpaths, cycle tracks and zebra crossings to identify safety deficiencies.
Based on the findings, the department will recommend engineering interventions such as improved road markings, safer pedestrian crossings, better lighting, speed-control measures and redesigned junctions to reduce the risk of accidents.

Hoax bomb threats target European airlines and airports for second time in a week
- Published
At least 21 aircraft and several airports across Europe have been targeted by bomb threats in the second such incident this week, with the UK calling it a "malicious hoax".
Flights to Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, France, Italy, Poland and Romania were affected. An Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome was diverted to an air base in France and Italian fighter jets escorted Finnair's Helsinki-Rome flight.
EasyJet said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were met by police in Prague as a precaution. London Heathrow and Birmingham airports received threats that were assessed as not credible.
No explosives have been found during searches, and it is not clear if the incidents, some claimed by a little known group, are related.
The airport authorities in Italy's capital Rome said the hoax threat against two inbound flights received on Thursday had come by email.
The warnings were signed on behalf of a group or individual calling themselves "Fighters of the Male State", claiming to be targeting a "feminist regime" and wanting to "make our mark on history".
They threatened to "turn the skies red" with explosions.
These details were first reported by Italian media and then confirmed to the BBC by Aeroporti di Roma, which manages both of the city airports.
"Fighters of the Male State" likely refers to the Russian group "Muzhskoi Legion" ( "Male Legion") - an ultra-right group with such extreme views it was banned by a Moscow court in 2021. Yet it retained tens of thousands of online followers as it cheered on the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in the following year.
But that email, even if genuine, is unlikely to provide the leads that police and airport authorities need to pin down who is generating these hoaxes and why.
UK Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander described Thursday's incidents as "malicious hoax threats."
She said the government was taking "these threats seriously", stressing that there were "established processes for dealing with hoax and malicious threats".
A UK government spokesperson later said the threats reported "in the early hours" of the day had been "resolved", without giving any further details.
Heathrow later said in a statement it had received a threat earlier in the day which was "deemed not credible", adding there was "no risk to passengers, colleagues or the aircraft".
"There are robust UK aviation security standards in place to assess and safely manage these types of situations," the statement said.
Meanwhile, a Birmingham Airport spokesperson told the BBC it had received a threat, after which "processes were immediately initiated in conjunction with emergency services and partners".
The following flights were targeted by threats on Thursday:
- Aer Lingus said its flight from Dublin to Rome diverted to Normandy, landing safely. The company added that it was working to "re-accommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible".
- Two Finnair flights from Helsinki landed at their destinations as normal, the airline said. One was escorted into Rome's Fiumicino airport by Italian Air Force fighter jets, Aeroporti di Roma told the BBC, while the other landed in Vienna, Austria
- Wizz Air said two flights which departed Milan were affected - one was heading to Warsaw, before being diverting to Vienna; the other landed safely in Bucharest, with teams inspecting the aircraft
- Polish airline LOT said its flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed as planned, and "no suspicious items were found". Another LOT flight from Warsaw to Paris was stopped before take-off and the plane and baggage underwent a security screening, with no hazardous items found
- Three Ryanair flights landed in Bulgaria, according to Bulgarian media - one from Copenhagen and another from Madrid landed in the capital Sofia, while a third coming from London bound for Sofia landed in Plovdiv. The flights were escorted by Bulgarian air force fighter jets
- No explosives were found on four flights which landed in Prague, Czech police said. EasyJet later said its flights from Newcastle and Glasgow were among those affected. "Passengers on both flights disembarked normally," the company said
- Aegean Airlines said it "was informed of a bomb threat" concerning two of its flights from Thessaloniki in Greece to Milan, and also from Athens to Vienna. It said threat was "unfounded", and both flights departed from the respective airports"
- A Ryanair flight from Porto in Portugal landed safely in Milan as planned, with bomb disposal experts checking them on arrival, Italy's Ansa news agency reported
- Spain's airport authority said it had received bomb threats affecting three flights at Madrid airport, but any threat was ruled out following inspections. Iberia later said two of its flights - Milan-Madrid and Rome-Madrid - were affected. It was not clear whether the third plane was the above reported Ryanair Madrid to Sofia flight
- Air Serbia said its flight from Belgrade to Bucharest "landed safely at its destination airport", and after checks, a reported bomb threat was "assessed as unfounded"
Emily Noble, who was aboard the diverted Aer Lingus plane from Dublin to Rome, said she was about an hour into her flight to attend a friend's wedding in the Italian capital when passengers were told about a "technical" problem.
Later, as the Aer Lingus plane began circling for an unplanned landing in France, the pilot said there was a "security" issue, the 26-year-old from Dublin told BBC Verify.
On board it was "an odd experience," Noble said. "It was worrying because we didn't know what was going on, but we were all trying to be as calm as we could."
Noble says she could hear fighter jets during the landing and saw one touch down behind the aircraft.
After landing at the Évreux-Fauville air base in Normandy, passengers learned the flight had been the subject of a bomb threat.
Noble said they remained on board for two-and-a-half hours while police and military personnel carried out checks, including searches with sniffer dogs.
The passengers were later told they would be taken to an airport in Paris and another plane would fly them on to Rome.
Philip Baum, professor of aviation security at the University of Coventry, said the industry "faces multiple bomb threats every single day" but he had been "surprised" by this week's incidents.
A flight is diverted "only when the threat is credible and the authorities believe there is a potential of explosive device on board", he said.
He said the concern was that "if you issue enough hoax threats, then complacency could set in and a real threat could be ignored - or they could be a diversion".
Marco Chan, an aviation expert at Kingston University, told the BBC the threats were "most likely a hoax, but the system is right to treat it as real".
He said they were being viewed by some experts as "possibly part of a pattern of cheap, deniable disruption" to air travel.
Hoaxes can also come from copycats, he said, but "three days of incidents is too small a sample to separate coordination from contagion".
Two days ago, seven European flights, including two from the UK, were searched after bomb threats were made. No explosives were found on any of the planes after searches.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia was escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.

ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline
- Published
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's biggest party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.
For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.
The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.
Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.
A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".
"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.
Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.
The same poll, along with others, points to a slight increase in electoral support for the Democratic Alliance (DA), especially in Johannesburg. Ipsos predicts the DA will garner 25% support in this election, up from 22% last time.
DA leader Helen Zille has been vying for the mayoral chain in the city and her unusual campaign has attracted a lot of attention.
The former Cape Town mayor has been captured swimming in crater-sized potholes, ziplining over sinkholes and riding into her final rally in the city in a classic BMW 325i, known locally as a "Gusheshe".
She believes the DA is the country's best choice for a government, telling local radio broadcaster 702 last week that "towns and cities that work best are under DA governance".
Verwoerd, a former ANC MP and South Africa's ambassador to Ireland, predicted that coalitions would continue being the order of the day across Gauteng.
These types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic at a local level and the constant change in leadership, usually caused by parties falling out with each other, has affected service delivery in many municipalities.
Verwoerd said in her view, the most stable coalitions would be those that replicate what the ANC and DA have done on a national level, where the historic rivals have agreed to share power.
Reflecting on Cape Town, she said it was unlikely that the DA would lose control of the municipality. The coastal city is widely considered the country's best-performing metro and has been run by the DA since the late 2000s when it unseated the ANC.
Ethekwini, which includes the port city of Durban in KwaZulu-Natal, would be a "different story", Verwoerd said.
The uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has been projected to perform well in the area but it is unclear if it will secure the outright majority needed to run the metro. Polls suggest it won't and will need partners to form a government.
The party was founded by former South African President Jacob Zuma and was the biggest party across his home province of KwaZulu-Natal in the 2024 provincial election.
Verwoerd reflected that while various options were on the table for the party, forming a government would be "very messy" given its refusal to work with either the ANC or DA.
A confident Zuma, addressing supporters on Sunday, vowed to take control of a number of municipalities after the elections.
Another political analyst Dr Levy Ndou echoed Verwoerd's assessment, saying that a coalition between the DA and ANC seemed unavoidable in most metros.
"We're not sure whether the arrangement of the government of national unity could have the potential to influence how the metros are going to be run," he said.
Both experts also spoke about the declining voter turnout in South Africa's elections. Over 29 million citizens are registered to vote, but the turnout, especially among young people, has seen a steady decline.
Ndou attributed this to the "calibre" of the candidates campaigning and the lack of visibility of local councillors, who are often the ones elected to lead their neighbourhoods, in election campaigns.
South Africa's electoral commission has seven days to announce the results, but parties have 14 days to form a governing structure.

The best smart ring does a lot without asking much of you, passively tracking your activity, health, and sleep. Some models go even further, with meal logging, AI coaching, and cycle tracking. No distracting screens. No bulky smartwatch banging you in the face while you're deep in REM sleep.
Once the preserve of wealthy wellness buffs, top-of-the-line smart rings are becoming increasingly affordable and available. Although our top pick is still Finnish pioneer Oura's Ring 5 (from $399), the company is no longer the only fish in the smart-ring sea, thanks to upstarts like Ultrahuman and RingConn, established fitness-tracking brands like Amazfit, and even tech giants like Samsung. I expect to see more entrants in the coming months, but for now, these are the best smart rings we’ve tried.
For more wearable recommendations, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Smartwatches, the Best Fitness Trackers, and the Best Fitbits.
Featured in This Guide
How I Test Smart Rings
WIRED has been testing smart rings since the NFC Ring and the first-ever Oura Ring. I wear each smart ring 24/7, for at least a month, to assess how it performs in everyday life. Every ring is worn during activities like commuting, exercising, and sleeping to see how comfortable it feels over extended use and whether the design causes irritation, scratches easily, or gets in the way of everyday tasks.
- Sleep tracking: Sleep tracking is one of the biggest reasons people buy smart rings, so I wear each device overnight for several weeks and compare data trends against other trackers I regularly use, including wearables and sleep-tracking mats. I also evaluate whether the personalized insights (readiness metrics, sleep apnea detection, and coaching recommendations) are useful.
- Fitness tracking: I wear each ring during a range of workouts—including walks, runs, and high-intensity training—to evaluate how accurately it tracks movement, heart rate variability (HRV), and other exertion metrics. I compare data trends against other fitness trackers I regularly use.
- Durability: I expose all smart rings to daily handwashing, temperature fluctuations, and bumps. I check for scratches, coating wear, and water resistance performance.
- Companion app: Since most smart rings lack screens, companion apps need to be user-friendly. I evaluate how easy the apps are to navigate, how clearly they present health data, and whether paywalled subscriptions lock away essential features.
- Battery life: Battery life claims are tested. I track how long each ring lasts with all available features, such as continuous heart-rate monitoring, workout recognition, and sleep tracking. I also look at how quickly each ring charges and whether its charging accessories are practical to use.
- Sizing: Because fit is critical for accurate readings and usability, I take note of sizing ranges and kits. I test multiple finger placements when possible and track performance to determine how dependable the readings are.
- Value: Some smart rings cost as much as a premium smartwatch, and many also require monthly subscriptions. To determine whether a ring is worth buying, I consider its build quality, the accuracy of its features, the app experience, and any ongoing fees.
What Am I Testing Next?
I am testing the new Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the RingConn Gen 3, and the Pulse Ring.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Smart Ring Overall
The original Oura Ring unilaterally created the health smart ring category. This stylish, unobtrusive ring, popularized by biohacking billionaires, soon brought miniaturized fitness tracking to the masses.
Why WIRED recommends: The latest Oura Ring 5 is 40 percent smaller than its predecessor, making it one of the comfiest wearables to keep on all day and night. The titanium exterior has a new coating applied with physical vapor deposition (PVD) to improve scratch resistance, and the ring itself features redesigned sensors, stronger signal detection, and consequently, better accuracy. It also has improved battery life, lasting up to nine days of use.
The biggest upgrade is Oura's push toward AI-powered health guidance. Similar to Google Health Coach, the Oura Advisor can answer wellness questions, provide personalized recommendations, and help identify patterns across your long-term data. New health features, including blood pressure signals and nighttime breathing insights, expand Oura's focus beyond basic fitness tracking.
The trade-offs: While it now supports live activity tracking through the app and can work with compatible heart rate monitors, the Ring 5 isn't the best choice for athletes who need live workout stats or a built-in GPS. If you already own a Ring 4, I'd probably wait another generation, considering that most software additions are coming to older hardware anyway. Finally, you'll need an Oura membership ($6 per month or $70 annually) to unlock most of its insights. (Without it, you can only view your Readiness, Activity, and Sleep Scores.)
Is There a Class-Action Lawsuit Against Oura?
Last August, San Francisco’s Clarkson Law Firm filed a class-action lawsuit alleging that Oura rings cannot measure one’s sleep stages and rely on the company’s AI models to do the guesswork. The complaint argues that sleep is “defined by brain electrical activity, eye movements, muscle tone, and other signals measured through electrodes placed on the scalp, leads on the eyes, and sensors on the chin. [Oura] doesn’t measure any of these parameters.”
In an email statement to WIRED responding to the lawsuit, an Oura spokesperson wrote, “Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature.”
According to Oura, its sleep-staging algorithm is informed by research based on more than 1,200 nights of collected data. “We published a peer-reviewed paper that describes how the sleep-staging algorithm was developed and how it uses the signals collected by the ring,” wrote the spokesperson. “Multiple third-party, independent studies support our claims of accuracy, and we have transparently reported on the mechanisms and measures that inform Oura’s sleep staging.”
As of November 2, the court has yet to rule on Oura’s response to the complaint. I’ll continue to monitor the lawsuit and report back on any significant developments. For now, though, nothing has surfaced that changes my judgment of Oura as my top pick.
TL;DR: Though still subscription-based, the Oura Ring 5 is the best sleep tracker, one of the best fitness trackers, and the best smart ring for most folks. Read my full review.

Best Subscription-Free Smart Ring
I'm currently testing the RingConn Gen 3, but the Gen 2 Air remains one of our budget picks thanks to its affordable price and subscription-free model.
Why WIRED recommends: The RingConn Gen 2 Air is slimmer, lighter, and much more comfortable than previous models. It tracks your steps, calories burned, heart rate, blood oxygen, and sleep. It's also compatible with colored ring protectors to swap out with your outfits if you're someone who likes to color-coordinate.
RingConn added an AI assistant to the app that generates a plan for you, adjusting your targets weekly based on your activity and feedback. This feature is fine. It also consistently overestimated reviewer Simon Hill's sleep and underestimated his steps and activity compared to the Oura and Apple Watch.

Best for Samsung Users
The Samsung Galaxy Ring works seamlessly with the Galaxy Watch8 series and Galaxy Watch Ultra, extending each device's battery life by trading tasks and keeping tabs on your activity while the other is charging.
Why WIRED recommends: Former WIRED editor Adrienne So found this ring's accuracy similar to the Apple Watch Ultra. It accurately auto-detected workouts—even pool workouts—and the heart rate tracking is also reliable. Its cycle-tracking feature, powered by the fertility-tracking app Natural Cycles, uses skin-temperature sensing to track when your period will come—and it works.
It comes in an attractive, clear charging case with an LED that shows you how much battery life you have left.
The trade-offs: While you can use the Galaxy Ring with most Android phones, it costs about as much as the Oura Ring 5 upfront and doesn’t require a subscription. The most useful features, like your daily Energy Score and wellness tips (what the company calls Booster Cards), also rely on Galaxy AI, which means you'll only be able to see them if you are using the ring with an Android phone and the Samsung Health app. Lastly, Adrienne found the Galaxy Ring to be a bit too generous with its sleep tracking, which makes sense since it lacks a gyroscope.

More Smart Rings We’ve Tested
Over the years, the WIRED Reviews team has tested several other entrants in this category. Here are some more smart rings to consider.
Oura Ring 4 for $349: While the Ring 5 is the smallest smart ring on the market, the Ring 4 is still slimmer and lighter than its predecessor. There's also a ceramic version. Reviewer Simon Hill had issues with dwindling battery life and some scuffing with his silver Ring 4, but he hasn't encountered those issues with the ceramic version.
Leep Ring for $199: A British smart ring that's affordable and subscription-free, and offers simplified stats on your activity, sleep, and stress. Unfortunately, sleep is woefully inaccurate and tends to report that I’ve been asleep for my entire time in bed, even if I was watching TV or reading. One night, it suggested I slept 8 hours and 43 minutes (Oura said 6 hours and 52 minutes). The app could also use some polish. For example, it doesn’t take into account that it’s only a couple of hours into the day before telling me my movement for today is “Bad.” I also lost data on the first night it ran out of battery, and there was no warning notification to tell me to recharge. A fully charged ring is meant to last up to eight days, but I’ve been getting closer to five. —Simon Hill
RingConn Gen 2 for $299: Despite being $100 more than the Gen 2 Air, this is still a relatively affordable, subscription-free smart ring. The main differences here are that the Gen 2 offers sleep apnea monitoring and it's a titanium build; the Gen 2 Air is made of stainless steel.
Avoid These Smart Rings
Amazfit Helio Ring: Amazfit is a purveyor of affordable fitness trackers like the Active 2, so I expected its smart ring to be competitive, but the Helio falls short in several areas. I like the textured bronze finish, but it is the only color you get. Sizes are limited to 8, 10, or 12 for now (sizes 7 to 13 are coming). Also, the Helio was often inaccurate, with heart rate measurements wildly out of step with other wearable tech. It lacks automatic workout tracking, battery life averaged three days for me, and it frequently disconnected from the busy and confusing Zepp app. There's no monthly subscription fee, but there is Aura AI ($70/year) for sleep insights and content or Fitness ($30/year), which includes an AI coach. They are expensive and confusing. (Why have two separate subscriptions?) The Helio works much better in conjunction with a smartwatch (I tried it with the Amazfit Cheetah Pro), as it can merge the data, but as a stand-alone device, it is impossible to recommend. —Adrienne So
Movano Evie Ring: When the subscription-free Movano Evie Ring first came out, it was touted as the fitness tracker for women’s health. However, its menstrual health features are pretty underbaked compared to those offered by its competitors. Now that the Oura and the Galaxy Ring can track cycles accurately, this ring's time may have passed. It's also currently sold out.
FAQs
How Do I Choose the Right Smart Ring Size?
Some smart rings come in standard sizes, but there is variation, and half sizes are rare, so it's worth taking some time to ensure you get the best possible fit. Most manufacturers will send you a free sizing kit, enabling you to wear a dummy ring for at least 24 hours. Your smart ring should be snug to enable the sensors to measure accurately, but you don't want it so tight that it restricts blood flow. Bear in mind that your fingers swell and shrink throughout the day.
Note: You may have to buy the ring directly from the manufacturer to get the sizing kit for free.
Which Finger Should I Wear My Smart Ring On?
You can wear your smart ring on any finger, but most manufacturers recommend wearing these gadgets on your index finger for the best accuracy, though the middle or ring finger can also work. These three fingers all have large blood vessels for more accurate pulse monitoring. What’s really important is that the ring fits tightly and securely around the base of your chosen finger, so if you have a big knuckle and a narrower finger base (more common with the middle or ring finger), this can be tricky. I recommend wearing it on the index finger of your less dominant hand, because I found wearing it on my right index finger, as a right-handed person, led to more damage on the ring and scrapes.
How Do I Care for My Smart Ring?
Regular cleaning can help maintain accurate tracking and prevent skin irritation. Use mild soap and water to remove buildup and oils. Wipe the inner sensors with a soft cloth. Always dry the ring and your finger completely after handwashing.
Most smart rings are built to handle everyday wear, but if you want to avoid damage, it's best to remove them when working with tools, lifting heavy weights, or playing contact sports. I'd also remove mine during chores like washing dishes or cooking, especially when abrasive products are involved.
How Often Do I Need to Charge My Smart Ring?
Most models need to be charged every five to eight days. I tested the smart rings above with all the functionalities turned on, so my battery life estimates are typically lower than the manufacturer's claims.
Smart rings come with a charging cable (and sometimes a charging case), but you will generally have to provide your own wall adapter. From dead, they take anywhere from an hour and a half to three hours to fully charge, but you should avoid letting the battery run down completely, or you run the risk of losing health data. Oura recommends charging your ring in short bursts and during moments of low activity, such as cooking or showering. The company also suggests charging your smart ring to at least 30 percent before bed to ensure uninterrupted sleep monitoring.
What Smart Ring Features Should I Look For?
Choosing the best smart ring for you comes down to a few key considerations:
- Biometric tracking: At a minimum, it's worth looking for essentials like continuous heart rate monitoring, sleep tracking accuracy, and daily activity tracking, all of which are pretty common across most modern models. For users who want deeper wellness insights, some devices offer more advanced features. These can include readiness or recovery scores that help you decide when to rest or push harder, body temperature sensing that can detect changes linked to stress or illness, and blood oxygen (SpO2) monitoring that may help flag potential breathing disturbances during sleep. Some smart rings also offer cycle tracking, which can help women monitor menstrual cycles, predict fertility windows, and better understand patterns related to hormonal changes.
- Materials and build: Materials like titanium and ceramic are popular choices because they're durable, lightweight, and often better suited for sensitive skin, thanks to their hypoallergenic properties.
- Water resistance: A rating of at least 5 ATM (or 5 atmospheres) is ideal, as it offers protection for swimming and showering.
- Companion app: Since smart rings don't have screens, the companion app becomes the only way you view and interact with your health data. A well-designed app makes all the difference, so make sure to choose one that feels intuitive, easy to navigate, and engaging to use daily. Compatibility matters too. Depending on your device ecosystem, you may want a ring that syncs with platforms like Apple Health, Google Health Connect, or Samsung Health.
- Battery life: Most smart rings last around five to eight days on a single charge, depending on usage and the specific model. Choose one that fits your lifestyle, especially if you plan to wear it overnight for sleep tracking. Some newer models also include a portable charging case, which can be useful if you travel often or tend to forget to charge your devices.
- Price and subscription costs: The upfront cost of a smart ring is important, but some brands also lock advanced insights behind a monthly membership. Before buying, consider whether the total long-term cost fits your budget. Otherwise, you may end up paying for a device without access to the features that make it most useful.
Are Smart Rings Better Than Smartwatches?
Neither is better per se. Smartwatches are designed to do more than just track health data, offering broader functionality and interactive features that allow users to check notifications, reply to messages, and even make calls right from their wrist. They're built to combine fitness tracking with everyday convenience, making them a versatile option for people who want multiple functions in one device. Smart rings take a more understated approach. Designed to be low-maintenance and discreet, they specialize in tracking health and wellness metrics in the background without the need for a display screen or interaction.
That said, here are a few reasons why you might consider a smart ring over a traditional fitness tracker or smartwatch:
- Better battery life. Smart rings are smaller and less power-hungry, which often translates to longer battery life. Most current models can run for about five to eight days on a single charge, though this varies depending on usage and brand. Smartwatches tend to require more frequent charging. Battery life varies widely, but many last around one to three days before needing a recharge. Some fitness-focused trackers—like Whoop and Fitbit—tend to last longer, offering battery life of up to two weeks.
- Reliable sleep tracking. When it comes to tracking sleep and resting heart rate, smart rings often have the edge. Because they fit securely on the finger, they maintain skin contact throughout the night, which ensures more consistent readings. Because of their longer battery life, you're more likely to keep a ring on overnight without needing to recharge it, whereas many smartwatches require overnight charging. Plus, smart rings are generally more comfortable to wear to bed than bulkier wrist-based devices.
- Looks like jewelry. Smart rings are compact and often available in a range of finishes that give them the look of everyday jewelry. Their discreet design makes them suitable to wear in almost any setting, including formal occasions where a smartwatch might look out of place. For users who prefer something low-profile, smart rings offer a more discreet option for health and fitness tracking.

Bose recalls S1 Pro battery packs due to fire and overheating risks
Over 670,000 units are being recalled in the US and Canada.
If you own a Bose S1 Pro or S1 Pro+, we have some good news and some bad news. The good news: the speaker itself is fine. The bad news: the battery pack inside may be less than fine. Bose and the US Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced a recall on Thursday, covering nearly 635,000 lithium-ion battery packs in the US, as well as about 35,400 in Canada.
The affected packs can overheat and ignite, risking fire and burn injuries, so stop using yours right away if it's affected. Bose has received seven reports of batteries melting, smoking or catching fire. Among those were six cases of property damage. Fortunately, no injuries have been reported.
The S1 Pro and S1 Pro+ are Bose's portable PA speakers, designed for parties, gigs and the like. The speakers have a built-in mixer, support Bluetooth streaming and can go mobile using the removable battery pack. The S1 Pro+ supports a wireless mic and instrument transmitter, a separate $159 purchase.
The affected packs were sold from December 2017 to July 2026 at Bose, Best Buy, Amazon, Walmart and other retailers. The battery packs came in the box with many of the speaker units, which cost about $700, and were available separately for between $100 and $160.
Not every battery pack is being recalled. To find out if yours is, you'll need to remove the battery, find its 17-digit serial number, and check it against the recalled batches. If the battery's serial starts with 083723, 078352, 084105, 078591, 078592, 084106 or 086409, you'll want to sign up to get a free replacement on Bose's recall page. The company also provides more detailed instructions. While you wait for the replacement, you can still use the speaker on AC power.
You don't want to just toss the recalled lithium-ion batteries in the trash. Check with your local household hazardous waste center to find out how to dispose of them safely.

- Wanted Posters are located in and around major POIs on the current Fortnite mini-season map; there are 126 in total.

Sticking to the theme of “Treasure Hunters,” Wanted Posters have replaced Cheat Codes in the Fortnite Mini Season. Instead of entering complex codes to get a Sprite, you can now find a Wanted Poster, track down the location of a Sprite Chest, and claim it for yourself. If you’re interested in knowing more, here’s where to find Wanted Posters in Treasure Hunters and how they work.
Where to Find Wanted Posters in Fortnite Treasure Hunters Mini Season
You can find Wanted Posters placed all over the new Crossbones Isle map in Fortnite Treasure Hunters mini-season. There are 126 Wanted Posters in total as of Fortnite update 43.00, with the majority of them located in and around major POIs. Wanted Posters grant you a Sprite Treasure Map that you can use in a Fortnite match to find a buried Sprite Chest and open it to claim a Sprite or a Pirate Shop Token.
Essentially, wherever there’s a place to hang a Wanted Poster, expect to see one. Here are all the locations you can find Wanted Posters in Fortnite Treasure Hunters:
- Rubber Resort: 8 Wanted Posters
- Southwest of The Chest: 1 Wanted Poster

- Giant’s Battlefield Landmark: 3 Wanted Posters
- East of Lantern Landing, along the road: 3 Wanted Posters
- Cursed Cavern: 13 Wanted Posters
- Between Cursed Cavern and Boogie Boat landmark: 2 Wanted Posters

- Busy Bay: 9 Wanted Posters
- Plunder Town: 7 Wanted Posters

To help you find them easily, we’ve marked their locations on the Fortnite Treasure Hunters mini-season map:
If you want to collect some of the rarest Sprites in Fortnite Treasure Hunters, we recommend going to Arlong Park, Cursed Cavern, Loguetown, or The $.$. Rocky. They have the highest concentration of Wanted Posters in Fortnite, which makes it easier to come across them often.
How to Use Wanted Posters in Fortnite Treasure Hunters
Similar to Cheat Codes in Fortnite, you need to interact with Wanted Posters to use them. They function as Treasure Maps that point the way to Buried Sprite Chests. Once you reach the designated location, you need to use your Pickaxe to dig up the chest and claim your reward. Here’s a step-by-step guide on how to do it:
- Find Wanted Posters using the map.
- Interact with it to get a Sprite Treasure Map and add it to your inventory.
- Equip it to see a red dotted line that shows you the direction in which you need to go.
- Follow the red dotted line till you reach an “X Marks the Spot”.
- Use your Pickaxe to dig up the buried chest.
- Interact with the chest to get a Sprite or a free Treasure Hunt Chest reward.
Keep in mind that there’s no limit to how many Wanted Posters you can interact with in a Battle Royale or Zero Build match, but you can only carry one at a time. However, don’t focus solely on collecting Sprites, as there are Fortnite Treasure Hunters Quests to complete as well for rewards.
Important Note: If your teammate or an opponent nearby uses a Lucky Locator to locate a buried Sprite Chest and opens it, the Sprite Treasure Map in your inventory will disappear, and you won’t be able to use it again.
Can You Get a Pirate Shop Token by Searching Wanted Posters in Fortnite?
Yes, you can get a Pirate Shop Access Token by searching (interacting) and completing Wanted Posters in the Fortnite mini-season. In fact, aside from containers such as Ammo Boxes, Barrels, and Produce Boxes, opening any Treasure Hunt Chests can reward you with the Pirate Shop Token.
Be sure to attend Treasure Hours in Fortnite, as you could stand a better chance of finding the Pirate Shop Access Token during this in-game event. If nothing else, XP boosts are going to activate, allowing you to level up and complete your Fortnite Treasure Hunters Battle Pass quicker.

'I don't fear for my safety from online abuse - because we're so used to it'
- Published
After struggling with her blood pressure as she lost her first WTA Tour singles match for 16 months, Jodie Burrage checked in with three things: a doctor, a physiotherapist, and her phone.
On her social media feed there were already messages promising punishment - and others making threats on her life - for losing 3-6 6-3 7-5 to Indian wildcard Vaishnavi Adkar.
"I try not to actually read what they say," Burrage told BBC Sport from Chennai, where she is still competing in the doubles.
"Because we are so used to it - which is really quite sad - I don't fear for my safety.
"You've got to have thick skin. There was some brutal stuff that was said, but I don't take it to heart.
"Sometimes it hurts more than others. If you've already got other stuff going on, or you're not in a great place, and that is put on top of everything else - this tour is tricky enough as it is."
Burrage, who says her blood pressure "tanked" towards the end of the match, decided to share screenshots of the abuse on Instagram to raise awareness of an everyday problem for professional players.
"It happens every match - whether it's win or lose," the 27-year-old Briton said.
"Playing in Wrexham [on the World Tennis Tour last month], I won three matches [and] lost one. But after every single match there was some sort of abuse.
"I think that's where tennis players get it pretty hard - because in tennis you can bet on so many things."
Abuse of players, particularly by angry gamblers, is not a new problem.
Burrage's compatriot Katie Boulter shared with the BBC last year the abuse and death threats she received on a near-daily basis.
This year's WTA and World Tennis report into online abuse, which was based on data from the Signify Group's Threat Matrix service, said "angry gamblers" were responsible for 42% of all verified abuse detected during the 2025 season.
It is why there is so much disquiet about the sponsorship deals some tournaments have struck with gambling firms.
The Davis Cup, for example, has an official sports betting partner, while in August self-described "prediction-market platform" Kalshi signed a multi-year deal with the US Open.
Burrage believes social media platforms "should do more to help".
"I think an ID should be put on every Instagram account, and then that way it makes more people more accountable for their actions on that platform," she said.
"I think it would limit what people would say. People should be accountable for what they say and that's where I think there could be more of a push to change.
"It's only getting worse."
All WTA and World Tennis players have access to Threat Matrix's services, which monitor all social media posts directed at players.
The first aim is to provide a rapid assessment of whether an individual's safety is under threat. They can then alert the platforms, and potentially law enforcement agencies, to the offending content.
Names can also be shared with gaming companies, so they have the option of banning offenders from their platforms.
The service can extend to direct messages and even the moderation of accounts, so players never see the message in the first place. But this is not foolproof - and players may feel they would rather know about any threats made against them.
Burrage has recently been able to improve her singles ranking to 474, from a low of 888 in July. Injury prevented her playing singles for nine months and when she returned for the grass court season, sickness held her back.
But she will not allow the abuse to throw her off course.
"I'm at a place where it's all bigger picture for me and everything I'm doing now is to have a good season in 2027," she added.
"I'm building a team that is really good around me. They know where I've been, what I've gone through.
"It's not what you want, but if I have to go through it, then I will."

A child may wake up after a full night’s sleep and still have dark circles under the eyes. For some children, this may simply be a family trait. While parents may immediately associate dark circles with inadequate sleep or nutritional deficiencies, their causes can be more varied.

Update | November 5, 19:43 After the story was published, RapidClaims founder and CEO Dushyant Mishra said the startup is not in talks with WestBridge Capital to raise any funding round. He also said that the $200 Mn valuation figure is “incorrect”. Original | October 5, 18:22 AI-powered SaaS startup RapidClaims is in talks to raise around $30 Mn in a funding round led by WestBridge Capital at a valuation of about $200 Mn, sources told Inc42. The round is expected to be its Series B, with existing investors Accel and Together Fund likely to participate, the sources added. RapidClaims did not respond to questions sent by Inc42, while WestBridge Capital declined to comment. Founded in 2023 by Dushyant Mishra, Abhinay Vyas, and Jot Sarup Singh, RapidClaims builds AI-powered revenue cycle management (RCM) software that helps healthcare providers automate medical coding, improve clinical documentation, prevent insurance claim denials, and recover outstanding payments. The startup primarily caters to healthcare providers in the US, helping them address billing errors, rejected claims, and delays in reimbursements. Automating Healthcare Revenue Workflows RapidClaims’ products include RapidCode for medical coding, RapidVBC for clinical documentation and risk adjustment, and RapidRecovery for managing denied claims, automating appeals, and detecting underpayments. The platform integrates with healthcare providers’ existing electronic health record systems. It serves physician groups, hospitals, health systems, federally qualified health centres (FQHCs), and ambulatory surgery centres, among other healthcare organisations. The startup is also developing inpatient coding capabilities with design partners, extending its automation tools to coding for hospital admissions. In April 2025, RapidClaims raised $8 Mn in a Series A round led by Accel, with participation from Together Fund. It also disclosed that it had previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding. RapidClaims had earmarked the Series A proceeds for expanding its go-to-market efforts, strengthening its technology and product capabilities, and growing its sales and marketing teams. At the time, the startup said it had grown sixfold over the preceding four months and served a double-digit client base. It was also looking to expand its presence among FQHCs, physician groups, outpatient facilities, and ambulatory surgery centres. Investors Bet On Automation The proposed fundraise comes amid increasing investor interest in startups looking to automate healthcare administration and insurance workflows. In October, Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in a Series A extension led by Z47, taking its total Series A funding to $22.5 Mn. The startup develops AI agents for tasks including appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills, and payment collection. Meanwhile, Consint.AI raised ₹22 Cr to expand internationally and develop its AI capabilities for fraud detection and claims processing. Its products automate claims processing, digitise documents, and standardise healthcare records.

The slew of new images was released by the developer on November 5, 2026, as part of its new “The Launch Gallery,” and you can check all 39 of them here:
All New Jason & Lucia Screenshots
The first slate of Rockstar’s new screenshots we see is GTA 6’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, together doing multiple criminal activities and spending quality time together, whether it’s robbing banks, dancing at the nightclub, chilling under Vice City’s sunset, or enjoying each other’s company. Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.
At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.
Last Monday, the central bank ordered Ueno into resolution over insolvency, freezing the deposits of 3 million customers, leaving hundreds of thousands of families without access to money for food and basic daily expenses. Bank executives were arrested, and people took to the streets in massive protests.
In power since August 2023 and with a term running until 2028, the 47-year-old economist was already facing impeachment proceedings that had broad support.
“Dear compatriots, today I address you at one of the most difficult moments of my life. With my heart set on Paraguay and with the conviction that our republic must always come before any person or circumstance, I have decided to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” said Peña in a video.
Ueno Bank began as a finance company in the 1970s and, in 2021, was bought by Grupo Vázquez, one of Paraguay’s largest business and industrial conglomerates. At the end of 2023, it received authorisation from the central bank, already under Peña’s administration, to operate as a digital bank.
The bank rapidly expanded its operations, attracting customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries and sponsoring Paraguay’s national football team. On Wednesday, the players released a letter “demanding” a “forceful response” from the government and the justice system.
The bank came to manage between $800m and $850m in deposits from state and pension entities, including retirement funds, prompting criticism over conflicts of interest because of Peña’s previous shareholding ties to Ueno Holding.
Peña said that, as an economist, he had merely made an “investment”, but that he had already disposed of all his shares. When the local press pointed to possible improper favouritism in directing state and pension funds to the bank, he called it a “false media campaign” aimed at weakening his government.
On Wednesday, opposition lawmakers and even members of Peña’s Colorado party filed an impeachment motion holding the president responsible for the collapse. He had been a shareholder in the group that ran the bank until early last year and, in recent months, had reportedly been ignoring warnings from the central bank and the media about its operations.
Political pressure intensified on Thursday morning when the ex-president Horacio Cartes, his former ally, posted a message endorsing the impeachment.
“We will not stand on the side of the theft of public, private and pensioners’ funds. We must think of the people and of the values we uphold in the Colorado party. We support the impeachment of the president of the republic, Santiago Peña, in order to restore the institutional order of the republic,” he wrote.
Other lawmakers followed suit and began debating impeachment when Peña released a video announcing his resignation.
“I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions,” said the now former president.
“I also want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed them … But today my priority is only one thing: the peace of mind of Paraguayans who trusted their savings to our financial system … My greatest wish is that the return of those funds is guaranteed,” he added.
Opposition senator Rafael Filizzola called the case “the biggest fraud carried out from political power in the democratic era … This is a bank created from political power, to use public money for private businesses linked to political power, with the president of the republic at the head of it,” he told 1020 AM radio.
Peña, a former finance minister who promised to rebuild a “great Paraguay”, was a key ally of the US president, Donald Trump, in the region – one of the few Latin American presidents to attend Trump’s second inauguration. US officials, including the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, repeatedly praised him as a “strategic partner”, and Peña recently flew to Washington to discuss critical minerals and economic cooperation. Neither Rubio nor Trump has yet commented on Peña’s resignation.
Vice-President Pedro Alliana automatically assumes the presidency to complete the constitutional term until August 2028.
About an hour after Peña’s announcement, the lower house unanimously approved the impeachment motion, which now goes to the senate. If approved, even after his resignation, he would lose his senate seat and, with it, parliamentary immunity, leaving him to face any criminal proceedings in the ordinary courts.

From groceries to tax credits, how much is in the federal budget for your wallet?
Push to spur investment overshadows affordability moves: economist
From a grocery benefit expansion to rental assistance and payments for more low-wage workers, Thursday's federal budget includes a number of measures aimed at making life more affordable.
But they were still eclipsed by a focus on investment.
One of the main direct pocketbook measures is a top-up to the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit — a pre-existing program that gives quarterly payments to Canadians with low and modest incomes.
The top-up will increase those payments by 50 per cent for the 2026-27 program year. Combined with previous increases, a single person could get up to $1,290. A couple with two children could get up to $2,570.
- Carney's 2nd budget earmarks billions for affordability and Canadian sovereignty
- live updates Budget 2026: Opposition leaders express disappointment in Liberal government's plan for Canada's economy
The government says the program will give Canadians collectively $4.1 billion more in support to help pay for essentials.
The plan also expands the Canada caregiver credit. Budget 2026 makes the tax credit refundable, helping caregivers who have incomes so low that they don't pay tax. The move would help extend the credit — which could give caregivers up to $1,260 back annually — to about 180,000 people who don't currently get it.
For those saving for retirement, the government also plans to merge Registered Retirement Savings Plans (RRSPs) and Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs). Right now, when Canadians turn 71 and can no longer contribute to their RRSPs, they have to convert that account into an RRIF and begin withdrawing from it.
The "RRSP-for-life" plan would eliminate the need to switch — and would also allow a surviving partner of the RRSP holder to transfer those savings tax free.
Other measures aimed at bringing down costs were already announced. The government suspended the excise tax on fuel — which saves Canadians about 10 cents a litre on the cost of gasoline — in April, and later extended that to the end of January 2027. The tax will come back at a 50 per cent rate until the end of March 2027 and then return to its regular level.
In all, the budget shows the government spending $5.3 billion on that relief at the pumps.
Overall, the federal government's fiscal plan pledges $22 billion for new spending on affordability measures.
But aside from that direct spending on things like groceries and gas — measures that will support Canadians in the short term — economist Armine Yalnizyan says there's little in the budget for everyday people.
"It's not like they're doing nothing," Yalnizyan said. "But the short answer is Canadians are going to need a lot of patience because this budget is not there to support them."
The biggest-ticket spending on affordability is related to housing, with $11.2 billion dedicated to ending homelessness within 10 years. That money would help build supportive and transitional housing and provide support to facilities that care for people in a mental health or substance abuse crisis.
